(Though Jesus himself baptized not, but his disciples,)
He left Judaea, and departed again into Galilee.
And he must needs go through Samaria.
Then cometh he to a city of Samaria, which is called Sychar, near to the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph.
Now Jacob’s well was there. Jesus therefore, being wearied with
his journey, sat thus on the well:
and it was about the sixth hour.
There cometh a woman of Samaria to draw water: Jesus saith unto her,
Give me to drink.
(For his disciples were gone away unto the city to buy meat.)
Then saith the woman of Samaria unto him, How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans.
Jesus answered and said unto her,
If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water.
The woman saith unto him, Sir, thou hast nothing to draw with, and the well is deep: from whence then hast thou that living water?
Art thou greater than our father Jacob, which gave us the well, and drank thereof himself, and his children, and his cattle?
Jesus answered and said unto her,
Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again:
But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.
The woman saith unto him, Sir, give me this water, that I thirst not, neither come hither to draw.
Jesus saith unto her,
Go, call thy husband, and come hither.
The woman answered and said, I have no husband. Jesus said unto her,
Thou hast well said, I have no husband:
For thou hast had five husbands; and he whom thou now hast is not thy husband: in that saidst thou truly.
The woman saith unto him, Sir, I perceive that thou art a prophet.
Our fathers worshipped in this mountain; and ye say, that in Jerusalem is the place where men ought to worship.
Jesus saith unto her,
Woman, believe me, the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father.
Ye worship ye know not what: we know what we worship: for salvation is of the Jews.
But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him.
God
is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship
him in spirit and in truth.
The woman saith unto him, I know that Messias cometh, which is called Christ: when he is come, he will tell us all things.
Jesus saith unto her,
I that speak unto thee am
he.And upon this came his disciples, and marvelled that he talked with the woman: yet no man said, What seekest thou? or, Why talkest thou with her?
The woman then left her waterpot, and went her way into the city, and saith to the men,
Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?
Then they went out of the city, and came unto him.
In the mean while his disciples prayed him, saying, Master, eat.
But he said unto them,
I have meat to eat that ye know not of.
Therefore said the disciples one to another, Hath any man brought him
ought to eat?
Jesus saith unto them,
My meat is to do the will of him that sent me, and to finish his work.
Say not ye, There are yet four months, and
then cometh harvest? behold, I say unto you, Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest.
And he that reapeth receiveth wages, and gathereth fruit unto life eternal: that both he that soweth and he that reapeth may rejoice together.
And herein is that saying true, One soweth, and another reapeth.
I sent you to reap that whereon ye bestowed no labour: other men laboured, and ye are entered into their labours.And many of the Samaritans of that city believed on him for the saying of the woman, which testified, He told me all that ever I did.
So when the Samaritans were come unto him, they besought him that he would tarry with them: and he abode there two days.
And many more believed because of his own word;
And said unto the woman, Now we believe, not because of thy saying: for we have heard
him ourselves, and know that this is indeed the Christ, the Saviour of the world.
stories.retelling:
The midday sun hung high over the dusty roads of Samaria. Jesus, weary from his travels, approached the ancient well of Jacob. The air shimmered with heat as he settled himself beside the stone rim, his eyes scanning the horizon. There, a solitary figure approached, a woman with a water jar balanced on her hip, her steps measured as she neared the well.

As she arrived, Jesus, with a gentle but firm voice, broke the silence. **“Give me to drink,”** he said, his words surprising the woman. She paused, her brow furrowed in disbelief. “How is it that you, a Jew, ask me, a Samaritan woman, for a drink?” she retorted, her voice carrying a mix of curiosity and caution. The animosity between Jews and Samaritans was well-known, after all.

Jesus leaned forward, his gaze steady and knowing. **“If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water,”** he replied, his words enigmatic and full of promise. The woman, taken aback, looked at the well and then back at him. “Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep,” she pointed out skeptically. “Are you greater than our ancestor Jacob, who gave us this well?”

With calm assurance, Jesus explained, **“Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again: But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst.”** The notion of a thirst that could be quenched forever intrigued her. “Sir, give me this water,” she said, longing evident in her voice, “that I thirst not, neither come hither to draw.”

Jesus shifted the conversation, asking her to call her husband. The woman hesitated, her voice dropping as she confessed, “I have no husband.” He nodded knowingly, revealing her truth, **“Thou hast well said, I have no husband: For thou hast had five husbands; and he whom thou now hast is not thy husband.”** This revelation left her speechless, a mix of awe and vulnerability in her eyes.

Realizing she was in the presence of someone extraordinary, she spoke of the Messiah who was to come. Jesus responded with profound clarity, **“I that speak unto thee am he.”** At that moment, his disciples returned, their expressions puzzled at the sight of him speaking with a Samaritan woman, yet they held their tongues.

The woman, now filled with a new purpose, abandoned her water jar and hurried back to the city. Her voice rang out to the people, urging them, “Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did. Could this be the Christ?” Her words stirred curiosity and hope, drawing many to the well.

Meanwhile, Jesus spoke to his disciples about a different kind of nourishment—the fulfillment found in doing the will of God. As the people from the city arrived, many believed because of the woman’s testimony and even more from hearing Jesus himself. They recognized him as the Savior, their hearts filled with newfound faith.

stories.title: Jesus Begins His Ministry in Galilee
stories.keyVerse: "And he saith unto them, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men."
stories.text:
Now when Jesus had heard that John was cast into prison, he departed into Galilee;
And leaving Nazareth, he came and dwelt in Capernaum, which is upon the sea coast, in the borders of Zabulon and Nephthalim:
That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying,
The land of Zabulon, and the land of Nephthalim,
by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles;
The people which sat in darkness saw great light; and to them which sat in the region and shadow of death light is sprung up.
From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say,
Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.And Jesus, walking by the sea of Galilee, saw two brethren, Simon called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea: for they were fishers.
And he saith unto them,
Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.
And they straightway left
their nets, and followed him.
And going on from thence, he saw other two brethren, James
the son
of Zebedee, and John his brother, in a ship with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he called them.
And they immediately left the ship and their father, and followed him.
And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing all manner of sickness and all manner of disease among the people.
And his fame went throughout all Syria: and they brought unto him all sick people that were taken with divers diseases and torments, and those which were possessed with devils, and those which were lunatick, and those that had the palsy; and he healed them.
And there followed him great multitudes of people from Galilee, and
from Decapolis, and
from Jerusalem, and
from
Judaea, and
from beyond Jordan.
stories.retelling:
The news of John the Baptist's imprisonment reached Jesus as he traveled through the dusty roads of Nazareth. Without hesitation, he turned his steps toward Galilee. The sun was setting as he entered Capernaum, a seaside town that would become his new home, nestled in the lands of Zebulun and Naphtali. The air there was different, infused with the scent of the sea and the chatter of fishermen preparing for the night’s work. This place, once shrouded in darkness, was about to witness the rise of a great light.

As dawn broke over the Sea of Galilee, Jesus walked along its shores, the waves lapping gently at the sand. He saw Simon, known as Peter, and his brother Andrew, their hands skillfully casting nets into the water. The brothers worked with a practiced rhythm, their focus on the sea's bounty. Jesus approached them, and with a voice that carried both promise and command, he spoke, **“Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.”**

The words hung in the air, an invitation to a different kind of catch, a life of purpose beyond the familiar waves. Without a moment's hesitation, Simon and Andrew dropped their nets, the ropes slipping through their fingers to lie abandoned on the sand. They turned and followed him, leaving behind the life they knew.

Walking further along the shore, Jesus came upon another pair of brothers, James and John, sons of Zebedee. They were in their boat, mending nets with their father, their hands busy with the day’s wear and tear. Jesus called out to them, a simple beckoning that stirred something deep within. The brothers exchanged a glance of understanding, and with quiet determination, they stepped out of the boat, leaving their father and their old lives behind to follow the man from Nazareth.

The days that followed were filled with movement and purpose. Jesus traveled through all of Galilee, entering synagogues with a message of hope and transformation. His teachings about the Kingdom of Heaven resonated with the crowds, speaking to their deepest longings. Everywhere he went, he healed the sick, the afflicted, and those tormented by unseen forces. His touch brought relief, his words offered solace.

As his fame spread like wildfire across Syria, people came from far and wide—Galilee, Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan—bringing their sick and suffering to him. The air was thick with anticipation, and the crowds grew larger with each passing day. Jesus’ presence was a beacon, a tangible sign of change and promise.

In this land that had once sat in shadow, light had truly sprung up, and it was just the beginning. The journey he had embarked upon with his new followers was destined to change not only them but the world around them.

stories.title: Rejected at Nazareth
stories.keyVerse: "And he began to say unto them, This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears."
stories.text:
And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up: and, as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read.
And there was delivered unto him the book of the prophet Esaias. And when he had opened the book, he found the place where it was written,
The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised,
To preach the acceptable year of the Lord.
And he closed the book, and he gave
it again to the minister, and sat down. And the eyes of all them that were in the synagogue were fastened on him.
And he began to say unto them,
This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.
And all bare him witness, and wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth. And they said, Is not this Joseph’s son?
And he said unto them,
Ye will surely say unto me this proverb, Physician, heal thyself: whatsoever we have heard done in Capernaum, do also here in thy country.
And he said,
Verily I say unto you, No prophet is accepted in his own country.
But I tell you of a truth, many widows were in Israel in the days of Elias, when the heaven was shut up three years and six months, when great famine was throughout all the land;
But unto none of them was Elias sent, save unto Sarepta,
a city of Sidon, unto a woman
that was a widow.
And many lepers were in Israel in the time of Eliseus the prophet; and none of them was cleansed, saving Naaman the Syrian.
And all they in the synagogue, when they heard these things, were filled with wrath,
And rose up, and thrust him out of the city, and led him unto the brow of the hill whereon their city was built, that they might cast him down headlong.
But he passing through the midst of them went his way,
stories.retelling:
In the dusty, sunlit village of Nazareth, where the air carried the scent of olive groves and the chatter of children playing in the streets, Jesus returned to his hometown. It was a place familiar to him, a place where every face bore the memory of his childhood. On the Sabbath, the synagogue hummed with anticipation as the townspeople gathered, filling the room with a quiet reverence. Jesus, as was his custom, walked into the synagogue and stood up to read, his presence commanding and calm.

The attendant handed him the scroll of the prophet Isaiah. Unrolling the parchment, Jesus found the passage he sought. The room fell silent, the only sound the soft rustle of the scroll as he read aloud. **“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,”** his voice echoed, **“because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised.”**

As he finished, he rolled up the scroll and handed it back, then sat down, a quiet confidence settling over him. The synagogue was still; every eye was on him, waiting, expectant. Then, he spoke, his words charged with a quiet power. **“This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.”**

At first, the crowd murmured with wonder, an undercurrent of disbelief and curiosity rippling through them. They whispered among themselves, questioning, **“Is not this Joseph’s son?”** Skepticism mingled with awe as they grappled with the implications of his words.

Sensing their doubt, Jesus addressed them, his voice steady. **“Ye will surely say unto me this proverb, ‘Physician, heal thyself: whatsoever we have heard done in Capernaum, do also here in thy country.’”** He paused, the weight of his message sinking in. **“Verily I say unto you, No prophet is accepted in his own country.”**

The tension in the room thickened as he reminded them of the prophets of old, of Elijah and Elisha, of miracles performed for outsiders, not for those within Israel. His words were a mirror, reflecting their disbelief and challenging their expectations.

The mood shifted violently. Anger flared in the eyes of those who moments before had listened with wonder. The synagogue erupted, a surge of wrath propelling the crowd to their feet. They pushed Jesus out of the building, their collective fury driving him toward the edge of town, to the steep cliff that marked the boundary of their village.

Heartbeats thundered, a chorus of indignation and fear, as they intended to hurl him down the rocky precipice. But in the midst of chaos, Jesus, calm and unflinching, walked through the crowd. With a serenity that defied their rage, he passed through them and went on his way, leaving behind a community grappling with their own disbelief and anger.

stories.title: The Miraculous Catch of Fish
stories.keyVerse: "When Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus’ knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord."
stories.text:
And it came to pass, that, as the people pressed upon him to hear the word of God, he stood by the lake of Gennesaret,
And saw two ships standing by the lake: but the fishermen were gone out of them, and were washing
their nets.
And he entered into one of the ships, which was Simon’s, and prayed him that he would thrust out a little from the land. And he sat down, and taught the people out of the ship.
Now when he had left speaking, he said unto Simon,
Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught.
And Simon answering said unto him, Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net.
And when they had this done, they inclosed a great multitude of fishes: and their net brake.
And they beckoned unto
their partners, which were in the other ship, that they should come and help them. And they came, and filled both the ships, so that they began to sink.
When Simon Peter saw
it, he fell down at Jesus’ knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord.
For he was astonished, and all that were with him, at the draught of the fishes which they had taken:
And so
was also James, and John, the sons of Zebedee, which were partners with Simon. And Jesus said unto Simon,
Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men.
And when they had brought their ships to land, they forsook all, and followed him.
stories.retelling:
The sun was just starting to rise over the Lake of Gennesaret, casting a pale glow on the water's surface. The air was crisp, and a gentle breeze rustled the reeds along the shore. A crowd gathered, eager to hear the teachings of Jesus, who stood by the water's edge. Nearby, two fishing boats were moored, their occupants not in the boats but on the shore, busy washing their nets after a long, unfruitful night at sea.

Jesus approached one of the boats, which belonged to Simon, a rugged fisherman with eyes that told tales of the sea. Jesus asked Simon to push the boat a little from the shore so he could address the crowd from the water. As the boat gently rocked on the waves, Jesus sat down and began to teach, his voice carrying over the water, holding the crowd in rapt attention.

After he finished speaking, Jesus turned to Simon, his eyes filled with an intriguing mixture of authority and warmth. He instructed, **"Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught."** Simon hesitated, the fatigue from the night's fruitless toil evident in his voice. **"Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing,"** he replied, a hint of resignation in his tone. Yet, something in Jesus' gaze prompted him to add, **"Nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net."**

Simon and his fellow fishermen, James and John, pushed the boat further into the lake. The water glistened under the morning sun as they lowered their nets. Almost immediately, the calm surface erupted with the thrashing of a multitude of fish. The nets strained under the weight, nearly breaking with the sheer volume.

Frantic, Simon signaled to his partners in the other boat to come and assist. Together, they hauled in the catch, the boats so laden with fish that they began to sink under the weight. The fishermen's faces were a mix of disbelief and exhilaration. Simon, overwhelmed by the miraculous catch, fell to his knees before Jesus amidst the piles of flopping fish. **"Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord,"** he declared, awestruck and trembling.

The others—James and John, the sons of Zebedee—were equally amazed, their eyes wide with astonishment. But Jesus, calm and reassuring, spoke to Simon with a promise that would change their lives forever. **"Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men."**

When they finally reached the shore, the boats were bursting with their miraculous haul. Yet, the fishermen, moved by what they had witnessed, felt the tug of a different kind of calling. Without hesitation, they left everything behind—their nets, their boats, their lives as they knew them—and followed Jesus, drawn by the profound promise of catching souls instead of fish.

stories.title: The Beatitudes
stories.keyVerse: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."
stories.text:
And seeing the multitudes, he went up into a mountain: and when he was set, his disciples came unto him:
And he opened his mouth, and taught them, saying,
Blessed
are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Blessed
are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted.
Blessed
are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.
Blessed
are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled.
Blessed
are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.
Blessed
are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.
Blessed
are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
Blessed
are they which are persecuted for righteousness sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Blessed are ye, when
men shall revile you, and persecute
you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.
Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great
is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you.
stories.retelling:
The sun rose gently over the hills, casting a warm, golden glow across the landscape. A crowd had gathered, their faces a mosaic of hope, curiosity, and longing. They came from all walks of life, drawn by whispers of a man whose words could touch hearts and change lives. This man, Jesus, climbed the mountain with a quiet grace, his presence commanding attention not through force, but through an unmistakable serenity and authority.

As he reached a natural plateau, he sat down, a gesture that signaled he was ready to speak. His disciples gathered close, eager to hear the wisdom he would impart. The crowd hushed, an expectant silence hanging in the air like the calm before a storm.

Jesus looked out over the multitude, his eyes meeting theirs with a warmth that seemed to reach into their souls. He opened his mouth, and his voice, though gentle, carried with it a strength that resonated with every listener. **"Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,"** he began, his words flowing like a soothing balm over the crowd.

He spoke of those who mourn, promising comfort; of the meek, who would inherit the earth. His words painted a picture of a world turned upside down, where the gentle and merciful would find favor, where those who hungered for righteousness would find satisfaction. As he spoke, a palpable sense of peace spread among the people, as if his words were a beacon guiding them through life's stormy seas.

Jesus continued, speaking of the pure in heart and the peacemakers, declaring them blessed. He acknowledged the pain of persecution, yet offered hope, assuring them that even in their suffering, they were not forgotten. His message was revolutionary, challenging the very fabric of society's understanding of power and blessing.

The sun climbed higher in the sky, its rays casting long shadows as Jesus spoke of joy amidst adversity. **"Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven,"** he urged, his voice infused with a conviction that ignited a spark of hope in each listener. His words resonated deeply, not just as teachings, but as promises of a new way of life, where love and humility triumphed over hate and pride.

As he finished speaking, the crowd remained silent for a moment, the weight and beauty of his words hanging in the air like a delicate tapestry. Slowly, they began to disperse, each person carrying with them a piece of the hope and promise that Jesus had so generously given. His words lingered in their hearts, seeds planted in fertile soil, ready to grow and change the world.

stories.title: Salt and Light, Fulfilling the Law
stories.keyVerse: "Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid."
stories.text:
Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men.
Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house.
Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.          Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.
For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled.
Whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven: but whosoever shall do and teach
them, the same shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.
For I say unto you, That except your righteousness shall exceed
the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven.          Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not kill; and whosoever shall kill shall be in danger of the judgment:
But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.
Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee;
Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift.
Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him; lest at any time the adversary deliver thee to the judge, and the judge deliver thee to the officer, and thou be cast into prison.
Verily I say unto thee, Thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing.          Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery:
But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.
And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast
it
from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not
that thy whole body should be cast into hell.
And if thy right hand offend thee, cut if off, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not
that thy whole body should be cast into hell.
It hath been said, Whosoever shall put away his wife, let him give her a writing of divorcement:
But I say unto you, That whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causeth her to commit adultery: and whosoever shall marry her that is divorced committeth adultery.
stories.retelling:
On a sunlit mountainside, a crowd gathered, their eager faces turned toward a solitary figure standing slightly above them. The air was filled with the gentle rustle of olive trees, their leaves shimmering in the soft breeze. Jesus, with a calm yet commanding presence, looked out over the sea of expectant eyes. He began to speak, his words like a melody that resonated deep within each listener.

"You are the salt of the earth," he told them, his voice clear and unwavering. His words painted vivid pictures in the minds of those gathered, the imagery of salt losing its flavor lingering in their thoughts. The importance of maintaining one’s essence, one’s purpose, was unmistakable.

As he continued, he spoke of light, drawing the crowd’s attention upwards where the sun illuminated the hilltop. **"Ye are the light of the world,"** he declared, the statement as bright and undeniable as the sun itself. He described how a city on a hill cannot be hidden, emphasizing the power and responsibility of being seen, of being a beacon for others. The image was striking, a city’s light visible for miles, guiding travelers through the night.

He urged them to let their light shine, to live in such a way that their actions illuminated the path for others, bringing glory to God. The crowd listened intently, absorbing the profound simplicity of the message.

Transitioning seamlessly, Jesus addressed the law, assuring them that he had not come to abolish it but to fulfill it. There was a quiet intensity in his voice as he emphasized that not even the smallest part of the law would disappear until everything was accomplished. The gravity of his mission was palpable, a tightrope walk between tradition and a new understanding of righteousness.

He spoke of the ancient laws, familiar commandments etched into their hearts since childhood. Yet, he expanded their meaning, challenging them to look beyond actions and into the realm of intentions and emotions. Anger, he warned, carried the same weight as murder in one’s heart. The crowd stirred, grappling with the depth of this teaching.

The imagery grew more intense as he spoke of reconciliation, urging them to prioritize mending broken relationships over ritual offerings. His words painted a vivid picture of someone leaving a gift at the altar to first seek peace with a brother. It was a call for deeper integrity and harmony.

Finally, Jesus addressed the matters of the heart. Lust, he explained, was as adulterous as the act itself, urging drastic measures to maintain purity of heart. His words were sharp, yet his tone was compassionate, inviting introspection rather than fear.

Through his teachings, Jesus illuminated a path of righteousness that transcended mere adherence to the law—a path that challenged his listeners to look inward, to be salt and light in a world in desperate need of both.

stories.title: Love Your Enemies
stories.keyVerse: "But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;"
stories.text:
Again, ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time, Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths:
But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God’s throne:
Nor by the earth; for it is his footstool: neither by Jerusalem; for it is the city of the great King.
Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black.
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.          Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth:
But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.
And if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have
thy cloke also.
And whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain.
Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away.          Ye have heard that it hath been said, Thou shalt love thy neighbour, and hate thine enemy.
But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;
That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.
For if ye love them which love you, what reward have ye? do not even the publicans the same?
And if ye salute your brethren only, what do ye more
than others? do not even the publicans so?
Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.
stories.retelling:
The sun cast long shadows over the hillside as a crowd gathered, eager to hear the teachings of the man who spoke with such authority. The air was thick with anticipation, and a quiet reverence settled over the multitude as Jesus began to teach. His words were unlike anything they had heard before, challenging the very fabric of their beliefs.

He spoke of oaths, advising them not to swear by heaven or earth, for these were not theirs to command. Instead, he urged simplicity and truthfulness, saying, “Let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’” His voice was calm yet firm, as if he were unveiling a new way of seeing the world.

As he continued, the crowd leaned in closer. They were familiar with the old laws, the ones that demanded fairness and retribution, an eye for an eye. But Jesus offered a different path. “If someone strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also,” he said, his words hanging in the air like a challenge to their instincts. Faces in the crowd showed a mix of confusion and wonder. Could such radical forgiveness truly be possible?

He went on, each statement more astonishing than the last. If someone sued them for their coat, they should give their cloak as well. If compelled to walk a mile, they should walk two. Generosity and patience were to replace retaliation and grudges. The crowd shifted, murmurs rippling through them like waves. This was a new law, one of compassion and unexpected kindness.

The teachings reached a crescendo with a call for radical love. **“Love your enemies, bless them that curse you,"** Jesus said, his voice filled with an earnestness that resonated deeply. The idea was revolutionary, almost unthinkable. To love those who hated them, to bless those who cursed them—these were not just words; they were a call to a higher standard of living. He explained that the sun rises on the evil and the good, that rain falls on the just and the unjust alike. In this, they were to emulate the perfection of their Father in heaven.

The crowd was silent now, absorbing the weight of his words. Some nodded slowly, while others stared into the distance, grappling with the implications. Jesus had painted a vision of a world transformed by love and grace, a world where enemies could become friends through acts of mercy and understanding.

As the sun dipped below the horizon, casting a warm glow over the gathered people, a sense of hope lingered in the air. They had been given a glimpse of a different way of living, one that challenged their deepest instincts but promised a profound peace. The message was clear: love was to be the guiding force, even in the face of hatred and adversity. And as they began to disperse, one by one, they carried with them the seed of this new vision, a vision that would slowly take root in their hearts and lives.

stories.title: The Lord's Prayer
stories.keyVerse: “After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.”
stories.text:
Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven.
Therefore when thou doest
thine alms, do not sound a trumpet before thee, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may have glory of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.
But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth:
That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly.          And when thou prayest, thou shalt not be as the hypocrites
are: for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.
But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.
But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen
do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking.
Be not ye therefore like unto them: for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him.
After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.
Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as
it is
in heaven.
Give us this day our daily bread.
And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.
For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you:
But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.          Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.
But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face;
That thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret: and thy Father, which seeth in secret, shall reward thee openly.
stories.retelling:
In the cool, quiet air of early morning, a small group gathered around the teacher on the hillside, their eyes fixed on him with a yearning to understand. The sun crept over the horizon, casting a warm glow across the landscape, while birds flitted about, their songs a gentle backdrop to the unfolding lesson. The teacher, known for his wisdom and simplicity, looked upon his followers with compassion, knowing the burdens they carried and the understanding they sought.

He began with a gentle warning, urging them to be mindful of their intentions when giving to others. **“Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them,”** he cautioned, his voice carrying a blend of authority and kindness. He spoke of those who sought public recognition, their loud proclamations echoing through synagogues and streets. These individuals, he said, had already received their reward in the form of fleeting admiration. Instead, he encouraged them to give quietly, without fanfare, so that even their left hand would be unaware of their right hand’s actions. In this secrecy, their deeds would be seen by the Father, who would reward them openly.

Turning to the subject of prayer, the teacher drew his listeners closer with a promise of simplicity and sincerity. He described the hypocrites, standing conspicuously in public places, their prayers long and loud, aimed at drawing attention rather than genuine communion. **“But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet,”** he advised, painting a picture of intimacy and solitude. In the quiet of their rooms, with doors closed, they could speak with the Father who valued their secrets and heartfelt petitions.

He then taught them a prayer, a simple yet profound invocation that bridged heaven and earth. **“Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name,”** he began, his voice resonating with reverence. The words flowed, asking for the kingdom to come, for daily sustenance, and for the forgiveness of debts as they forgave others. It was a prayer for guidance, for deliverance from evil, and an acknowledgment of the Father’s eternal power and glory.

The teacher’s voice softened as he spoke of forgiveness, a gentle reminder that forgiving others opened the way for their own forgiveness. He emphasized that these acts, done in secret, held a deeper significance to the Father than any public display.

Finally, he addressed fasting, another practice often marred by performative acts. He urged them not to disfigure their faces to gain sympathy or attention, but to present themselves normally, with washed faces and anointed heads. In this way, their fasting would be a private matter between them and the Father, who saw all that was done in secret and would reward them accordingly.

The teacher's words lingered in the morning air, leaving the group with a sense of purpose, their hearts filled with the quiet assurance that their humble acts and sincere prayers would not go unnoticed.

stories.title: Do Not Worry
stories.keyVerse: "Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?"
stories.text:
Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:
But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:
For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great
is
that darkness!          No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?
Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they?
Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?
And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin:
And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.
Wherefore, if God so clothe the grass of the field, which to day is, and to morrow is cast into the oven,
shall he not much more
clothe you, O ye of little faith?
Therefore take no thought, saying, What shall we eat? or, What shall we drink? or, Wherewithal shall we be clothed?
(For after all these things do the Gentiles seek:) for your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of all these things.
But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.
Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day
is the evil thereof.
stories.retelling:
Under a sky painted in hues of gold and orange, Jesus stood amidst a large gathering on the slope of a gentle hill. The air was cool, carrying the scent of wildflowers and damp earth, as people sat on the grassy ground, their eyes fixed on Him. Murmurs of anticipation rippled through the crowd, like the rustling leaves in the breeze. Jesus, His presence both calming and commanding, began to speak.

He pointed out how fleeting earthly possessions were. **"Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth,"** He said, a gentle urgency in His voice. He spoke of moths that gnaw through fabric and rust that erodes metal, and of thieves who slip through the night to steal. Instead, He urged them to seek treasures in heaven, where nothing could destroy. As His words settled over them, a thoughtful silence fell, broken only by the distant chirp of crickets and the rustle of leaves.

He explained that the eye is the lamp of the body. If the eye is clear and focused, the whole body is illuminated, brimming with light. But if the eye is clouded by greed or malice, the body is consumed by darkness. His words painted vivid images in the listeners' minds, as they pondered the clarity of their own vision.

With a shift in tone, Jesus addressed the impossibility of serving two masters. **"Ye cannot serve God and mammon,"** He declared, His voice firm yet gentle. The crowd stirred, reflecting on their own divided loyalties between material wealth and spiritual devotion.

Then, with a compassionate gaze, He urged them not to be consumed by worry. **"Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life,"** He said, His words a soothing balm to their anxious hearts. He pointed to the birds soaring above them, carefree and unworried about their next meal, yet fed by the hand of God. The people followed His gesture, watching the swallows dip and dive with a newfound appreciation.

He then drew their attention to the wildflowers blanketing the fields in vibrant colors. They neither toiled nor spun, yet they were clothed in beauty that even Solomon, in all his splendor, could not match. If God adorned the grass, which lives but a short time, how much more would He care for them? His words were a gentle reminder, spoken with such love that it resonated deep within their souls.

Finally, Jesus encouraged them to focus on seeking God's kingdom and righteousness, assuring them that all their needs would be met. **"Take therefore no thought for the morrow,"** He advised, as the sun began to dip below the horizon, casting long shadows across the hillside. His message lingered in the cool evening air, a call to trust and live in the present, free from the burdens of tomorrow's worries.

stories.title: Judging Others, Ask Seek Knock
stories.keyVerse: "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you."
stories.text:
Judge not, that ye be not judged.
For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.
And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?
Or how wilt thou say to thy brother, Let me pull out the mote out of thine eye; and, behold, a beam
is in thine own eye?
Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother’s eye.
Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.          Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you:
For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened.
Or what man is there of you, whom if his son ask bread, will he give him a stone?
Or if he ask a fish, will he give him a serpent?
If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children, how much more shall your Father which is in heaven give good things to them that ask him?
Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.          Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide
is the gate, and broad
is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat:
Because strait
is the gate, and narrow
is
the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.
stories.retelling:
As the sun began its ascent over the horizon, casting a warm, golden hue over the gathering, Jesus stood before the crowd, his voice a calm yet powerful beacon. He addressed them with a gentle authority, sharing wisdom that pierced the heart like an arrow finding its mark. He spoke of judgment, a topic that weighed heavily on the minds of many.

Pausing, he let his eyes roam over the multitude, each person a unique story waiting to be told. "Why do you notice the tiny speck in your brother’s eye," he asked, his voice resonating with clarity, "while ignoring the massive beam in your own?" The crowd murmured, a ripple of understanding passing through them. He urged them to remove the beam from their own eyes first, allowing them to see clearly before pointing out the faults in others. The lesson was simple yet profound, a call to introspection and humility.

Jesus then shifted his message, speaking of a more intimate connection with the divine. **"Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you,"** he declared, his words a promise, an assurance that resonated with hope. He painted a vivid picture of a father and child, asking who among them, when their child requested bread, would hand them a stone instead. The crowd chuckled softly, the imagery striking a chord of shared humanity. If earthly parents knew how to give good gifts, how much more would their heavenly Father offer good things to those who asked?

His words were not only a promise of divine generosity but also a call to action. He encouraged them to treat others as they wished to be treated, a principle that encompassed the essence of the law and the prophets. The crowd nodded in agreement, the weight of his message settling over them like a comforting cloak.

Finally, Jesus spoke of paths and gates, his tone turning serious. The wide gate, he explained, led to destruction, a path many would take, drawn by its ease and appeal. In contrast, the narrow gate, though difficult and less traveled, led to life. His words were a map, a guide to those willing to listen and choose wisely.

As the crowd absorbed his teachings, the air seemed to shimmer with possibility. They realized that the choice was theirs—to judge or to forgive, to ask or to ignore, to seek or to remain stagnant. Jesus had given them the tools, the guidance, and now it was up to them to act. The sun continued its climb, illuminating the path ahead, and as the people began to disperse, they carried with them a renewed sense of purpose, ready to knock on doors of opportunity and seek the treasures of the heart.

stories.title: The Wise and Foolish Builders
stories.keyVerse: "Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:"
stories.text:
Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.
Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?
Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit.
A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither
can
a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit.
Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.
Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.          Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.
Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?
And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.          Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:
And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.
And every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man, which built his house upon the sand:
And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell: and great was the fall of it.
And it came to pass, when Jesus had ended these sayings, the people were astonished at his doctrine:
For he taught them as
one having authority, and not as the scribes.
stories.retelling:
As the sun began its descent, casting a golden glow over the Galilean hillside, a crowd gathered, their eyes fixed on the solitary figure standing on the slope. Jesus, with a quiet authority that seemed to resonate with the earth itself, spoke words that hung heavy in the air, each syllable weaving its way into the hearts of those who listened.

“Be wary of those who come cloaked as friends yet harbor intentions as fierce as wolves,” he warned, his voice clear and unwavering. The crowd shifted, murmuring softly among themselves, as he continued. “You will know them by the fruits they bear. Good cannot spring from evil, just as grapes do not grow on thorns.”

He paused, letting the truth settle over them, before painting a vivid scene. “Imagine a man,” he said, gesturing to the horizon. “A wise man, who, hearing my words, chooses to build his house upon the rock.” His audience could almost see it—a sturdy home standing resolute against the elements. “The rains come,” he described, his arms sweeping downward like the falling deluge, “the floods rise, and the winds howl and beat against it. Yet, it stands firm, unshaken and secure.”

The listeners nodded, their imaginations carrying them through the storm-tossed night, feeling the strength of the foundation beneath them. But then, Jesus turned the picture dark. “Now consider the foolish man,” he urged, the tone in his voice deepening. “Who hears my words but does not act upon them, like a man who builds his house on the shifting sands.”

The crowd leaned in, caught in the vivid contrast, the tension rising as Jesus spoke of the rains descending upon this second house. The imagery was stark and vivid; they could almost hear the creaking of wood and feel the ground slipping away beneath their feet. “The winds lash out, and with a great crash, the house falls,” he concluded, his words echoing like thunder.

Silence followed, thick and contemplative, as the crowd absorbed the lesson. They exchanged glances, the weight of his teaching pressing heavily upon them. Jesus had spoken with an authority that differed from the dry, distant tones of the scribes. His words were alive, reaching into the depths of their souls with a truth that was both piercing and liberating.

As he finished, the people were left in awe, their hearts stirred by the simplicity yet profound depth of his words. They began to disperse, each carrying with them the vision of those two houses—a choice between the rock and the sand, between wisdom and folly. The hillside cleared, but the echo of Jesus’s teachings lingered, weaving its way into the evening breeze, leaving an indelible mark on the landscape of their lives.

stories.title: The Sermon on the Plain
stories.keyVerse: "And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said, Blessed be ye poor: for yours is the kingdom of God."
stories.text:
And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said,
Blessed
be ye poor: for yours is the kingdom of God.
Blessed
are ye that hunger now: for ye shall be filled. Blessed
are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh.
Blessed are ye, when men shall hate you, and when they shall separate you
from their company, and shall reproach
you, and cast out your name as evil, for the Son of man’s sake.
Rejoice ye in that day, and leap for joy: for, behold, your reward
is great in heaven: for in the like manner did their fathers unto the prophets.
But woe unto you that are rich! for ye have received your consolation.
Woe unto you that are full! for ye shall hunger. Woe unto you that laugh now! for ye shall mourn and weep.
Woe unto you, when all men shall speak well of you! for so did their fathers to the false prophets.          But I say unto you which hear, Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you,
Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you.
And unto him that smiteth thee on the
one cheek offer also the other; and him that taketh away thy cloke forbid not
to take thy coat also.
Give to every man that asketh of thee; and of him that taketh away thy goods ask
them not again.
And as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise.
For if ye love them which love you, what thank have ye? for sinners also love those that love them.
And if ye do good to them which do good to you, what thank have ye? for sinners also do even the same.
And if ye lend
to them of whom ye hope to receive, what thank have ye? for sinners also lend to sinners, to receive as much again.
But love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and
to the evil.
Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful.
Judge not, and ye shall not be judged: condemn not, and ye shall not be condemned: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven:
Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom. For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again.
And he spake a parable unto them,
Can the blind lead the blind? shall they not both fall into the ditch?The disciple is not above his master: but every one that is perfect shall be as his master.
And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye, but perceivest not the beam that is in thine own eye?
Either how canst thou say to thy brother, Brother, let me pull out the mote that is in thine eye, when thou thyself beholdest not the beam that is in thine own eye? Thou hypocrite, cast out first the beam out of thine own eye, and then shalt thou see clearly to pull out the mote that is in thy brother’s eye.
For a good tree bringeth not forth corrupt fruit; neither doth a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit.
For every tree is known by his own fruit. For of thorns men do not gather figs, nor of a bramble bush gather they grapes.
A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good; and an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is evil: for of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh.          And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?
Whosoever cometh to me, and heareth my sayings, and doeth them, I will shew you to whom he is like:
He is like a man which built an house, and digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock: and when the flood arose, the stream beat vehemently upon that house, and could not shake it: for it was founded upon a rock.
But he that heareth, and doeth not, is like a man that without a foundation built an house upon the earth; against which the stream did beat vehemently, and immediately it fell; and the ruin of that house was great.
stories.retelling:
As the sun began its descent, casting a warm glow over the gathering, Jesus stood on the gentle slope of the plain. The air was filled with anticipation as a diverse crowd, drawn by whispers of wisdom and healing, gathered around him. His disciples were closest, their eyes fixed on him, eager to capture every word.

With a serene gaze that seemed to embrace each person, Jesus lifted his eyes to his disciples. His voice carried across the plain, gentle but firm. **"Blessed be ye poor,"** he declared, the words hanging in the air like a promise. **"For yours is the kingdom of God."** A ripple of surprise mixed with hope washed over the listeners. The poor, the hungry, those who wept—these were the ones he called blessed, their eyes widening with a flicker of newfound dignity and purpose.

He spoke of hunger and sorrow, acknowledging the deep aches that life often brought. **"Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh,"** he assured them, his words a balm to the weary and the grieving. He continued, warning those who were rich and content, foretelling a time when their abundance would turn to want, their laughter to mourning.

The crowd listened, captivated by this radical inversion of the world's values. Jesus spoke of loving one's enemies, a notion so contrary to human instinct that it drew murmurs of disbelief. Yet, his conviction was unwavering. He urged them to turn the other cheek, to give without expectation, to love without boundaries. The challenge was immense, yet his vision of a compassionate world was compelling.

He told a parable, his voice weaving a vivid image. **"Can the blind lead the blind?"** he asked, his rhetorical question echoing across the plain. He spoke of the futility of judging others without first examining oneself, a call to self-awareness and humility. The metaphor of the blind leading the blind was as clear as the sky above, illustrating the folly of hypocrisy.

Jesus then moved to the imagery of trees and fruit. He painted a picture of a good tree, laden with healthy fruit, contrasting it with a corrupt tree bearing rotten produce. It was a simple yet powerful analogy, driving home the truth that one's actions reveal the true nature of the heart.

He concluded with a vivid parable of builders, emphasizing the importance of a strong foundation. Those who listened to his words and acted upon them were like the wise builder who laid the foundation on a rock, unshaken by storms. In contrast, those who ignored his teachings were like the foolish builder, whose house crumbled under the flood.

As his words settled over the crowd, they carried with them a profound call to action, an invitation to live differently, to embody the kingdom of God in their everyday lives.

stories.title: Jesus Heals Many
stories.keyVerse: "And Jesus put forth his hand, and touched him, saying, I will; be thou clean. And immediately his leprosy was cleansed."
stories.text:
When he was come down from the mountain, great multitudes followed him.
And, behold, there came a leper and worshipped him, saying, Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean.
And Jesus put forth
his hand, and touched him, saying,
I will; be thou clean. And immediately his leprosy was cleansed.
And Jesus saith unto him,
See thou tell no man; but go thy way, shew thyself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses commanded, for a testimony unto them.And when Jesus was entered into Capernaum, there came unto him a centurion, beseeching him,
And saying, Lord, my servant lieth at home sick of the palsy, grievously tormented.
And Jesus saith unto him,
I will come and heal him.
The centurion answered and said, Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof: but speak the word only, and my servant shall be healed.
For I am a man under authority, having soldiers under me: and I say to this
man, Go, and he goeth; and to another, Come, and he cometh; and to my servant, Do this, and he doeth
it.
When Jesus heard
it, he marvelled, and said to them that followed,
Verily I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel.
And I say unto you, That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven.
But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
And Jesus said unto the centurion,
Go thy way; and as thou hast believed, so be it done unto thee. And his servant was healed in the selfsame hour.
And when Jesus was come into Peter’s house, he saw his wife’s mother laid, and sick of a fever.
And he touched her hand, and the fever left her: and she arose, and ministered unto them.
When the even was come, they brought unto him many that were possessed with devils: and he cast out the spirits with
his word, and healed all that were sick:
That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying, Himself took our infirmities, and bare
our sicknesses.
stories.retelling:
Descending from the mountain, Jesus was greeted by the sight of a vast crowd trailing behind him, their whispers and eager gazes filled with anticipation. Suddenly, a figure emerged from among them—a man, cloaked in the tattered rags of an outcast, his skin marred by the telltale signs of leprosy. The crowd instinctively recoiled, creating a wide berth around the man as he fell to his knees before Jesus. His voice, though cracked and weary, was filled with desperate hope. "Lord, if you want to, you can make me clean," he implored.

Without hesitation, Jesus reached out. His touch was gentle, yet it carried with it the power of certainty and compassion. **"I will; be thou clean,"** he declared, and with those words, the man's skin was transformed. The leprosy vanished, leaving him whole and clean. Jesus instructed him to keep this miracle private, to show himself to the priest and offer the gift Moses had commanded as a testimony.

As Jesus continued his journey into Capernaum, a Roman centurion approached, his demeanor respectful yet urgent. "Lord, my servant lies at home, paralyzed and in agony," he explained. Jesus, unwavering, responded, **"I will come and heal him."**

But the centurion, understanding the weight of authority, replied with humility, "Lord, I am not worthy for you to enter my home. Just say the word, and my servant will be healed. I, too, am a man of authority and know the power of a command." 

Jesus paused, marveling at the centurion's faith. Turning to the crowd, he expressed admiration, noting that such faith was unparalleled even among his own people. Then, addressing the centurion, he assured him, **"Go thy way; and as thou hast believed, so be it done unto thee."** At that moment, miles away, the centurion's servant was restored to health.

Later, Jesus entered the house of Peter. Inside, the warmth of the hearth contrasted with the pallor of Peter’s mother-in-law, bedridden and feverish. Jesus approached her, gently grasping her hand. Instantly, the fever dissipated, leaving her revitalized. Rising from her bed, she began to serve them, her gratitude evident in her every action.

As dusk settled over the town, shadows lengthening into the night, people from all around brought to Jesus those possessed by demons and afflicted by various ailments. The air was thick with cries and whispers of hope as Jesus, with a word, cast out spirits and healed the sick, fulfilling the prophecy that he would bear their infirmities.

The night sky stretched above, a backdrop to the miracles unfolding on earth, as the town of Capernaum witnessed the boundless compassion and power of Jesus, leaving the people in awe of the day’s extraordinary events.

stories.title: The Cost of Following, Calming the Storm
stories.keyVerse: But the men marvelled, saying, What manner of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him!
stories.text:
Now when Jesus saw great multitudes about him, he gave commandment to depart unto the other side.
And a certain scribe came, and said unto him, Master, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest.
And Jesus saith unto him,
The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air
have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay
his head.
And another of his disciples said unto him, Lord, suffer me first to go and bury my father.
But Jesus said unto him,
Follow me; and let the dead bury their dead.And when he was entered into a ship, his disciples followed him.
And, behold, there arose a great tempest in the sea, insomuch that the ship was covered with the waves: but he was asleep.
And his disciples came to
him, and awoke him, saying, Lord, save us: we perish.
And he saith unto them,
Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith? Then he arose, and rebuked the winds and the sea; and there was a great calm.
But the men marvelled, saying, What manner of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him!
And when he was come to the other side into the country of the Gergesenes, there met him two possessed with devils, coming out of the tombs, exceeding fierce, so that no man might pass by that way.
And, behold, they cried out, saying, What have we to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of God? art thou come hither to torment us before the time?
And there was a good way off from them an herd of many swine feeding.
So the devils besought him, saying, If thou cast us out, suffer us to go away into the herd of swine.
And he said unto them,
Go. And when they were come out, they went into the herd of swine: and, behold, the whole herd of swine ran violently down a steep place into the sea, and perished in the waters.
And they that kept them fled, and went their ways into the city, and told every thing, and what was befallen to the possessed of the devils.
And, behold, the whole city came out to meet Jesus: and when they saw him, they besought
him that he would depart out of their coasts.
stories.retelling:
The sun dipped below the horizon, casting a golden hue across the sea as Jesus stood at the shore, watching the crowd swell around him. The air was filled with anticipation, but there was something more pressing in his gaze. He turned to his disciples and instructed them to prepare for departure to the other side of the lake. As the disciples scrambled to ready the boat, a scribe approached, eyes alight with determination. "Master," he declared, "I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest." Jesus paused, his voice carrying a gentle warning. **"The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head."**

Another disciple approached, conflicted and hesitant. “Lord, allow me first to go and bury my father,” he pleaded. Jesus, with unwavering purpose, responded, **"Follow me; and let the dead bury their dead."**

The boat rocked gently as the disciples climbed aboard, the wood creaking underfoot. Once they were all settled, Jesus found a place to rest at the stern, exhaustion weighing heavy upon him. As the boat glided over the darkening waters, a sudden wind whipped across the surface, the sea rising in tumultuous waves. The sky turned an ominous gray, and the boat was soon swamped by the angry sea.

Amidst the chaos, Jesus slept, his peace unbroken by the storm that raged around him. Panicked, the disciples shook him awake, their voices laced with fear. "Lord, save us: we perish." They cried out, desperation palpable.

Jesus awoke, calm and unruffled by the squall. He looked at his disciples, a hint of disappointment in his eyes. **"Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith?"** His voice, though gentle, carried the weight of authority. Rising, he faced the storm, his command cutting through the roar of the wind and crashing waves. There was silence as the tempest obeyed, the sea smoothing itself under the power of his rebuke.

The disciples, soaked and shivering, could only stare in awe and bewilderment. **"What manner of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him!"** they murmured amongst themselves.

The boat glided onto the shores of the Gergesenes, a land shrouded in eerie quiet. As Jesus stepped onto the land, two men, wild and tormented, emerged from the tombs, their presence a grim reminder of the darkness that lingered in the world. "What have we to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of God?" they cried, their voices echoing through the still air. A herd of swine grazed in the distance, oblivious to the unfolding drama.

The demons within the men begged for release, and Jesus, with a single word, granted their plea. **"Go,"** he commanded, and the unclean spirits fled into the swine, sending the herd plunging into the sea, where their cries were swallowed by the depths.

News spread quickly, the keepers of the swine running to the city to tell of what they had witnessed. Soon, the townspeople gathered, their curiosity overshadowed by fear. They pleaded with Jesus to leave, unable to comprehend the power they had seen. And so, he departed, leaving behind a land forever changed by his presence.

stories.title: The Paralytic Forgiven and Healed
stories.keyVerse: "But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power on earth to forgive sins, (then saith he to the sick of the palsy,) Arise, take up thy bed, and go unto thine house."
stories.text:
And he entered into a ship, and passed over, and came into his own city.
And, behold, they brought to him a man sick of the palsy, lying on a bed: and Jesus seeing their faith said unto the sick of the palsy;
Son, be of good cheer; thy sins be forgiven thee.
And, behold, certain of the scribes said within themselves, This
man blasphemeth.
And Jesus knowing their thoughts said,
Wherefore think ye evil in your hearts?
For whether is easier, to say,
Thy sins be forgiven thee; or to say, Arise, and walk?
But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power on earth to forgive sins, (then saith he to the sick of the palsy,)
Arise, take up thy bed, and go unto thine house.
And he arose, and departed to his house.
But when the multitudes saw
it, they marvelled, and glorified God, which had given such power unto men.
And as Jesus passed forth from thence, he saw a man, named Matthew, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he saith unto him,
Follow me.
And he arose, and followed him.
And it came to pass, as Jesus sat at meat in the house, behold, many publicans and sinners came and sat down with him and his disciples.
And when the Pharisees saw
it, they said unto his disciples, Why eateth your Master with publicans and sinners?
But when Jesus heard
that, he said unto them,
They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick.
But go ye and learn what
that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.Then came to him the disciples of John, saying, Why do we and the Pharisees fast oft, but thy disciples fast not?
And Jesus said unto them,
Can the children of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? but the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then shall they fast.
No man putteth a piece of new cloth unto an old garment, for that which is put in to fill it up taketh from the garment, and the rent is made worse.
Neither do men put new wine into old bottles: else the bottles break, and the wine runneth out, and the bottles perish: but they put new wine into new bottles, and both are preserved.
stories.retelling:
The sun cast a golden glow over the bustling streets of Capernaum as Jesus returned to his hometown, the air alive with anticipation and curiosity. Word had spread like wildfire about the miracles he performed, and people gathered with hope and skepticism in equal measure. Among the crowd, a group of determined men carried their paralyzed friend on a makeshift stretcher, their eyes set on reaching the healer. They pushed through the throngs, their faith unwavering despite the clamor around them.

Finally, they reached Jesus. Seeing their earnest belief, he turned to the paralyzed man, who lay silently on the bed, eyes wide with a mixture of fear and hope. **"Son, be of good cheer; thy sins be forgiven thee,"** Jesus declared, his voice calm and assuring. The crowd fell into hushed whispers. Some marveled at his words, while others, especially the scribes, muttered amongst themselves, questioning his audacious claim to forgive sins.

Aware of their murmurs, Jesus addressed them directly, his voice cutting through the tension. **"Wherefore think ye evil in your hearts?"** he asked, challenging their silent judgments. **"For whether is easier, to say, 'Thy sins be forgiven thee;' or to say, 'Arise, and walk?'** The crowd held its breath, the air thick with expectation.

To prove his authority, Jesus turned back to the paralyzed man, eyes kind yet commanding. **"Arise, take up thy bed, and go unto thine house,"** he instructed. In an astonishing moment, the man, once bound by his condition, rose to his feet. His legs, once useless, now supported him as he picked up his bed and walked home, each step a testament to newfound strength and freedom. The crowds erupted in amazement, glorifying God for the extraordinary power displayed right before their eyes.

Later, as Jesus walked through the bustling streets, he spotted Matthew, a tax collector, sitting at his post, surrounded by ledgers and coins. With a simple invitation, **"Follow me,"** Jesus called him. Without hesitation, Matthew stood up, leaving behind his life of numbers and transactions to join the growing group of disciples.

The day continued with a feast at a house where Jesus sat among tax collectors and other outcasts. The aroma of food mingled with laughter and conversation, filling the room with warmth and acceptance. But outside, the Pharisees looked on with disdain, questioning the choice of company Jesus kept. When they confronted his disciples about it, Jesus replied with a quiet yet firm conviction, **"They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick."**

As the evening wore on, the depth of Jesus’ ministry became clear. He was not there to uphold the status quo but to challenge it, to extend mercy rather than demand sacrifice, reaching out to those most in need of hope and healing.

stories.title: Jairus' Daughter and the Harvest
stories.keyVerse: "Give place: for the maid is not dead, but sleepeth." And they laughed him to scorn.
stories.text:
While he spake these things unto them, behold, there came a certain ruler, and worshipped him, saying, My daughter is even now dead: but come and lay thy hand upon her, and she shall live.
And Jesus arose, and followed him, and
so did his disciples.
And, behold, a woman, which was diseased with an issue of blood twelve years, came behind
him, and touched the hem of his garment:
For she said within herself, If I may but touch his garment, I shall be whole.
But Jesus turned him about, and when he saw her, he said,
Daughter, be of good comfort; thy faith hath made thee whole. And the woman was made whole from that hour.
And when Jesus came into the ruler’s house, and saw the minstrels and the people making a noise,
He said unto them,
Give place: for the maid is not dead, but sleepeth. And they laughed him to scorn.
But when the people were put forth, he went in, and took her by the hand, and the maid arose.
And the fame hereof went abroad into all that land.
And when Jesus departed thence, two blind men followed him, crying, and saying,
Thou Son of David, have mercy on us.
And when he was come into the house, the blind men came to him: and Jesus saith unto them,
Believe ye that I am able to do this? They said unto him, Yea, Lord.
Then touched he their eyes, saying,
According to your faith be it unto you.
And their eyes were opened; and Jesus straitly charged them, saying,
See
that no man know
it.
But they, when they were departed, spread abroad his fame in all that country.
As they went out, behold, they brought to him a dumb man possessed with a devil.
And when the devil was cast out, the dumb spake: and the multitudes marvelled, saying, It was never so seen in Israel.
But the Pharisees said, He casteth out devils through the prince of the devils.
And Jesus went about all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every sickness and every disease among the people.
But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd.
Then saith he unto his disciples,
The harvest truly
is
plenteous, but the labourers
are few;
Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.
stories.retelling:
In the bustling town, a sense of urgency hung in the air as a desperate father, a respected ruler, rushed through the crowd, his heart heavy with grief.
