He approached Jesus, falling to his knees with a plea that broke through the noise: **"My daughter is even now dead: but come and lay thy hand upon her, and she shall live."** Without a moment's hesitation, Jesus rose to his feet and followed the man, his disciples trailing close behind.

As they wove through the throng of people, a woman, fragile yet determined, reached out from the crowd. For twelve long years, she had suffered, her hope dwindling with each passing year. Yet, today, she believed. If only she could touch the hem of Jesus' garment, she might be healed. Her fingers brushed the fabric, and instantly, she felt a change within her. Jesus turned, his eyes meeting hers. **"Daughter, be of good comfort; thy faith hath made thee whole."** In that moment, her suffering ceased, leaving her whole and renewed.

They continued to the ruler's home, where the scene was one of chaos. Flute players and mourners filled the air with a cacophony of grief. Jesus stepped into the disarray and spoke with calm authority, **"Give place: for the maid is not dead, but sleepeth."** Laughter erupted, mocking the absurdity of his words, but undeterred, he asked for the room to be cleared.

Inside, the still form of the young girl lay untouched by time's passage. Jesus took her hand gently, and life flowed back into her cheeks. Her eyes fluttered open, and she rose, alive and vibrant. News of this miracle spread swiftly, igniting wonder and awe across the land.

As Jesus departed, two blind men followed, their voices lifted in earnest prayer, "Thou Son of David, have mercy on us." Inside the house, Jesus asked them, **"Believe ye that I am able to do this?"** With unwavering faith, they affirmed, "Yea, Lord." With a touch, their eyes were opened, and they saw the world anew. Despite Jesus' instruction to keep this miracle quiet, the news spread like wildfire.

Immediately after, a man unable to speak was brought before him, tormented by unseen forces. Jesus cast out the demon, and the man spoke, his voice marvelously restored. The crowd was astounded, exclaiming that such wonders had never been seen in Israel. Yet, the Pharisees, skeptical and scornful, muttered their disbelief, attributing the miracle to dark forces.

Undeterred, Jesus continued his journey through towns and villages, teaching and healing, his heart moved by the scattered and weary crowds. He turned to his disciples, his voice carrying a note of urgency and hope. **"The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few."** His words called for more hearts to join in the work, for the fields were ripe with promise.

stories.title: The Twelve Sent Out
stories.keyVerse: "Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves."
stories.text:
And when he had called unto
him his twelve disciples, he gave them power
against unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal all manner of sickness and all manner of disease.
Now the names of the twelve apostles are these; The first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James
the son of Zebedee, and John his brother;
Philip, and Bartholomew; Thomas, and Matthew the publican; James
the son of Alphaeus, and Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus;
Simon the Canaanite, and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him.
These twelve Jesus sent forth, and commanded them, saying,
Go not into the way of the Gentiles, and into
any city of the Samaritans enter ye not:
But go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.
And as ye go, preach, saying, The kingdom of heaven is at hand.
Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, raise the dead, cast out devils: freely ye have received, freely give.
Provide neither gold, nor silver, nor brass in your purses,
Nor scrip for
your journey, neither two coats, neither shoes, nor yet staves: for the workman is worthy of his meat.
And into whatsoever city or town ye shall enter, enquire who in it is worthy; and there abide till ye go thence.
And when ye come into an house, salute it.
And if the house be worthy, let your peace come upon it: but if it be not worthy, let your peace return to you.
And whosoever shall not receive you, nor hear your words, when ye depart out of that house or city, shake off the dust of your feet.
Verily I say unto you, It shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrha in the day of judgment, than for that city.          Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
But beware of men: for they will deliver you up to the councils, and they will scourge you in their synagogues;
And ye shall be brought before governors and kings for my sake, for a testimony against them and the Gentiles.
But when they deliver you up, take no thought how or what ye shall speak: for it shall be given you in that same hour what ye shall speak.
For it is not ye that speak, but the Spirit of your Father which speaketh in you.
And the brother shall deliver up the brother to death, and the father the child: and the children shall rise up against
their
parents, and cause them to be put to death.
And ye shall be hated of all
men for my name’s sake: but he that endureth to the end shall be saved.
But when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another: for verily I say unto you, Ye shall not have gone over the cities of Israel, till the Son of man be come.
The disciple is not above
his master, nor the servant above his lord.
It is enough for the disciple that he be as his master, and the servant as his lord. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more
shall they call them of his household?
Fear them not therefore: for there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; and hid, that shall not be known.
What I tell you in darkness,
that speak ye in light: and what ye hear in the ear,
that preach ye upon the housetops.
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father.
But the very hairs of your head are all numbered.
Fear ye not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows.
Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven.
But whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven.
Think not that I am come to send peace on earth: I came not to send peace, but a sword.
For I am come to set a man at variance against his father, and the daughter against her mother, and the daughter in law against her mother in law.
And a man’s foes
shall be they of his own household.
He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me: and he that loveth son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me.
And he that taketh not his cross, and followeth after me, is not worthy of me.
He that findeth his life shall lose it: and he that loseth his life for my sake shall find it.          He that receiveth you receiveth me, and he that receiveth me receiveth him that sent me.
He that receiveth a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward; and he that receiveth a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man’s reward.
And whosoever shall give to drink unto one of these little ones a cup of cold
water only in the name of a disciple, verily I say unto you, he shall in no wise lose his reward.
stories.retelling:
In the soft morning light, Jesus gathered his twelve disciples around him on a gentle hillside. The air was crisp, carrying the scent of wild herbs and distant wood smoke. As the men knelt on the cool grass, each looked at Jesus with a mixture of awe and anticipation. Today, he was sending them out, not just as followers, but as apostles, armed with a mission and a purpose that would test the boundaries of their faith and courage.

Jesus began by bestowing upon them a gift, one that shimmered in the early sun like a promise. He gave them authority—an invisible mantle of power to cast out unclean spirits and heal all kinds of sickness and disease. The disciples felt the weight and wonder of this responsibility settle on their shoulders, a gravity that was both exhilarating and daunting.

As Jesus spoke, his voice was calm, yet each word carried a depth that resonated within them. He laid out their path clearly: **"Go not into the way of the Gentiles, and into any city of the Samaritans enter ye not: but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel."** The directive was clear; their mission was to spread the message of the Kingdom of Heaven to their own people.

He instructed them to travel light—no gold, silver, or even an extra coat—relying instead on the hospitality of those they would meet. Each town and village they would enter was a new opportunity, a chance to bring peace to homes that welcomed them. **"Freely ye have received, freely give,"** he urged, encouraging them to heal the sick, cleanse lepers, and cast out demons without expecting anything in return.

The tone shifted as Jesus prepared them for the challenges ahead. **"Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves,"** he warned, urging them to be both wise and gentle. He spoke of the trials they would face: betrayals, arrests, and standing before governors and kings. Yet, he assured them that when these moments came, they need not worry about what to say; the Spirit of their Father would speak through them.

In a world full of dangers, Jesus reminded them of their worth. **"Fear ye not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows,"** he said, his voice a soothing balm against the coming storm. Each disciple, in that moment, felt the warmth of divine protection, a shield against the physical threats they would endure.

As they prepared to leave, Jesus' words lingered in the air, a sacred echo guiding their steps: **"He that receiveth you receiveth me, and he that receiveth me receiveth him that sent me."** With their hearts full and their mission clear, the twelve rose, ready to spread their message of hope and healing across the land, every footstep a testament to the light they carried within.

stories.title: Come Unto Me
stories.keyVerse: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."
stories.text:
And it came to pass, when Jesus had made an end of commanding his twelve disciples, he departed thence to teach and to preach in their cities.
Now when John had heard in the prison the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples,
And said unto him, Art thou he that should come, or do we look for another?
Jesus answered and said unto them,
Go and shew John again those things which ye do hear and see:
The blind receive their sight, and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the gospel preached to them.
And blessed is
he, whosoever shall not be offended in me.And as they departed, Jesus began to say unto the multitudes concerning John,
What went ye out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken with the wind?
But what went ye out for to see? A man clothed in soft raiment? behold, they that wear soft
clothing are in kings’ houses.
But what went ye out for to see? A prophet? yea, I say unto you, and more than a prophet.
For this is
he, of whom it is written, Behold, I send my messenger before thy face, which shall prepare thy way before thee.
Verily I say unto you, Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist: notwithstanding he that is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.
And from the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent take it by force.
For all the prophets and the law prophesied until John.
And if ye will receive
it, this is Elias, which was for to come.
He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.          But whereunto shall I liken this generation? It is like unto children sitting in the markets, and calling unto their fellows,
And saying, We have piped unto you, and ye have not danced; we have mourned unto you, and ye have not lamented.
For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, He hath a devil.
The Son of man came eating and drinking, and they say, Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners. But wisdom is justified of her children.Then began he to upbraid the cities wherein most of his mighty works were done, because they repented not:
Woe unto thee, Chorazin! woe unto thee, Bethsaida! for if the mighty works, which were done in you, had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.
But I say unto you, It shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon at the day of judgment, than for you.
And thou, Capernaum, which art exalted unto heaven, shalt be brought down to hell: for if the mighty works, which have been done in thee, had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day.
But I say unto you, That it shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom in the day of judgment, than for thee.At that time Jesus answered and said,
I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes.
Even so, Father: for so it seemed good in thy sight.
All things are delivered unto me of my Father: and no man knoweth the Son, but the Father; neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and
he to whomsoever the Son will reveal
him.
Come unto me, all
ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.
For my yoke
is easy, and my burden is light.
stories.retelling:
The sun cast golden light over the dusty streets as Jesus moved through the towns, his disciples trailing behind him like shadows. He had just finished instructing them, and now he was on a mission to spread his message far and wide across the bustling cities. Meanwhile, far from the vibrant crowds and open skies, John the Baptist languished in a dim, oppressive prison. Confined and isolated, he heard murmurs of Jesus’ miraculous works echoing through the stone walls. Intrigued and perhaps a bit uncertain, John sent two of his own followers to find Jesus and ask a pressing question.

They found Jesus among the throng of people, healing and teaching. Approaching with purpose, they conveyed John's question, "Are you the one we have been waiting for, or should we expect another?" Jesus, calm and unperturbed, responded not with words alone but with evidence. He gestured to the miracles unfolding around them. **"Go and shew John again those things which ye do hear and see,"** he said. **"The blind receive their sight, and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the gospel preached to them."**

As John's disciples departed, their minds filled with wonder, Jesus turned to address the crowd. His voice carried over the noise of the marketplace, drawing everyone in. He spoke of John, challenging the people’s perceptions. What were they expecting when they journeyed into the wilderness? A weak reed swaying in the wind, or a man dressed in finery? No, they sought a prophet—and indeed, John was more than that. He was the herald of the one to come, the messenger who prepared the way.

With fervor, Jesus continued, speaking of the greatness of John, yet emphasizing that even the least in the kingdom of heaven held a higher place. He painted vivid images of a generation that neither danced to the joyful tunes nor mourned with the lamenters. They judged John for his abstinence, and Jesus for his openness. But in a world of contradictions, wisdom would be justified by her deeds.

Then, with a heavy but resolute heart, Jesus turned his attention to the unrepentant cities where he had performed many of his miracles. "Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!" he cried, lamenting their hardened hearts. He spoke of judgment with a voice that resonated with sorrow and disappointment, comparing them to the infamous cities of Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom.

In a moment of quiet reflection, Jesus looked up and thanked his Father for revealing these truths not to the wise and learned, but to those with the simplicity of children. His gaze softened as he addressed the weary crowd, offering an invitation that transcended time and circumstance. **"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."** It was a promise of solace and peace, an invitation to find rest in the gentle embrace of his words.

stories.title: Lord of the Sabbath
stories.keyVerse: “How much then is a man better than a sheep? Wherefore it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days.”
stories.text:
At that time Jesus went on the sabbath day through the corn; and his disciples were an hungred, and began to pluck the ears of corn, and to eat.
But when the Pharisees saw
it, they said unto him, Behold, thy disciples do that which is not lawful to do upon the sabbath day.
But he said unto them,
Have ye not read what David did, when he was an hungred, and they that were with him;
How he entered into the house of God, and did eat the shewbread, which was not lawful for him to eat, neither for them which were with him, but only for the priests?
Or have ye not read in the law, how that on the sabbath days the priests in the temple profane the sabbath, and are blameless?
But I say unto you, That in this place is
one greater than the temple.
But if ye had known what
this meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice, ye would not have condemned the guiltless.
For the Son of man is Lord even of the sabbath day.
And when he was departed thence, he went into their synagogue:
And, behold, there was a man which had
his hand withered. And they asked him, saying, Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath days? that they might accuse him.
And he said unto them,
What man shall there be among you, that shall have one sheep, and if it fall into a pit on the sabbath day, will he not lay hold on it, and lift
it out?
How much then is a man better than a sheep? Wherefore it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days.
Then saith he to the man,
Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched
it forth; and it was restored whole, like as the other.
Then the Pharisees went out, and held a council against him, how they might destroy him.
But when Jesus knew
it, he withdrew himself from thence: and great multitudes followed him, and he healed them all;
And charged them that they should not make him known:
That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying,
Behold my servant, whom I have chosen; my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased: I will put my spirit upon him, and he shall shew judgment to the Gentiles.
He shall not strive, nor cry; neither shall any man hear his voice in the streets.
A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory.
And in his name shall the Gentiles trust.
stories.retelling:
The morning sun cast long shadows across a field of golden grain as Jesus and his disciples walked slowly through, their sandals brushing against the dew-covered stalks. The disciples, their stomachs grumbling with hunger, began to pluck the grain and eat. But lurking nearby, the ever-watchful Pharisees observed with disapproval. They approached Jesus, their robes rustling with indignation. "Behold," they said, voices sharp with accusation, "thy disciples do that which is not lawful to do upon the sabbath day."  

Jesus turned to them, his eyes calm yet piercing. He spoke with a steady voice, reminding them of a time when David, hungry and in need, ate the sacred bread meant only for priests. He spoke of the priests who worked on the Sabbath and yet remained blameless. **“But I say unto you, That in this place is one greater than the temple,”** he declared, his words hanging in the air like a challenge.  

Leaving the field behind, Jesus entered the synagogue. Inside, the atmosphere was tense, charged with the energy of the waiting crowd. In the corner, a man stood alone, his hand withered and useless. The Pharisees saw an opportunity. "Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath days?" they asked, their voices dripping with cunning as they tried to trap Jesus in his own words.  

Jesus turned his gaze to them, his eyes filled with a mix of patience and disappointment. He spoke to their hearts, illustrating with a simple truth. **“What man shall there be among you, that shall have one sheep, and if it fall into a pit on the sabbath day, will he not lay hold on it, and lift it out?”** His words painted a vivid picture in their minds, a sheep bleating helplessly in a pit while its owner, filled with compassion, rushes to its aid. **“How much then is a man better than a sheep?”** he continued, his voice layered with a quiet authority. **“Wherefore it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days.”**  

Turning to the man with the withered hand, Jesus spoke gently yet commandingly, **“Stretch forth thine hand.”** The man, eyes wide with hope and disbelief, obeyed. As he extended his hand, it transformed before the eyes of the crowd, becoming whole and strong, a mirror of its twin. Gasps of amazement filled the room, but the Pharisees, instead of rejoicing, felt their anger deepen. They withdrew, whispering among themselves, plotting their next move against him.  

Sensing the brewing danger, Jesus quietly left the synagogue. Yet, as he withdrew, the people followed, drawn by the hope and healing he offered. In their midst, he continued to heal, his presence a living testament to the words of the prophet Isaiah, promising justice and hope to all nations. And so, the Sabbath day unfolded, marked not by the restrictions of man, but by acts of kindness and mercy that transcended time and tradition.

stories.title: A House Divided
stories.keyVerse: "Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand."
stories.text:
Then was brought unto him one possessed with a devil, blind, and dumb: and he healed him, insomuch that the blind and dumb both spake and saw.
And all the people were amazed, and said, Is not this the son of David?
But when the Pharisees heard
it, they said, This
fellow
doth not cast out devils, but by Beelzebub the prince of the devils.
And Jesus knew their thoughts, and said unto them,
Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand:
And if Satan cast out Satan, he is divided against himself; how shall then his kingdom stand?
And if I by Beelzebub cast out devils, by whom do your children cast
them out? therefore they shall be your judges.
But if I cast out devils by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God is come unto you.
Or else how can one enter into a strong man’s house, and spoil his goods, except he first bind the strong man? and then he will spoil his house.
He that is not with me is against me; and he that gathereth not with me scattereth abroad.          Wherefore I say unto you, All manner of sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men: but the blasphemy
against the
Holy
Ghost shall not be forgiven unto men.
And whosoever speaketh a word against the Son of man, it shall be forgiven him: but whosoever speaketh against the Holy Ghost, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world, neither in the
world to come.
Either make the tree good, and his fruit good; or else make the tree corrupt, and his fruit corrupt: for the tree is known by
his fruit.O generation of vipers, how can ye, being evil, speak good things? for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.
A good man out of the good treasure of the heart bringeth forth good things: and an evil man out of the evil treasure bringeth forth evil things.
But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.
For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned.Then certain of the scribes and of the Pharisees answered, saying, Master, we would see a sign from thee.
But he answered and said unto them,
An evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign; and there shall no sign be given to it, but the sign of the prophet Jonas:
For as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale’s belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.
The men of Nineveh shall rise in judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it: because they repented at the preaching of Jonas; and, behold, a greater than Jonas
is here.
The queen of the south shall rise up in the judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it: for she came from the uttermost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and, behold, a greater than Solomon
is here.
When the unclean spirit is gone out of a man, he walketh through dry places, seeking rest, and findeth none.
Then he saith, I will return into my house from whence I came out; and when he is come, he findeth
it empty, swept, and garnished.
Then goeth he, and taketh with himself seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter in and dwell there: and the last
state of that man is worse than the first. Even so shall it be also unto this wicked generation.While he yet talked to the people, behold,
his mother and his brethren stood without, desiring to speak with him.
Then one said unto him, Behold, thy mother and thy brethren stand without, desiring to speak with thee.
But he answered and said unto him that told him,
Who is my mother? and who are my brethren?
And he stretched forth his hand toward his disciples, and said,
Behold my mother and my brethren!
For whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother.
stories.retelling:
Amidst a sea of faces, Jesus stood, his presence commanding and serene. The sun cast warm rays over the gathered crowd, illuminating their eager expressions. In the throng, a man was brought forward, his eyes vacant and his voice silent. Possessed by a demon, he was both blind and mute, his world shrouded in darkness and silence. The crowd watched with bated breath as Jesus approached the man.

With a gentle touch, Jesus restored his sight and voice. The man's eyes widened with clarity, and his first words rang out, free from the demon's grip. A collective gasp of amazement rippled through the crowd. **"Is not this the son of David?"** someone whispered, awe thickening the air.

Yet, not everyone was impressed. In the background, the Pharisees, draped in their robes, exchanged skeptical glances. One of them sneered, **"This fellow doth not cast out devils, but by Beelzebub the prince of the devils."** Their words were laced with disdain, aiming to undermine the miraculous event.

Jesus, perceiving their thoughts, turned to face them. His voice was steady and clear as he spoke to the naysayers. **"Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand."** His words sliced through the tension, challenging their baseless accusations. He continued, pointing out the absurdity of Satan working against himself and questioned by what power their own followers cast out demons.

The Pharisees shifted uncomfortably, their skepticism met by the unwavering truth in Jesus' words. He spoke of the Spirit of God, suggesting that if he drove out demons by this power, then the kingdom of God was indeed upon them. The crowd listened intently, the weight of his words settling in their hearts.

As Jesus continued, his teachings turned to the nature of good and evil, likening it to trees and their fruits. He warned them of the consequences of their words and actions, implying that their own judgments would reflect back upon them. The Pharisees, visibly unsettled, demanded a sign from Jesus, an indisputable proof of his divine authority.

Jesus, unwavering in his stance, responded, **"An evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign; and there shall no sign be given to it, but the sign of the prophet Jonas."** He spoke of Jonah's time in the whale, drawing a parallel to his own destiny, hinting at the greater truths that lay beyond their comprehension.

As he spoke, his mother and brothers arrived, waiting to speak with him. A voice from the crowd called out, bringing their presence to his attention. Jesus, gesturing towards his disciples, declared, **"Behold my mother and my brethren! For whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother."** His words redefined family, extending it to all who embraced his teachings, leaving an indelible mark on those who heard.

stories.title: Healing at the Pool of Bethesda
stories.keyVerse: "Rise, take up thy bed, and walk."
stories.text:
After this there was a feast of the Jews; and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.
Now there is at Jerusalem by the sheep
market a pool, which is called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda, having five porches.
In these lay a great multitude of impotent folk, of blind, halt, withered, waiting for the moving of the water.
For an angel went down at a certain season into the pool, and troubled the water: whosoever then first after the troubling of the water stepped in was made whole of whatsoever disease he had.
And a certain man was there, which had an infirmity thirty and eight years.
When Jesus saw him lie, and knew that he had been now a long time
in that case, he saith unto him,
Wilt thou be made whole?
The impotent man answered him, Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pool: but while I am coming, another steppeth down before me.
Jesus saith unto him,
Rise, take up thy bed, and walk.
And immediately the man was made whole, and took up his bed, and walked: and on the same day was the sabbath.
The Jews therefore said unto him that was cured, It is the sabbath day: it is not lawful for thee to carry
thy bed.
He answered them, He that made me whole, the same said unto me,
Take up thy bed, and walk.
Then asked they him, What man is that which said unto thee,
Take up thy bed, and walk?
And he that was healed wist not who it was: for Jesus had conveyed himself away, a multitude being in
that place.
Afterward Jesus findeth him in the temple, and said unto him,
Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee.
The man departed, and told the Jews that it was Jesus, which had made him whole.
And therefore did the Jews persecute Jesus, and sought to slay him, because he had done these things on the sabbath day.
But Jesus answered them,
My Father worketh hitherto, and I work.
Therefore the Jews sought the more to kill him, because he not only had broken the sabbath, but said also that God was his Father, making himself equal with God.
Then answered Jesus and said unto them,
Verily, verily, I say unto you, The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do: for what things soever he doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise.
For the Father loveth the Son, and sheweth him all things that himself doeth: and he will shew him greater works than these, that ye may marvel.
For as the Father raiseth up the dead, and quickeneth
them;
even so the Son quickeneth whom he will.
For the Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son:
That all
men should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father. He that honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father which hath sent him.
Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation; but is passed from death unto life.
Verily, verily, I say unto you, The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God: and they that hear shall live.
For as the Father hath life in himself; so hath he given to the Son to have life in himself;
And hath given him authority to execute judgment also, because he is the Son of man.
Marvel not at this: for the hour is coming, in the which all that are in the graves shall hear his voice,
And shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation.
I can of mine own self do nothing: as I hear, I judge: and my judgment is just; because I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me.
If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true.          There is another that beareth witness of me; and I know that the witness which he witnesseth of me is true.
Ye sent unto John, and he bare witness unto the truth.
But I receive not testimony from man: but these things I say, that ye might be saved.
He was a burning and a shining light: and ye were willing for a season to rejoice in his light.          But I have greater witness than
that of John: for the works which the Father hath given me to finish, the same works that I do, bear witness of me, that the Father hath sent me.
And the Father himself, which hath sent me, hath borne witness of me. Ye have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his shape.
And ye have not his word abiding in you: for whom he hath sent, him ye believe not.          Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life.
I receive not honour from men.
But I know you, that ye have not the love of God in you.
I am come in my Father’s name, and ye receive me not: if another shall come in his own name, him ye will receive.
How can ye believe, which receive honour one of another, and seek not the honour that
cometh from God only?
Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father: there is
one that accuseth you,
even Moses, in whom ye trust.
For had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me.
But if ye believe not his writings, how shall ye believe my words?
stories.retelling:
The bustling city of Jerusalem was alive with the celebration of a Jewish feast. Among the throngs, Jesus walked with quiet purpose towards a place known as Bethesda. This area, near the sheep gate, was known not for its beauty but for the crowd of suffering souls who gathered there, seeking hope in the waters of its pool. The five covered porches were filled with the sick, the blind, the lame, and the paralyzed—each waiting for the water to stir, believing that an angel would come to heal the first to enter after the disturbance.

Among them was a man who had been ill for thirty-eight long years. His eyes, heavy with the weight of unfulfilled hope, watched as once again others reached the water before him. His heart ached with resignation.

Then, quietly, almost unnoticed, Jesus approached him. He saw the man lying there, the years of illness etched into his very being. Jesus understood the depth of his struggle. He leaned in and asked a simple question that carried the weight of possibility, **"Wilt thou be made whole?"**

The man, surprised by the attention, responded with a hint of bitterness mixed with yearning. "Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred, and while I am coming, another steps down before me."

Jesus, with a gentle yet commanding presence, looked into his soul. In that moment, the air around them seemed to still, as if the world itself paused to listen. Jesus said, **"Rise, take up thy bed, and walk."**

With those words, a miracle unfolded. Strength surged through the man’s body. He stood, the sensation of standing unfamiliar yet exhilarating. He rolled up his mat, his heart pounding with disbelief and joy as he walked.

It was on the Sabbath, and as the man moved through the streets, carrying his mat, he caught the attention of the Jewish leaders. They confronted him with stern faces, reminding him that it was not lawful to carry his mat on the Sabbath. Undeterred, he replied, **"He that made me whole, the same said unto me, 'Take up thy bed, and walk.'"**

The leaders, intrigued, demanded to know who had instructed him to do so. The man, however, did not know, for Jesus had slipped away into the crowd.

Later, Jesus found him in the temple. He spoke to him again, reminding him to live a life free from sin to avoid further suffering. Realizing who Jesus was, the man hurried to the leaders, revealing his healer’s identity.

The revelation ignited anger among the leaders. Jesus had not only healed on the Sabbath but had also spoken of God in a way that equated Himself with the Father. Confronted by their hostility, Jesus calmly explained that His actions mirrored those of the Father, and that greater works would be revealed. But His words only deepened their resolve against Him, as they failed to see the wonder of what had unfolded at Bethesda.

stories.title: The Parable of the Sower
stories.keyVerse: "Who hath ears to hear, let him hear."
stories.text:
The same day went Jesus out of the house, and sat by the sea side.
And great multitudes were gathered together unto him, so that he went into a ship, and sat; and the whole multitude stood on the shore.
And he spake many things unto them in parables, saying,
Behold, a sower went forth to sow;
And when he sowed, some
seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up:
Some fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth: and forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth:
And when the sun was up, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away.
And some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprung up, and choked them:
But other fell into good ground, and brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold.
Who hath ears to hear, let him hear.
And the disciples came, and said unto him, Why speakest thou unto them in parables?
He answered and said unto them,
Because it is given unto you to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it is not given.
For whosoever hath, to him shall be given, and he shall have more abundance: but whosoever hath not, from him shall be taken away even that he hath.
Therefore speak I to them in parables: because they seeing see not; and hearing they hear not, neither do they understand.
And in them is fulfilled the prophecy of Esaias, which saith, By hearing ye shall hear, and shall not understand; and seeing ye shall see, and shall not perceive:
For this people’s heart is waxed gross, and
their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes they have closed; lest at any time they should see with
their eyes, and hear with
their ears, and should understand with
their
heart, and should be converted, and I should heal them.
But blessed
are your eyes, for they see: and your ears, for they hear.
For verily I say unto you, That many prophets and righteous
men have desired to see
those things which ye see, and have not seen
them; and to hear
those things which ye hear, and have not heard
them.
Hear ye therefore the parable of the sower.
When any one heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth
it not, then cometh the wicked
one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart. This is he which received seed by the way side.
But he that received the seed into stony places, the same is he that heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it;
Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended.
He also that received seed among the thorns is he that heareth the word; and the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word, and he becometh unfruitful.
But he that received seed into the good ground is he that heareth the word, and understandeth
it; which also beareth fruit, and bringeth forth, some an hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty.Another parable put he forth unto them, saying,
The kingdom of heaven is likened unto a man which sowed good seed in his field:
But while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat, and went his way.
But when the blade was sprung up, and brought forth fruit, then appeared the tares also.
So the servants of the householder came and said unto him, Sir, didst not thou sow good seed in thy field? from whence then hath it tares?
He said unto them, An enemy hath done this. The servants said unto him, Wilt thou then that we go and gather them up?
But he said, Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them.
Let both grow together until the harvest: and in the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them: but gather the wheat into my barn.
stories.retelling:
It was a typical day near the Sea of Galilee, where the sun kissed the rolling waves, and the scent of salt lingered in the air. Jesus emerged from a house, stepping into the open, where a great crowd eagerly awaited him. Their eyes followed him as he made his way to a small boat by the shore. He climbed aboard and sat down, the vessel gently rocking beneath him. The multitude, carried by their desire for wisdom, gathered along the sandy beach, their feet sinking into the warm grains.

From his seat in the boat, Jesus looked out at the sea of faces stretching along the shore. He began to weave a story, his words like a soft breeze that captured their attention. “Imagine a farmer,” he said, casting seeds with a practiced hand. The crowd could almost see him, a solitary figure sowing his fields with hope for a bountiful harvest.

Some seeds, he explained, fell by the side of the path, where the soil was hard and unyielding. Birds, sharp-eyed and opportunistic, swooped down and devoured the seeds before they had a chance to take root. Others landed on rocky ground, where the earth was thin and deceptive. The seeds sprouted quickly, but the sun scorched them, and without deep roots, they withered and died. **"And some fell among thorns,"** Jesus continued, his voice steady and clear, **"and the thorns sprung up, and choked them."**

Even as he spoke, the crowd could almost feel the scratch of thorns and the oppressive heat of the sun. But then, Jesus described the seeds that found good soil—rich and welcoming. They took root and flourished, producing a harvest that far exceeded expectations. **"Some an hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty,"** he shared, painting a picture of abundance and growth.

As Jesus finished the parable, a contemplative silence fell over the crowd, broken only by the gentle lapping of waves against the boat. Then, he added a mysterious invitation, **"Who hath ears to hear, let him hear."** His words lingered in the air, leaving the crowd pondering their deeper meaning.

Later, away from the crowd, the disciples approached Jesus with a question that had been weighing on their minds. “Why do you speak to them in parables?” they asked, seeking to understand the purpose behind his stories. Jesus explained that the parables were like keys to the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven, given to those ready to unlock their truths.

He spoke of how some people see and hear yet fail to understand, their hearts hardened like the paths by the wayside. But for the disciples, who were eager and open, their eyes and ears were blessed, able to perceive what others could not. The stories, simple yet profound, were meant to reveal truths to those willing to listen and understand deeply. As the disciples absorbed his words, the sea continued its rhythmic dance, echoing the timeless resonance of Jesus’ teachings.

stories.title: The Kingdom Parables
stories.keyVerse: "That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying, I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things which have been kept secret from the foundation of the world."
stories.text:
Another parable put he forth unto them, saying,
The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and sowed in his field:
Which indeed is the least of all seeds: but when it is grown, it is the greatest among herbs, and becometh a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in the branches thereof.Another parable spake he unto them;
The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven, which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened.
All these things spake Jesus unto the multitude in parables; and without a parable spake he not unto them:
That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying, I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things which have been kept secret from the foundation of the world.
Then Jesus sent the multitude away, and went into the house: and his disciples came unto him, saying, Declare unto us the parable of the tares of the field.
He answered and said unto them,
He that soweth the good seed is the Son of man;
The field is the world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom; but the tares are the children of the wicked
one;
The enemy that sowed them is the devil; the harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels.
As therefore the tares are gathered and burned in the fire; so shall it be in the end of this world.
The Son of man shall send forth his angels, and they shall gather out of his kingdom all things that offend, and them which do iniquity;
And shall cast them into a furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth.
Then shall the righteous shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father. Who hath ears to hear, let him hear.          Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field.          Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls:
Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it.          Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a net, that was cast into the sea, and gathered of every kind:
Which, when it was full, they drew to shore, and sat down, and gathered the good into vessels, but cast the bad away.
So shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just,
And shall cast them into the furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth.
Jesus saith unto them,
Have ye understood all these things?
They say unto him, Yea, Lord.
Then said he unto them,
Therefore every scribe
which is
instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man
that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure
things new and old.And it came to pass,
that when Jesus had finished these parables, he departed thence.
And when he was come into his own country, he taught them in their synagogue, insomuch that they were astonished, and said, Whence hath this
man this wisdom, and
these mighty works?
Is not this the carpenter’s son? is not his mother called Mary? and his brethren, James, and Joses, and Simon, and Judas?
And his sisters, are they not all with us? Whence then hath this
man all these things?
And they were offended in him. But Jesus said unto them, A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country, and in his own house.
And he did not many mighty works there because of their unbelief.
stories.retelling:
The sun hung low in the sky, casting a golden glow over the crowd gathered on the hillside. They had come from near and far, drawn by the whispers of a teacher who spoke in parables—stories wrapped in mystery, yet rich with meaning. Jesus stood before them, his eyes scanning the multitude, ready to share truths hidden since the world began.

He began with the tale of a mustard seed, tiny and unassuming, planted by a farmer in his field. With time, it grew beyond expectation, becoming a tree where birds nested among its branches. The crowd murmured, imagining the surprising transformation from the smallest of seeds to a towering tree. 

Next, Jesus spoke of a woman working dough. As she mixed in a bit of yeast, it slowly spread, permeating the entire batch. The image of the yeast, unseen yet powerful, lingered in the minds of his listeners, hinting at the subtle growth of the Kingdom of Heaven.

After sharing these parables with the crowd, Jesus sent them away, retreating to a house with his disciples. Curious and eager for understanding, they approached him, seeking clarity about the tale of weeds among wheat. **“Declare unto us the parable of the tares of the field,”** one disciple requested.

Jesus explained that the good seed represented the children of the kingdom, while the weeds were the offspring of evil. The enemy, the devil, had sowed these weeds, and at the end of the age, angels would gather and separate them. **“The harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels,”** he said, his voice carrying the weight of the revelation. The righteous would shine like the sun in their Father's kingdom—an image both hopeful and solemn.

The room fell silent, each disciple absorbing the gravity of Jesus' words. Then, Jesus spoke of treasure hidden in a field, found by a man who sold everything he owned to buy it. He likened the kingdom to a merchant seeking fine pearls, who, upon finding one of great value, sold all he had to acquire it. The parables painted vivid pictures of sacrifice and the incomparable worth of the kingdom.

Lastly, he described a net cast into the sea, gathering fish of all kinds. Once the net was full, fishermen sorted the good from the bad, just as angels would separate the righteous from the wicked at the world's end.

“Have you understood all these things?” Jesus asked, breaking the contemplative silence. His disciples nodded, acknowledging their newfound insight.

When Jesus returned to his hometown, he spoke in the synagogue. The townspeople marveled at his wisdom, yet questioned his origins. **“Is not this the carpenter’s son?”** they asked, their skepticism clouding their acceptance. In their doubt, they missed the depth of truth before them. Jesus, undeterred, remarked, **“A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country, and in his own house.”** And there, limited by their unbelief, he performed few miracles.

stories.title: The Gerasene Demoniac
stories.keyVerse: "And they come to Jesus, and see him that was possessed with the devil, and had the legion, sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid."
stories.text:
And the same day, when the even was come, he saith unto them,
Let us pass over unto the other side.
And when they had sent away the multitude, they took him even as he was in the ship. And there were also with him other little ships.
And there arose a great storm of wind, and the waves beat into the ship, so that it was now full.
And he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow: and they awake him, and say unto him, Master, carest thou not that we perish?
And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea,
Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.
And he said unto them,
Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith?
And they feared exceedingly, and said one to another, What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?
And they came over unto the other side of the sea, into the country of the Gadarenes.
And when he was come out of the ship, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit,
Who had
his dwelling among the tombs; and no man could bind him, no, not with chains:
Because that he had been often bound with fetters and chains, and the chains had been plucked asunder by him, and the fetters broken in pieces: neither could any
man tame him.
And always, night and day, he was in the mountains, and in the tombs, crying, and cutting himself with stones.
But when he saw Jesus afar off, he ran and worshipped him,
And cried with a loud voice, and said, What have I to do with thee, Jesus,
thou Son of the most high God? I adjure thee by God, that thou torment me not.
For he said unto him,
Come out of the man,
thou unclean spirit.
And he asked him,
What
is thy name? And he answered, saying, My name
is Legion: for we are many.
And he besought him much that he would not send them away out of the country.
Now there was there nigh unto the mountains a great herd of swine feeding.
And all the devils besought him, saying, Send us into the swine, that we may enter into them.
And forthwith Jesus gave them leave. And the unclean spirits went out, and entered into the swine: and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea, (they were about two thousand;) and were choked in the sea.
And they that fed the swine fled, and told
it in the city, and in the country. And they went out to see what it was that was done.
And they come to Jesus, and see him that was possessed with the devil, and had the legion, sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid.
And they that saw
it told them how it befell to him that was possessed with the devil, and
also concerning the swine.
And they began to pray him to depart out of their coasts.
And when he was come into the ship, he that had been possessed with the devil prayed him that he might be with him.
Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him,
Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee.
And he departed, and began to publish in Decapolis how great things Jesus had done for him: and all
men did marvel.
stories.retelling:
As twilight descended, Jesus and his disciples set sail across the lake. The air was calm at first, but soon, dark clouds gathered and a fierce wind whipped the water into a frenzy. Waves crashed violently over the sides of the boat, filling it with water. Amidst the chaos, Jesus lay asleep on a cushion in the stern. The disciples, their faces pale with fear, shook him awake. **“Master, carest thou not that we perish?”** one of them cried out, desperation etched in his voice.

Awakening, Jesus stood and faced the tumult. With a commanding voice, he spoke to the elements, **“Peace, be still.”** Instantly, the wind died down, and the waves settled into a serene calm. The sudden tranquility was almost as unsettling as the storm had been. The disciples exchanged glances, awe-struck and whispering, **“What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”**

Once they reached the opposite shore, in the country of the Gadarenes, a new challenge awaited. As Jesus stepped ashore, a man emerged from the tombs, his eyes wild and tormented. This man, possessed by a legion of unclean spirits, lived among the graves. His body bore scars from the stones he used to cut himself, and no chains had ever held him for long. Seeing Jesus, he ran and fell before him, shouting, **“What have I to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of the most high God?”**

Jesus commanded the unclean spirit to leave the man. **“What is thy name?”** he asked, and the voice that answered was many, **“My name is Legion, for we are many.”** The spirits begged not to be sent away but instead asked to enter a nearby herd of pigs. Jesus permitted them, and as the spirits departed the man, the pigs—about two thousand in number—rushed headlong down the steep bank into the sea, drowning in the depths.

Witnesses of this event, the swineherds fled into the town, telling all they had seen. Soon, a crowd gathered by the shore. They found the once-tormented man sitting peacefully at Jesus' feet, clothed and in his right mind. The transformation was so profound that fear gripped the onlookers. They pleaded with Jesus to leave their region, unable to comprehend the power they had witnessed.

As Jesus prepared to depart, the man who had been freed begged to go with him. But Jesus shook his head, saying, **“Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee.”** The man did as he was told, spreading the news throughout Decapolis. And those who heard his story marveled at the wonders that had unfolded on their shores.

stories.title: The Death of John the Baptist
stories.keyVerse: "And the king was sorry: nevertheless for the oath’s sake, and them which sat with him at meat, he commanded it to be given her."
stories.text:
At that time Herod the tetrarch heard of the fame of Jesus,
And said unto his servants, This is John the Baptist; he is risen from the dead; and therefore mighty works do shew forth themselves in him.
For Herod had laid hold on John, and bound him, and put
him
in prison for Herodias’ sake, his brother Philip’s wife.
For John said unto him, It is not lawful for thee to have her.
And when he would have put him to death, he feared the multitude, because they counted him as a prophet.
But when Herod’s birthday was kept, the daughter of Herodias danced before them, and pleased Herod.
Whereupon he promised with an oath to give her whatsoever she would ask.
And she, being before instructed of her mother, said, Give me here John Baptist’s head in a charger.
And the king was sorry: nevertheless for the oath’s sake, and them which sat with him at meat, he commanded
it to be given
her.
And he sent, and beheaded John in the prison.
And his head was brought in a charger, and given to the damsel: and she brought
it to her mother.
And his disciples came, and took up the body, and buried it, and went and told Jesus.
stories.retelling:
In the dimly lit halls of Herod's palace, shadows flickered as news of a man called Jesus stirred whispers and concern. Herod Antipas, the tetrarch, sat brooding in his chamber. He had heard of Jesus’ growing fame and miraculous deeds, and a chill ran down his spine as he said to his servants, **“This is John the Baptist; he is risen from the dead; and therefore mighty works do shew forth themselves in him.”** The name John the Baptist was a haunting echo in Herod’s mind, one that carried the weight of guilt and fear.

Not long ago, Herod had seized John, shackling him in the cold stone confines of a prison. It was a move spurred by Herodias, his wife, who had once been married to Herod’s brother, Philip. John had openly condemned their union, declaring, **“It is not lawful for thee to have her.”** Herodias seethed with anger, but Herod hesitated to harm John, fearing the people's reverence for him as a prophet.

The palace was abuzz with preparations for Herod's birthday feast, an affair of opulence and indulgence. Nobles and dignitaries gathered, their laughter and chatter rising above the strains of music. Amidst the revelry, Salome, the daughter of Herodias, took to the center, her dance a mesmerizing display of grace and allure. Herod watched, captivated, and when she finished, he rose, his voice echoing in the hall as he made a grand promise—an oath to grant her any wish.

Salome, with a glint of mischief and manipulation in her eyes, approached her mother. Herodias, quick with her own dark intentions, instructed her daughter with a chilling request. With a poised and deliberate step, Salome returned to Herod, her voice unwavering as she asked for the head of John the Baptist on a platter.

The room fell silent, the air thick with anticipation. Herod's heart sank. He was trapped by his own words, the oath he had made in a moment of folly. His mind raced, the weight of the guests' expectant gazes heavy upon him. **“And the king was sorry: nevertheless for the oath’s sake, and them which sat with him at meat, he commanded it to be given her.”** 

The order was swift, his decision final. In the dim light of the prison, the executioner carried out the grim task. Soon after, John’s severed head was presented to Salome on a gleaming platter. She carried it to her mother, Herodias, who accepted it with a twisted satisfaction.

Meanwhile, John's disciples, stricken with grief, came to collect his body. They bore it away quietly, laying it to rest with reverence. With heavy hearts, they went to inform Jesus, carrying with them the weight of loss and the knowledge of a life unjustly taken.

stories.title: Feeding the Five Thousand
stories.keyVerse: "But Jesus said unto them, They need not depart; give ye them to eat."
stories.text:
When Jesus heard
of it, he departed thence by ship into a desert place apart: and when the people had heard
thereof, they followed him on foot out of the cities.
And Jesus went forth, and saw a great multitude, and was moved with compassion toward them, and he healed their sick.
And when it was evening, his disciples came to him, saying, This is a desert place, and the time is now past; send the multitude away, that they may go into the villages, and buy themselves victuals.
But Jesus said unto them,
They need not depart; give ye them to eat.
And they say unto him, We have here but five loaves, and two fishes.
He said,
Bring them hither to me.
And he commanded the multitude to sit down on the grass, and took the five loaves, and the two fishes, and looking up to heaven, he blessed, and brake, and gave the loaves to
his disciples, and the disciples to the multitude.
And they did all eat, and were filled: and they took up of the fragments that remained twelve baskets full.
And they that had eaten were about five thousand men, beside women and children.
stories.retelling:
As the sun began its descent, casting a warm, golden hue over the barren landscape, Jesus sought a moment of solitude. He had retreated by boat to a remote, desert-like place, hoping for a brief escape from the throngs of people. However, news of his whereabouts spread like wildfire, and soon, a massive crowd had gathered, their figures dotting the horizon as they approached on foot from nearby cities.

Stepping ashore, Jesus was met with a sea of expectant faces. Despite his own need for rest, compassion swelled within him. He moved among them, healing the sick, his hands bringing solace and relief to the ailing.

As the day wore on and shadows grew long, the disciples approached, concern etched on their faces. They surveyed the great multitude and the desolate landscape. **"This is a desert place,"** they said, worry seeping into their voices. **"The time is now past; send the multitude away, that they may go into the villages, and buy themselves victuals."**

But Jesus, with a calm certainty, replied, **"They need not depart; give ye them to eat."** The disciples exchanged puzzled glances, their minds grappling with the impossibility of the command. They gathered what little provisions they had—merely five loaves and two small fish—and presented them to Jesus, their expressions a mix of doubt and resignation. **"We have here but five loaves, and two fishes,"** they explained.

Undeterred, Jesus instructed, **"Bring them hither to me."** The crowd, sensing something extraordinary was about to unfold, settled down on the grass, each person finding a comfortable spot amidst the throng. Silence fell over the multitude as Jesus took the meager offering in his hands. He gazed skyward, his lips moving in prayer, blessing the food with a reverence that seemed to fuse heaven and earth.

Then, with an air of serene authority, he broke the bread and fish, handing pieces to his disciples. They, in turn, distributed them among the people. The crowd watched, a mix of wonder and disbelief, as the food kept coming, seemingly multiplying in their very hands.

The initial apprehension transformed into joy and satisfaction as everyone ate their fill. The once-anxious disciples moved among the satisfied masses, gathering the leftovers. To their astonishment, they collected twelve baskets full of fragments, more than what they had begun with.

As dusk cloaked the land in its cool embrace, the crowd of five thousand men, along with countless women and children, began to disperse, their hearts full and their spirits lifted. Jesus had not only met their physical hunger but had also touched them with a glimpse of the divine. The miracle of abundance lingered in the air, a testament to the boundless compassion and power of the man they followed.

stories.title: Jesus Walks on Water
stories.keyVerse: "And he said, Come. And when Peter was come down out of the ship, he walked on the water, to go to Jesus."
stories.text:
And straightway Jesus constrained his disciples to get into a ship, and to go before him unto the other side, while he sent the multitudes away.
And when he had sent the multitudes away, he went up into a mountain apart to pray: and when the evening was come, he was there alone.
But the ship was now in the midst of the sea, tossed with waves: for the wind was contrary.
And in the fourth watch of the night Jesus went unto them, walking on the sea.
And when the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were troubled, saying, It is a spirit; and they cried out for fear.
But straightway Jesus spake unto them, saying,
Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.
And Peter answered him and said, Lord, if it be thou, bid me come unto thee on the water.
And he said,
Come. And when Peter was come down out of the ship, he walked on the water, to go to Jesus.
But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me.
And immediately Jesus stretched forth
his hand, and caught him, and said unto him,
O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?
And when they were come into the ship, the wind ceased.
Then they that were in the ship came and worshipped him, saying, Of a truth thou art the Son of God.
And when they were gone over, they came into the land of Gennesaret.
And when the men of that place had knowledge of him, they sent out into all that country round about, and brought unto him all that were diseased;
And besought him that they might only touch the hem of his garment: and as many as touched were made perfectly whole.
stories.retelling:
As twilight deepened into night, the sea churned with restless energy, waves rising and crashing against the sides of a lone boat. The disciples, weary and tense, struggled to keep their vessel steady in the turbulent waters. They had set out earlier, at Jesus' insistence, to cross to the other side while he remained behind to dismiss the crowd and find solitude on the mountainside for prayer.

Now, in the darkest hours before dawn, the wind howled fiercely, and the boat rocked violently beneath them. Exhausted, the men fought the elements, their strained eyes scanning the horizon for any sign of relief. Suddenly, amidst the chaos of wind and sea, they spotted a figure approaching, treading the roiling waters with an impossible grace.

Fear gripped them. "It's a ghost!" someone shouted, as anxiety rippled through the group, their voices rising in a mix of disbelief and terror. But then, cutting through the wind, came a voice, calm and clear. **"Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid."**

Peter, heart pounding, leaned over the edge of the boat, compelled by a mix of faith and wonder. "Lord, if it is really you," he called out into the darkness, "command me to come to you on the water."

Jesus' reply was simple and commanding. **"Come."** The word hung in the air, a lifeline thrown across the tumultuous sea. Peter, steeling himself with a deep breath, stepped over the side. The water, impossibly, held him. He took another step, then another, his eyes fixed on Jesus. For a moment, all was calm within him, the storm around him forgotten.

But then the wind gusted, a fierce reminder of the chaos surrounding him. Doubt crept in, and Peter faltered, his focus broken. Terror surged as he felt himself sinking into the cold embrace of the sea. Desperate, he cried out, **"Lord, save me!"**

Without hesitation, Jesus reached out, his hand strong and sure, pulling Peter from the abyss. Standing together on the water, Jesus looked at Peter, his voice gentle yet firm. **"O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?"** His words, though a rebuke, were a reminder of the faith that had brought Peter this far.

Together, they climbed into the boat, and as if in awe of the miracle, the winds ceased their howling, the sea calming to a gentle ripple under the moonlit sky. The disciples, breathless and overwhelmed, fell silent, their hearts moved by the man who had walked upon the waves. In reverence, they turned to Jesus, their voices united in awe and belief, **"Of a truth thou art the Son of God."**

With dawn breaking, they reached the shores of Gennesaret, where recognition spread quickly among the people. Word of Jesus' presence drew crowds, the sick and suffering eager for healing. They reached out in faith, touching the hem of his garment, and as they did, each was made whole.

stories.title: The Bread of Life
stories.keyVerse: And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
stories.text:
The day following, when the people which stood on the other side of the sea saw that there was none other boat there, save that one whereinto his disciples were entered, and that Jesus went not with his disciples into the boat, but
that his disciples were gone away alone;
(Howbeit there came other boats from Tiberias nigh unto the place where they did eat bread, after that the Lord had given thanks:)
When the people therefore saw that Jesus was not there, neither his disciples, they also took shipping, and came to Capernaum, seeking for Jesus.
And when they had found him on the other side of the sea, they said unto him, Rabbi, when camest thou hither?
Jesus answered them and said,
Verily, verily, I say unto you, Ye seek me, not because ye saw the miracles, but because ye did eat of the loaves, and were filled.
Labour not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life, which the Son of man shall give unto you: for him hath God the Father sealed.
Then said they unto him, What shall we do, that we might work the works of God?
Jesus answered and said unto them,
This is the work of God, that ye believe on him whom he hath sent.
They said therefore unto him, What sign shewest thou then, that we may see, and believe thee? what dost thou work?
Our fathers did eat manna in the desert; as it is written, He gave them bread from heaven to eat.
Then Jesus said unto them,
Verily, verily, I say unto you, Moses gave you not that bread from heaven; but my Father giveth you the true bread from heaven.
For the bread of God is he which cometh down from heaven, and giveth life unto the world.
Then said they unto him, Lord, evermore give us this bread.
And Jesus said unto them,
I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
But I said unto you, That ye also have seen me, and believe not.
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
For I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me.
And this is the Father’s will which hath sent me, that of all which he hath given me I should lose nothing, but should raise it up again at the last day.
And this is the will of him that sent me, that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life: and I will raise him up at the last day.
The Jews then murmured at him, because he said,
I am the bread which came down from heaven.
And they said, Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? how is it then that he saith,
I came down from heaven?
Jesus therefore answered and said unto them,
Murmur not among yourselves.
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
It is written in the prophets, And they shall be all taught of God. Every man therefore that hath heard, and hath learned of the Father, cometh unto me.
Not that any man hath seen the Father, save he which is of God, he hath seen the Father.
Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me hath everlasting life.
I am that bread of life.
Your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead.
This is the bread which cometh down from heaven, that a man may eat thereof, and not die.
I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world.
The Jews therefore strove among themselves, saying, How can this man give us
his flesh to eat?
Then Jesus said unto them,
Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you.
Whoso eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, hath eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day.
For my flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed.
He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him.
As the living Father hath sent me, and I live by the Father: so he that eateth me, even he shall live by me.
This is that bread which came down from heaven: not as your fathers did eat manna, and are dead: he that eateth of this bread shall live for ever.
These things said he in the synagogue, as he taught in Capernaum.
Many therefore of his disciples, when they had heard
this,
said, This is an hard saying; who can hear it?
When Jesus knew in himself that his disciples murmured at it, he said unto them,
Doth this offend you?
What and if ye shall see the Son of man ascend up where he was before?
It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you,
they are spirit, and
they are life.
But there are some of you that believe not. For Jesus knew from the beginning who they were that believed not, and who should betray him.
And he said,
Therefore said I unto you, that no man can come unto me, except it were given unto him of my Father.From that
time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him.
Then said Jesus unto the twelve,
Will ye also go away?
Then Simon Peter answered him, Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life.
And we believe and are sure that thou art that Christ, the Son of the living God.
Jesus answered them,
Have not I chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?
He spake of Judas Iscariot
the son of Simon: for he it was that should betray him, being one of the twelve.
stories.retelling:
The sun rose over the Sea of Galilee, casting a golden glow on the restless crowd gathered on the far shore. They had witnessed a miracle—bread multiplied to feed thousands—and now their eyes sought the one who had performed it. They knew the disciples had left in the only boat, yet Jesus had not been with them. How had he reached the other side? Confused but determined, they clambered into boats from Tiberias, drawn to Capernaum by an insatiable curiosity and hunger for more than just food.

Upon finding Jesus, their questions tumbled out, urgent and inquisitive. “Rabbi, when did you come here?” they asked, puzzled by his presence. Jesus looked at them knowingly, recognizing their true intentions. He spoke with a voice that carried the weight of truth, **“Ye seek me, not because ye saw the miracles, but because ye did eat of the loaves, and were filled.”** His words pierced through the crowd's superficial desires, beckoning them to seek sustenance of a different kind.

He urged them to pursue not the perishable, but the eternal. The crowd, eager to grasp this new teaching, asked, “What must we do to perform the works of God?” Jesus answered with a simple yet profound directive, **“This is the work of God, that ye believe on him whom he hath sent.”** Yet they demanded a sign, invoking the manna their ancestors received in the wilderness.

Jesus’ response was striking, filled with a promise that echoed beyond the ages. **“I am the bread of life,”** he declared, his words resonating through the synagogue like a bell. He offered a sustenance that transcended earthly needs, a spiritual nourishment promising eternal life. Those who believed would never hunger or thirst again.

The crowd murmured, struggling to comprehend. Wasn’t this Jesus, the carpenter’s son? How could he claim such divine origin? Yet Jesus stood firm, elucidating the mystery of faith, the unseen hand of the Father drawing people to him. As he spoke of eating his flesh and drinking his blood, many faltered, unable to digest his challenging words.

A tense silence fell as disciples turned away, their faith shaken. Jesus addressed the twelve, a gentle yet probing inquiry in his eyes, **“Will ye also go away?”** Simon Peter, ever the voice of steadfast devotion, replied with conviction, **“Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life.”**

Amidst the dwindling crowd, one presence remained ominous and silent—Judas, the betrayer, standing among the loyal. Jesus acknowledged the shadow among them, aware of his looming betrayal. Yet even this moment was woven into the divine tapestry, a step along the path toward ultimate redemption.

The scene closed with echoes of Peter’s confession and the lingering question of faith. In the gentle ripple of the sea and the whispering winds, the promise of the bread of life hovered, inviting all who had ears to hear and hearts to believe.

stories.title: What Defiles, The Canaanite Woman
stories.keyVerse: "Then Jesus answered and said unto her, O woman, great is thy faith: be it unto thee even as thou wilt. And her daughter was made whole from that very hour."
stories.text:
Then came to Jesus scribes and Pharisees, which were of Jerusalem, saying,
Why do thy disciples transgress the tradition of the elders? for they wash not their hands when they eat bread.
But he answered and said unto them,
Why do ye also transgress the commandment of God by your tradition?
For God commanded, saying, Honour thy father and mother: and, He that curseth father or mother, let him die the death.
But ye say, Whosoever shall say to
his father or
his mother,
It is a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me;
And honour not his father or his mother,
he shall be free.
Thus have ye made the commandment of God of none effect by your tradition.
Ye hypocrites, well did Esaias prophesy of you, saying,
This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth, and honoureth me with
their lips; but their heart is far from me.
But in vain they do worship me, teaching
for doctrines the commandments of men.And he called the multitude, and said unto them,
Hear, and understand:
Not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man; but that which cometh out of the mouth, this defileth a man.
Then came his disciples, and said unto him, Knowest thou that the Pharisees were offended, after they heard this saying?
But he answered and said,
Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up.
Let them alone: they be blind leaders of the blind. And if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch.
Then answered Peter and said unto him, Declare unto us this parable.
And Jesus said,
Are ye also yet without understanding?
Do not ye yet understand, that whatsoever entereth in at the mouth goeth into the belly, and is cast out into the draught?
But those things which proceed out of the mouth come forth from the heart; and they defile the man.
For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies:
These are
