Why was not this ointment sold for three hundred pence, and given to the poor?
This he said, not that he cared for the poor; but because he was a thief, and had the bag, and bare what was put therein.
Then said Jesus,
Let her alone: against the day of my burying hath she kept this.
For the poor always ye have with you; but me ye have not always.
Much people of the Jews therefore knew that he was there: and they came not for Jesus’ sake only, but that they might see Lazarus also, whom he had raised from the dead.
But the chief priests consulted that they might put Lazarus also to death;
Because that by reason of him many of the Jews went away, and believed on Jesus.
stories.retelling:
In the hushed, dim light of a council room, the tension was palpable. The chief priests and Pharisees gathered urgently, their faces etched with concern and fear. News had spread rapidly—Jesus had performed yet another miraculous sign, this time raising Lazarus from the dead. Many who witnessed this were now fervent believers, their faith in Jesus growing stronger with each miracle.  

The leaders whispered anxiously among themselves. "What are we doing?" one voice cut through. "If we let him continue like this, everyone will believe in him, and then the Romans will come and strip us of our power and destroy our nation." Worry shadowed their eyes as they faced the possibility of losing everything they held dear.  

Caiaphas, the high priest for that year, stood with an air of authority. "Ye know nothing at all," he said, his voice steady and commanding. **"Nor consider that it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not."** His words carried a chilling finality, a prophecy that sealed their intentions. From that moment, they conspired to put Jesus to death.  

Meanwhile, Jesus, aware of the growing threat, withdrew to a remote area near the wilderness, to the quiet town of Ephraim. There, he found refuge with his disciples, away from the looming danger.  

As the Passover approached, Jerusalem buzzed with anticipation. Pilgrims filled the city, cleansing themselves in preparation for the holy feast. Whispers circulated in the temple courtyards—would Jesus dare to come to the festival? The chief priests and Pharisees had decreed that anyone who knew of his whereabouts must report it, so they could seize him.  

Six days before Passover, Jesus returned to Bethany, to the home of Lazarus, the very man he had brought back from the grave. That evening, a supper was prepared in his honor. Martha busied herself serving, while Lazarus reclined at the table, alive and well.  

Mary entered, carrying a small jar of precious ointment. As she knelt, she gently poured the fragrant oil over Jesus' feet, filling the room with its rich aroma. With tender devotion, she wiped his feet with her hair.  

Judas Iscariot, one of the disciples, watched with a calculating eye. "Why was not this ointment sold for three hundred pence, and given to the poor?" he questioned, his voice tinged with feigned concern. In truth, his motives were far from noble; he was known to pilfer from their collective funds.  

Jesus responded, his voice gentle yet firm. **"Let her alone: against the day of my burying hath she kept this. For the poor always ye have with you; but me ye have not always."**  

The fragrance lingered, a testament to Mary's act of love and foreshadowing the sorrow to come. Meanwhile, the plot against Jesus grew ever more sinister, and now even Lazarus was in danger, for his resurrection had led many to believe in Jesus. The chief priests knew that to extinguish this light, they might need to snuff out its reflections too.

stories.title: The Triumphal Entry
stories.keyVerse: "And the multitudes that went before, and that followed, cried, saying, Hosanna to the Son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest."
stories.text:
And when they drew nigh unto Jerusalem, and were come to Bethphage, unto the mount of Olives, then sent Jesus two disciples,
Saying unto them,
Go into the village over against you, and straightway ye shall find an ass tied, and a colt with her: loose
them,
and bring
them unto me.
And if any
man say ought unto you, ye shall say, The Lord hath need of them; and straightway he will send them.
All this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying,
Tell ye the daughter of Sion, Behold, thy King cometh unto thee, meek, and sitting upon an ass, and a colt the foal of an ass.
And the disciples went, and did as Jesus commanded them,
And brought the ass, and the colt, and put on them their clothes, and they set
him thereon.
And a very great multitude spread their garments in the way; others cut down branches from the trees, and strawed
them in the way.
And the multitudes that went before, and that followed, cried, saying, Hosanna to the Son of David: Blessed
is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest.
And when he was come into Jerusalem, all the city was moved, saying, Who is this?
And the multitude said, This is Jesus the prophet of Nazareth of Galilee.
And Jesus went into the temple of God, and cast out all them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves,
And said unto them,
It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves.
And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple; and he healed them.
And when the chief priests and scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children crying in the temple, and saying, Hosanna to the Son of David; they were sore displeased,
And said unto him, Hearest thou what these say? And Jesus saith unto them,
Yea; have ye never read, Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings thou hast perfected praise?And he left them, and went out of the city into Bethany; and he lodged there.
stories.retelling:
As the sun rose over the Mount of Olives, the air was filled with anticipation. Jesus and his disciples approached the outskirts of Jerusalem, reaching the village of Bethphage. The landscape was serene yet buzzing with a sense of something monumental about to unfold. Jesus paused, turning to two of his disciples with a clear instruction. They were to go into the nearby village where they would find a donkey and her colt tied up. **“Loose them, and bring them unto me,”** he instructed with purpose. **“If any man say ought unto you, ye shall say, The Lord hath need of them.”** 

Following his instructions, the disciples ventured into the village. The air was still, with only the faint sounds of their footsteps and the occasional rustle of leaves. As Jesus had said, they found the animals tied just ahead. Untying them, they sensed a sacredness in their mission, as if fulfilling an age-old prophecy.

With the donkey and colt brought to him, Jesus sat astride them, and a great crowd gathered around. The atmosphere shifted as people began laying their garments and freshly cut branches on the dusty path. It was a tapestry of vibrant colors and green leaves, creating a royal carpet for the humble king. 

The crowd swelled, their voices rising in unison. **“Hosanna to the Son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest,”** they shouted, each word echoing off the walls of the city. The air was electric with enthusiasm, and the people were caught up in the moment, their cheers reverberating like a tidal wave.

As Jesus entered Jerusalem, the city was alive with whispers and questions. **“Who is this?”** curious onlookers asked, their faces a mix of intrigue and skepticism. The answer came with conviction from those who recognized him: **“This is Jesus the prophet of Nazareth of Galilee.”**

Once inside the temple, the atmosphere changed. Jesus, filled with righteous anger, witnessed the merchants and money changers who had turned this sacred space into a marketplace. With a forceful resolve, he overturned the tables and drove them out, declaring, **“It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves.”**

In the aftermath, the temple became a place of healing and hope. The blind and the lame approached him, and with gentle hands, he restored them. Children’s voices rang out, echoing the earlier cries of “Hosanna,” much to the chagrin of the chief priests and scribes. They questioned his acceptance of such praises, to which Jesus responded, calm and assured, **“Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings thou hast perfected praise.”**

As evening approached, Jesus departed the city, leaving behind a day that would be remembered as a turning point. He retreated to the quiet refuge of Bethany, the city still vibrating with the echoes of his presence.

stories.title: The Fig Tree and Authority Questioned
stories.keyVerse: "Did ye never read in the scriptures, The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner: this is the Lord’s doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes?"
stories.text:
Now in the morning as he returned into the city, he hungered.
And when he saw a fig tree in the way, he came to it, and found nothing thereon, but leaves only, and said unto it,
Let no fruit grow on thee henceforward for ever. And presently the fig tree withered away.
And when the disciples saw
it, they marvelled, saying, How soon is the fig tree withered away!
Jesus answered and said unto them,
Verily I say unto you, If ye have faith, and doubt not, ye shall not only do this
which is done to the fig tree, but also if ye shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea; it shall be done.
And all things, whatsoever ye shall ask in prayer, believing, ye shall receive.And when he was come into the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came unto him as he was teaching, and said, By what authority doest thou these things? and who gave thee this authority?
And Jesus answered and said unto them,
I also will ask you one thing, which if ye tell me, I in like wise will tell you by what authority I do these things.
The baptism of John, whence was it? from heaven, or of men? And they reasoned with themselves, saying, If we shall say, From heaven; he will say unto us, Why did ye not then believe him?
But if we shall say, Of men; we fear the people; for all hold John as a prophet.
And they answered Jesus, and said, We cannot tell. And he said unto them,
Neither tell I you by what authority I do these things.          But what think ye? A
certain man had two sons; and he came to the first, and said, Son, go work to day in my vineyard.
He answered and said, I will not: but afterward he repented, and went.
And he came to the second, and said likewise. And he answered and said, I
go, sir: and went not.
Whether of them twain did the will of
his father?
They say unto him, The first. Jesus saith unto them,
Verily I say unto you, That the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you.
For John came unto you in the way of righteousness, and ye believed him not: but the publicans and the harlots believed him: and ye, when ye had seen
it, repented not afterward, that ye might believe him.
Hear another parable: There was a certain householder, which planted a vineyard, and hedged it round about, and digged a winepress in it, and built a tower, and let it out to husbandmen, and went into a far country:
And when the time of the fruit drew near, he sent his servants to the husbandmen, that they might receive the fruits of it.
And the husbandmen took his servants, and beat one, and killed another, and stoned another.
Again, he sent other servants more than the first: and they did unto them likewise.
But last of all he sent unto them his son, saying, They will reverence my son.
But when the husbandmen saw the son, they said among themselves, This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance.
And they caught him, and cast
him out of the vineyard, and slew
him.When the lord therefore of the vineyard cometh, what will he do unto those husbandmen?
They say unto him, He will miserably destroy those wicked men, and will let out
his vineyard unto other husbandmen, which shall render him the fruits in their seasons.
Jesus saith unto them,
Did ye never read in the scriptures, The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner: this is the Lord’s doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes?
Therefore say I unto you, The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof.
And whosoever shall fall on this stone shall be broken: but on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder.
And when the chief priests and Pharisees had heard his parables, they perceived that he spake of them.
But when they sought to lay hands on him, they feared the multitude, because they took him for a prophet.
stories.retelling:
The sun had just begun its ascent, painting the morning sky in soft hues as Jesus and his disciples made their way back into the city. Hunger gnawed at him, and as they traveled along the dusty road, a fig tree caught Jesus' eye. Hopeful, he approached it, but his anticipation turned to disappointment as he found it barren, adorned only with leaves. In a voice that resonated with quiet authority, he declared, **"Let no fruit grow on thee henceforward for ever."** The tree immediately withered, its leaves crumbling into brittle shards. The disciples stood in awe, whispering among themselves, marveling at how swiftly the tree had succumbed.

In the temple, a different kind of confrontation awaited. Jesus was teaching, his words drawing people in when the chief priests and elders approached, their faces masked with skepticism. They demanded to know by what authority he acted. In response, Jesus posed a question about John’s baptism, knowing it would leave them tangled in their own reasoning. **"I also will ask you one thing,"** he replied, turning the tables. Caught between the fear of the people's reverence for John and their own disbelief, the priests were cornered into admitting ignorance. Jesus, unfazed, refused to reveal the source of his authority.

As the tension simmered, Jesus shared a parable. He spoke of a man with two sons, asking each to work in his vineyard. The first son initially refused but later went, while the second promised compliance but never followed through. The crowd murmured, recognizing the first son as the one who fulfilled his father’s wish. Jesus pointed out that tax collectors and prostitutes, those often scorned, were entering God’s Kingdom ahead of them because they believed, unlike the priests.

Jesus continued with another parable about a landowner who planted a vineyard and leased it to farmers. When harvest time came, servants were sent to collect the fruit, only to be met with violence. Finally, the landowner sent his son, thinking they would respect him. However, the farmers, blinded by greed, killed the son to seize his inheritance. Jesus asked what the landowner would do, and the answer was clear—justice would be served, and the vineyard entrusted to those who would honor the agreement.

Then, with piercing clarity, Jesus quoted the scriptures, **"Did ye never read in the scriptures, The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner: this is the Lord’s doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes?"** His words laid bare the truth, unsettling the priests and Pharisees, who realized he was speaking of them. Fearful of the crowd, yet unwilling to accept his authority, they seethed in silence, unable to act against the prophet revered by the people.

stories.title: The Wedding Banquet, Render to Caesar
stories.keyVerse: "Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s."
stories.text:
And Jesus answered and spake unto them again by parables, and said,
The kingdom of heaven is like unto a certain king, which made a marriage for his son,
And sent forth his servants to call them that were bidden to the wedding: and they would not come.
Again, he sent forth other servants, saying, Tell them which are bidden, Behold, I have prepared my dinner: my oxen and
my fatlings
are killed, and all things
are
ready: come unto the marriage.But they made light of
it, and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise:
And the remnant took his servants, and entreated
them
spitefully, and slew
them.But when the king heard
thereof, he was wroth: and he sent forth his armies, and destroyed those murderers, and burned up their city.
Then saith he to his servants, The wedding is ready, but they which were bidden were not worthy.
Go ye therefore into the highways, and as many as ye shall find, bid to the marriage.
So those servants went out into the highways, and gathered together all as many as they found, both bad and good: and the wedding was furnished with guests.          And when the king came in to see the guests, he saw there a man which had not on a wedding garment:
And he saith unto him, Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless.
Then said the king to the servants, Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast
him into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
For many are called, but few
are chosen.Then went the Pharisees, and took counsel how they might entangle him in
his talk.
And they sent out unto him their disciples with the Herodians, saying, Master, we know that thou art true, and teachest the way of God in truth, neither carest thou for any
man: for thou regardest not the person of men.
Tell us therefore, What thinkest thou? Is it lawful to give tribute unto Caesar, or not?
But Jesus perceived their wickedness, and said,
Why tempt ye me,
ye hypocrites?
Shew me the tribute money. And they brought unto him a penny.
And he saith unto them,
Whose
is this image and superscription?
They say unto him, Caesar’s. Then saith he unto them,
Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s.
When they had heard
these words, they marvelled, and left him, and went their way.
stories.retelling:
In a grand palace, a king prepared a splendid wedding feast for his beloved son. The aroma of roasted oxen and fattened cattle wafted through the halls, and the air buzzed with anticipation. The king sent his servants to invite the carefully selected guests, but they refused to come. Undeterred, the king sent more servants, insisting, **“Behold, I have prepared my dinner. My cattle and my fatlings are killed, and all things are ready: come unto the marriage.”** Yet, the guests scoffed at the invitation. They turned away, preoccupied with their farms and shops, while others seized the servants, mistreating them mercilessly.

The king, upon hearing this, was furious. In his wrath, he dispatched his armies, who swiftly avenged the mistreatment and destruction, leaving ruin in their wake. The king then turned to his loyal servants, his voice resolute. **“The wedding is ready, but they which were bidden were not worthy. Go ye therefore into the highways, and as many as ye shall find, bid to the marriage.”** The servants ventured far and wide, gathering all they encountered, both the good and the bad, until the feast was filled with a diverse crowd.

As the king surveyed the bustling hall, his eyes fell upon a man not dressed in a wedding garment. Approaching him, the king asked, **“Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment?”** The man stood speechless, unable to explain. The king commanded his servants to bind the man and cast him into the outer darkness, a place of sorrow and regret. The echoes of **“many are called, but few are chosen”** lingered in the air.

Meanwhile, the Pharisees and Herodians plotted, seeking to ensnare Jesus with a tricky question. They approached him, feigning respect, and asked about the legality of paying taxes to the Roman emperor, Caesar. Jesus, sensing their deceit, requested to see a coin. Holding it up, he asked, **“Whose is this image and superscription?”** They replied, “Caesar’s.” With a calm, piercing gaze, Jesus declared, **“Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s.”**

The onlookers were taken aback by his wisdom, unable to trap him with their cunning question. Awed by his profound response, they left him, their scheme thwarted, and whispers of his insight spreading like wildfire.

stories.title: The Greatest Commandment
stories.keyVerse: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind.”
stories.text:
The same day came to him the Sadducees, which say that there is no resurrection, and asked him,
Saying, Master, Moses said, If a man die, having no children, his brother shall marry his wife, and raise up seed unto his brother.
Now there were with us seven brethren: and the first, when he had married a wife, deceased, and, having no issue, left his wife unto his brother:
Likewise the second also, and the third, unto the seventh.
And last of all the woman died also.
Therefore in the resurrection whose wife shall she be of the seven? for they all had her.
Jesus answered and said unto them,
Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God.
For in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven.
But as touching the resurrection of the dead, have ye not read that which was spoken unto you by God, saying,
I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.
And when the multitude heard
this, they were astonished at his doctrine.
But when the Pharisees had heard that he had put the Sadducees to silence, they were gathered together.
Then one of them,
which was a lawyer, asked
him a question,
tempting him, and saying,
Master, which
is the great commandment in the law?
Jesus said unto him,
Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind.
This is the first and great commandment.
And the second
is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.
On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.
While the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them,
Saying, What think ye of Christ? whose son is he? They say unto him,
The Son of David.
He saith unto them,
How then doth David in spirit call him Lord, saying,
The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand, till I make thine enemies thy footstool?
If David then call him Lord, how is he his son?
And no man was able to answer him a word, neither durst any
man
from that day forth ask him any more
questions.
stories.retelling:
Under the blinding midday sun in the bustling courtyards of Jerusalem, the air buzzed with tension and anticipation. Jesus, surrounded by a diverse crowd of followers and skeptics, stood calmly as the Sadducees approached. Known for their denial of the resurrection, they sought to entrap him with a question steeped in the complexities of Mosaic Law.

“Teacher,” one began, his voice smooth and calculated, “Moses said if a man dies without children, his brother must marry the widow to preserve the family line. Imagine there are seven brothers. The first marries and dies childless, leaving his wife to the second brother. This continues until all seven brothers have married her, and finally, the woman herself dies. In the resurrection, whose wife will she be?”

The question hung in the air, a carefully crafted snare. But Jesus, unperturbed, met their challenge head-on. **“Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God,”** he replied, his voice resonating with authority. He explained that in the resurrection, human institutions like marriage would not bind them. Instead, they would be like angels, living in a divine realm beyond earthly ties.

The crowd murmured in awe as Jesus continued, invoking the words of God: **“I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.”** His point was clear—God is the God of the living, not the dead. The Sadducees, caught off guard by his profound understanding, fell silent, their trap dismantled.

Among the crowd, the Pharisees, always eager to challenge him, seized the moment to regroup. One of their number, a lawyer, stepped forward, his eyes gleaming with the prospect of a fresh test. “Teacher, which is the greatest commandment in the law?” he asked, testing the limits of Jesus' wisdom.

Without hesitation, Jesus spoke, his words cutting through the crowd like a beacon. **“Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind.”** He paused, allowing the gravity of the commandment to settle over them. **“This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.”** The simplicity and depth of his words swept through the crowd, leaving a profound impact.

As the Pharisees huddled together, contemplating their next move, Jesus turned the tables with a question of his own. “What do you think of the Christ? Whose son is he?” They answered, “The son of David.” But Jesus pressed further, citing the scriptures: **“How then doth David in spirit call him Lord?”** His question left them speechless, unable to counter his divine insight.

In the silence that followed, a sense of awe and respect settled over the gathered crowd. From that day, no one dared to question him further, his wisdom having extinguished the fires of their skepticism.

stories.title: Woes to the Scribes and Pharisees
stories.keyVerse: "Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men’s bones, and of all uncleanness."
stories.text:
Then spake Jesus to the multitude, and to his disciples,
Saying,
The scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat:
All therefore whatsoever they bid you observe,
that observe and do; but do not ye after their works: for they say, and do not.
For they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay
them on men’s shoulders; but they
themselves
will not move them with one of their fingers.
But all their works they do for to be seen of men: they make broad their phylacteries, and enlarge the borders of their garments,
And love the uppermost rooms at feasts, and the chief seats in the synagogues,
And greetings in the markets, and to be called of men, Rabbi, Rabbi.
But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master,
even
Christ; and all ye are brethren.
And call no
man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven.
Neither be ye called masters: for one is your Master,
even
Christ.
But he that is greatest among you shall be your servant.
And whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased; and he that shall humble himself shall be exalted.          But woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye shut up the kingdom of heaven against men: for ye neither go in
yourselves,
neither suffer ye them that are entering to go in.
Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye devour widows’ houses, and for a pretence make long prayer: therefore ye shall receive the greater damnation.
Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves.
Woe unto you,
ye blind guides, which say, Whosoever shall swear by the temple, it is nothing; but whosoever shall swear by the gold of the temple, he is a debtor!
Ye fools and blind: for whether is greater, the gold, or the temple that sanctifieth the gold?
And, Whosoever shall swear by the altar, it is nothing; but whosoever sweareth by the gift that is upon it, he is guilty.
Ye fools and blind: for whether
is
greater, the gift, or the altar that sanctifieth the gift?
Whoso therefore shall swear by the altar, sweareth by it, and by all things thereon.
And whoso shall swear by the temple, sweareth by it, and by him that dwelleth therein.
And he that shall swear by heaven, sweareth by the throne of God, and by him that sitteth thereon.
Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier
matters
of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.
Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel.
Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess.
Thou blind Pharisee, cleanse first that
which is within the cup and platter, that the outside of them may be clean also.
Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead
men’s bones, and of all uncleanness.
Even so ye also outwardly appear righteous unto men, but within ye are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.
Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! because ye build the tombs of the prophets, and garnish the sepulchres of the righteous,
And say, If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partakers with them in the blood of the prophets.
Wherefore ye be witnesses unto yourselves, that ye are the children of them which killed the prophets.
Fill ye up then the measure of your fathers.
Ye serpents,
ye generation of vipers, how can ye escape the damnation of hell?          Wherefore, behold, I send unto you prophets, and wise men, and scribes: and
some of them ye shall kill and crucify; and
some of them shall ye scourge in your synagogues, and persecute
them from city to city:
That upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel unto the blood of Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar.
Verily I say unto you, All these things shall come upon this generation.
O Jerusalem, Jerusalem,
thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under
her wings, and ye would not!
Behold, your house is left unto you desolate.
For I say unto you, Ye shall not see me henceforth, till ye shall say, Blessed
is he that cometh in the name of the Lord.
stories.retelling:
The afternoon sun hung high above Jerusalem, casting long shadows across the crowded marketplace. The murmur of merchants haggling and the rustle of people moving about filled the air. Among the bustling crowd, Jesus stood, his presence drawing a gathering of people eager to hear his words. His disciples were close by, watching intently as he spoke.

Jesus began, addressing the crowd with a voice both firm and resonant. He spoke of the scribes and Pharisees, the religious leaders who held positions of authority and were revered by many. They occupied the seat of Moses, teaching the law to the people, yet Jesus cautioned against their actions. **“All therefore whatsoever they bid you observe, that observe and do; but do not ye after their works: for they say, and do not.”** His words echoed with a piercing truth, cutting through the façade of their outward piety.

The Pharisees, with their flowing robes and broad phylacteries, loved to be seen. They thrived on attention, relishing the best seats at feasts and the respectful greetings in public places. Yet, behind this polished exterior lay a different reality. Jesus described them as burdening the people with laws they themselves would not lift a finger to ease. 

With each woe, Jesus peeled back another layer of hypocrisy. **“Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye devour widows’ houses, and for a pretence make long prayer.”** His words painted a vivid picture of leaders who hid behind long prayers while exploiting the vulnerable. He cast a light on the darkness within their hearts, their actions cloaked in deceit.

The crowd listened, hanging on each word, as Jesus likened the Pharisees to whitewashed tombs—beautiful on the outside but filled with decay and death inside. **“Woe unto you…for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men’s bones, and of all uncleanness.”** His voice was both a lament and a call to see beyond the surface, to understand the depth of their hypocrisy.

As Jesus continued, he foretold of the prophets and wise men who would come, only to be persecuted by these very leaders. He spoke with sorrow of Jerusalem, the city that had killed the prophets sent to her. **“O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee.”** His words carried a yearning, a desire to gather the people as a hen gathers her chicks, if only they would come.

The crowd was silent, the weight of his words settling over them like a heavy cloud. The marketplace, once filled with the clamor of daily life, now held a tense stillness. Jesus’ message was clear, his voice a beacon calling for truth and sincerity over empty gestures. The people left, their hearts stirred, the echoes of his words lingering long after he had finished speaking.

stories.title: The Widow's Offering
stories.keyVerse: "Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury:"
stories.text:
And Jesus sat over against the treasury, and beheld how the people cast money into the treasury: and many that were rich cast in much.
And there came a certain poor widow, and she threw in two mites, which make a farthing.
And he called
unto him his disciples, and saith unto them,
Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury:
For all
they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had,
even all her living.
stories.retelling:
The temple courtyard buzzed with activity. Sunlight glinted off polished coins as they slipped from the hands of the wealthy, clinking into the treasury boxes with a satisfying ring. Men and women in fine robes moved with practiced ease, their generous contributions a testament to their abundance. Jesus sat quietly nearby, observing the scene with a thoughtful gaze. His eyes followed the steady stream of donors, noting not just the size of their offerings but the hearts behind them.

Amidst the throng, an unassuming figure approached the treasury. She was a widow, her garments worn and her steps slow, yet there was a quiet dignity in her demeanor. Clutched in her hand were two small bronze coins, nearly insignificant in their value—a mere whisper against the symphony of wealth around her. She paused for a moment, her gaze steady, before dropping the coins into the treasury. The sound was barely audible, swallowed by the grander gestures of those around her.

Jesus watched her closely, a deep understanding in his eyes. He shifted his gaze to his disciples, who were scattered nearby, observing the scene with varying degrees of interest. He called them over, his voice firm yet filled with a certain urgency. As they gathered around him, he pointed towards the retreating figure of the widow. 

**"Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury,"** he declared, his words cutting through the bustling noise of the courtyard. The disciples looked at him, puzzled. How could those two tiny coins compare to the lavish donations of the rich?

Sensing their confusion, Jesus continued, his voice carrying a note of profound insight. He explained that while the wealthy had given from their surplus, the widow had given everything she had, holding nothing back. She had entrusted her livelihood to God, her faith a stark contrast to the calculated generosity of those who surrounded her.

As the widow disappeared into the crowd, her heart likely lightened by the act of giving, the disciples stood in silent reflection. The lesson was clear, echoing in their minds long after the widow had gone. Jesus had shown them that the true measure of giving was not in the amount, but in the spirit and sacrifice behind it.

The temple courtyard continued to hum with activity, but for those who had heard Jesus’ words, the widow’s humble offering had become a beacon—a small act of profound significance that transcended the clatter of wealth and the noise of the world. In that moment, she had given more than anyone else, and her story would resonate far beyond the temple walls.

stories.title: Unless a Grain of Wheat Dies
stories.keyVerse: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit."
stories.text:
And there were certain Greeks among them that came up to worship at the feast:
The same came therefore to Philip, which was of Bethsaida of Galilee, and desired him, saying, Sir, we would see Jesus.
Philip cometh and telleth Andrew: and again Andrew and Philip tell Jesus.
And Jesus answered them, saying,
The hour is come, that the Son of man should be glorified.
Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.
He that loveth his life shall lose it; and he that hateth his life in this world shall keep it unto life eternal.
If any man serve me, let him follow me; and where I am, there shall also my servant be: if any man serve me, him will
my Father honour.
Now is my soul troubled; and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour: but for this cause came I unto this hour.
Father, glorify thy name. Then came there a voice from heaven,
saying, I have both glorified
it, and will glorify
it again.
The people therefore, that stood by, and heard
it, said that it thundered: others said, An angel spake to him.
Jesus answered and said,
This voice came not because of me, but for your sakes.
Now is the judgment of this world: now shall the prince of this world be cast out.
And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all
men
unto me.
This he said, signifying what death he should die.
The people answered him, We have heard out of the law that Christ abideth for ever: and how sayest thou,
The Son of man must be lifted up?
who is this Son of man?
Then Jesus said unto them,
Yet a little while is the light with you. Walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you: for he that walketh in darkness knoweth not whither he goeth.
While ye have light, believe in the light, that ye may be the children of light. These things spake Jesus, and departed, and did hide himself from them.
But though he had done so many miracles before them, yet they believed not on him:
That the saying of Esaias the prophet might be fulfilled, which he spake, Lord, who hath believed our report? and to whom hath the arm of the Lord been revealed?
Therefore they could not believe, because that Esaias said again,
He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart; that they should not see with
their eyes, nor understand with
their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them.
These things said Esaias, when he saw his glory, and spake of him.
Nevertheless among the chief rulers also many believed on him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess
him, lest they should be put out of the synagogue:
For they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God.
Jesus cried and said,
He that believeth on me, believeth not on me, but on him that sent me.
And he that seeth me seeth him that sent me.
I am come a light into the world, that whosoever believeth on me should not abide in darkness.
And if any man hear my words, and believe not, I judge him not: for I came not to judge the world, but to save the world.
He that rejecteth me, and receiveth not my words, hath one that judgeth him: the word that I have spoken, the same shall judge him in the last day.
For I have not spoken of myself; but the Father which sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak.
And I know that his commandment is life everlasting: whatsoever I speak therefore, even as the Father said unto me, so I speak.
stories.retelling:
The air in Jerusalem was thick with anticipation as the feast drew a diverse crowd, including a group of curious Greeks. Amid the bustling energy, they approached Philip, a disciple from Bethsaida, their eyes filled with earnest intent. “Sir, we want to see Jesus,” they requested, their voices blending with the surrounding chatter. 

Philip, slightly taken aback by their boldness, nodded and quickly sought out Andrew. Together, they approached Jesus, relaying the visitors' request. Jesus, standing in the midst of the pressing crowd, looked contemplative. His gaze seemed to peer beyond the horizon as he spoke, his voice both solemn and resolute. **“The hour is come, that the Son of man should be glorified.”**

His words hung in the air, charged with an unspoken gravity. He continued, drawing a vivid image that seized the imagination of those listening. **“Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.”** The simple yet profound metaphor left the crowd in thoughtful silence, each person considering the sacrifice and rebirth that echoed in his words.

As if burdened by the weight of what lay ahead, Jesus confessed, “Now my soul is troubled.” The admission was raw, a rare glimpse into his humanity. Yet, steeling himself, he looked toward the heavens. **“Father, glorify thy name.”** Suddenly, a voice rumbled from the sky, majestic and powerful, affirming, “I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again.” The crowd shifted uneasily, some murmuring that it was thunder, others whispering of angels.

Jesus, addressing their confusion, declared, **“This voice came not because of me, but for your sakes.”** His words hinted at the cosmic scale of the unfolding events—a pivotal moment that would alter the course of history. He spoke of the impending judgment on the world and of being lifted up, drawing all people to himself.

Confused, the crowd questioned, “Who is this Son of Man?” Jesus, with an urgency born of limited time, urged them, **“Yet a little while is the light with you. Walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you.”** It was an invitation, a call to believe and embrace the light before it was gone.

Despite the signs and miracles he had performed, many still did not believe, their hearts hardened, as if fulfilling ancient prophecies. Yet, even among the leaders, there were those who believed but remained silent, fearing exclusion from their community.

In a final, impassioned cry, Jesus declared, **“I am come a light into the world, that whosoever believeth on me should not abide in darkness.”** His voice carried the promise of salvation, a beacon of hope against the encroaching night. Then, as the day waned, he withdrew from the crowd, leaving them to ponder the light that flickered just within reach.

stories.title: Signs of the End
stories.keyVerse: "For as the lightning cometh out of the east, and shineth even unto the west; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be."
stories.text:
And Jesus went out, and departed from the temple: and his disciples came to
him for to shew him the buildings of the temple.
And Jesus said unto them, See ye not all these things? verily I say unto you, There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down.And as he sat upon the mount of Olives, the disciples came unto him privately, saying, Tell us, when shall these things be? and what
shall be the sign of thy coming, and of the end of the world?
And Jesus answered and said unto them,
Take heed that no man deceive you.
For many shall come in my name, saying, I am Christ; and shall deceive many.
And ye shall hear of wars and rumours of wars: see that ye be not troubled: for all
these things must come to pass, but the end is not yet.
For nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom: and there shall be famines, and pestilences, and earthquakes, in divers places.
All these
are the beginning of sorrows.
Then shall they deliver you up to be afflicted, and shall kill you: and ye shall be hated of all nations for my name’s sake.
And then shall many be offended, and shall betray one another, and shall hate one another.
And many false prophets shall rise, and shall deceive many.
And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold.
But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved.
And this gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in all the world for a witness unto all nations; and then shall the end come.
When ye therefore shall see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, stand in the holy place, (whoso readeth, let him understand:)Then let them which be in Judaea flee into the mountains:
Let him which is on the housetop not come down to take any thing out of his house:
Neither let him which is in the field return back to take his clothes.
And woe unto them that are with child, and to them that give suck in those days!
But pray ye that your flight be not in the winter, neither on the sabbath day:
For then shall be great tribulation, such as was not since the beginning of the world to this time, no, nor ever shall be.
And except those days should be shortened, there should no flesh be saved: but for the elect’s sake those days shall be shortened.
Then if any man shall say unto you, Lo, here
is Christ, or there; believe
it not.
For there shall arise false Christs, and false prophets, and shall shew great signs and wonders; insomuch that, if
it were possible, they shall deceive the very elect.
Behold, I have told you before.
Wherefore if they shall say unto you, Behold,
he is in the desert; go not forth: behold, he is in the secret chambers; believe
it not.
For as the lightning cometh out of the east, and shineth even unto the west; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be.
For wheresoever the carcase is, there will the eagles be gathered together.          Immediately after the tribulation of those days shall the sun be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens shall be shaken:
And then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven: and then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn, and they shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.
And he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other.
Now learn a parable of the fig tree; When his branch is yet tender, and putteth forth leaves, ye know that summer is nigh:
So likewise ye, when ye shall see all these things, know that it is near,
even at the doors.
Verily I say unto you, This generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled.
Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.
stories.retelling:
As the sun began to dip behind the horizon, casting long shadows across the city, Jesus and his disciples moved away from the temple, its towering structures gleaming in the fading light. The disciples couldn't help but admire the grandeur of the temple buildings, their intricate designs a testament to human craftsmanship and devotion.

But Jesus, with a gaze that seemed to pierce through time itself, turned to them and spoke with a quiet certainty. **"See ye not all these things?"** he asked, gesturing towards the majestic stone edifices. **"Verily I say unto you, There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down."** The disciples, their curiosity piqued and perhaps a touch of fear creeping in, followed him to the Mount of Olives. There, under the vast expanse of the sky, they gathered around him as the first stars began to twinkle.

In hushed tones, they asked him about the future, about the signs of his return and the end of the age. Their voices were tinged with a mix of anticipation and apprehension. Jesus, seated among them, warned them of the dangers ahead, his words weaving a tapestry of caution and hope. **"Take heed that no man deceive you,"** he began, his voice carrying the weight of impending trials.

He spoke of false prophets who would claim his name and lead many astray, of wars and whispers of wars that would echo across the lands. Yet, amid the chaos, he urged them not to be troubled, for these events were not the end. Nations would clash, kingdoms would crumble, and the earth itself would shudder with famines, plagues, and earthquakes. These, he said, were merely the beginning of sorrows.

The air grew heavy with his words as he painted a picture of tribulation, of followers persecuted and betrayed, their love growing cold in a world awash with iniquity. Yet, amid the darkness, a light of endurance flickered—a promise that those who held firm to the end would find salvation.

He spoke of a time when the gospel would reach every corner of the earth, a testimony to all nations before the final act. And when the ominous "abomination of desolation" appeared, he advised them to flee, leaving everything behind, for the tribulation would be unlike anything the world had seen.

His words echoed in the quiet night as he spoke of false messiahs and prophets, warning them not to be swayed by miraculous signs and wonders. Instead, they should look to the sky, for **"as the lightning cometh out of the east, and shineth even unto the west; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be."**

In the end, he spoke of celestial upheaval—darkened skies and falling stars—before the Son of Man appeared in glory, gathering his chosen ones from across the globe. It was a vision both terrifying and hopeful, a promise that, despite heaven and earth passing away, his words would remain.

stories.title: Be Ready, The Ten Virgins
stories.keyVerse: "And at midnight there was a cry made, Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him."
stories.text:
But of that day and hour knoweth no
man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only.
But as the days of Noe
were, so shall also the coming of the Son of man be.
For as in the days that were before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day that Noe entered into the ark,
And knew not until the flood came, and took them all away; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be.
Then shall two be in the field; the one shall be taken, and the other left.
Two
women shall be grinding at the mill; the one shall be taken, and the other left.          Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come.
But know this, that if the goodman of the house had known in what watch the thief would come, he would have watched, and would not have suffered his house to be broken up.
Therefore be ye also ready: for in such an hour as ye think not the Son of man cometh.
Who then is a faithful and wise servant, whom his lord hath made ruler over his household, to give them meat in due season?
Blessed
is that servant, whom his lord when he cometh shall find so doing.
Verily I say unto you, That he shall make him ruler over all his goods.
But and if that evil servant shall say in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming;
And shall begin to smite
his fellowservants, and to eat and drink with the drunken;
The lord of that servant shall come in a day when he looketh not for
him, and in an hour that he is not aware of,
And shall cut him asunder, and appoint
him his portion with the hypocrites: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
Then shall the kingdom of heaven be likened unto ten virgins, which took their lamps, and went forth to meet the bridegroom.
And five of them were wise, and five
were foolish.
They that
were foolish took their lamps, and took no oil with them:
But the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps.
While the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept.
And at midnight there was a cry made, Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him.
Then all those virgins arose, and trimmed their lamps.
And the foolish said unto the wise, Give us of your oil; for our lamps are gone out.
But the wise answered, saying,
Not so; lest there be not enough for us and you: but go ye rather to them that sell, and buy for yourselves.
And while they went to buy, the bridegroom came; and they that were ready went in with him to the marriage: and the door was shut.
Afterward came also the other virgins, saying, Lord, Lord, open to us.
But he answered and said, Verily I say unto you, I know you not.
Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh.
stories.retelling:
The night was still, with stars scattered like diamonds across the black velvet sky. The air was cool, brushing lightly against the faces of ten young women gathered outside a grand house, each holding a lamp, waiting for the bridegroom. Anticipation buzzed among them, a mix of excitement and tension filling the air.

Five of the women, the wise ones, had prepared diligently, carrying extra oil in small flasks tucked into their robes. They stood calmly, their lamps shining brightly. The other five, the foolish ones, held their lamps aloft, but the anxious looks on their faces betrayed their oversight—they had brought no extra oil. 

As the hours slipped by, the night deepened, and weariness crept over the group. One by one, they nestled into the grass, the soft sounds of their breathing mingling with the night’s quiet hum. Time drifted, and they slept.

Suddenly, a cry pierced the silence, sharp and urgent: **"Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him."** The women jolted awake, hearts pounding with the sudden rush of adrenaline. In the scramble, the foolish ones discovered their lamps flickering weakly, the oil nearly gone. Panic seized them.

“Help us!” they pleaded, turning to the wise women. “Our lamps are going out.”

The wise women exchanged glances, their expressions a mix of sympathy and resolve. “We can't,” they replied, their voices steady. **“Lest there be not enough for us and you: but go ye rather to them that sell, and buy for yourselves.”**

With no other choice, the foolish women dashed off into the night, their footsteps echoing as they searched desperately for a merchant to sell them oil. Meanwhile, the bridegroom arrived, a figure of joy and celebration. The wise women, ready and waiting, joined him in the procession, their lamps casting a warm glow around them.

As they entered the grand hall, the doors swung closed with a heavy thud, sealing the jubilant celebration inside. Laughter and music spilled out through the walls, a stark contrast to the anxious darkness where the foolish women returned, oil in hand, too late.

They knocked frantically on the door, their voices rising in desperation, “Lord, Lord, open to us!”

The door remained closed, the bridegroom’s voice firm but tinged with sadness as it echoed through the barrier: **“Verily I say unto you, I know you not.”**

Silence fell, broken only by the distant echoes of celebration. The five outside stood in the shadows, realizing the weight of their missed opportunity. They had not been ready, and now the night seemed colder, the stars above indifferent to their plight.

Inside, the festivities continued, a testament to those who had prepared and waited with vigilance in the quiet hours of the night. The lesson was stark and unforgettable, etched into the hearts of all who witnessed the bridegroom's coming.

stories.title: The Parable of the Talents
stories.keyVerse: "His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord."
stories.text:
For
the kingdom of heaven is as a man travelling into a far country,
who called his own servants, and delivered unto them his goods.
And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability; and straightway took his journey.
Then he that had received the five talents went and traded with the same, and made
them other five talents.
And likewise he that
had received two, he also gained other two.
But he that had received one went and digged in the earth, and hid his lord’s money.
After a long time the lord of those servants cometh, and reckoneth with them.
And so he that had received five talents came and brought other five talents, saying, Lord, thou deliveredst unto me five talents: behold, I have gained beside them five talents more.
His lord said unto him, Well done,
thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
He also that had received two talents came and said, Lord, thou deliveredst unto me two talents: behold, I have gained two other talents beside them.
His lord said unto him, Well done, good and faithful servant; thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
Then he which had received the one talent came and said, Lord, I knew thee that thou art an hard man, reaping where thou hast not sown, and gathering where thou hast not strawed:
And I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth: lo,
there thou hast
that is thine.
His lord answered and said unto him,
Thou wicked and slothful servant, thou knewest that I reap where I sowed not, and gather where I have not strawed:
Thou oughtest therefore to have put my money to the exchangers, and
then at my coming I should have received mine own with usury.
Take therefore the talent from him, and give
it unto him which hath ten talents.
For unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance: but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath.
And cast ye the unprofitable servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
stories.retelling:
A wealthy man prepared to embark on a long journey, deciding to entrust his wealth to his three servants. With a calculating eye, he assessed each one’s capability. To the first, he handed over five talents, a significant sum, a nod to the servant's proven diligence. The second received two talents, a reflection of his steady, reliable nature. The third, less experienced, was given one talent, a trust nonetheless, but of a more cautious measure.

The master departed, leaving behind whispered promises of opportunity and responsibility. The first servant, eyes gleaming with determination, immediately set out to trade. His days were filled with negotiations and exchanges, the clink of coins a constant melody as he doubled his master's wealth to ten talents. The second servant, though less ambitious, was no less industrious. He also engaged in trade, carefully doubling his two talents to four.

The third servant, however, was gripped by fear. He saw the master's gift not as an opportunity but as a burden. Distrustful of his own ability, he chose the path of safety. In the quiet solitude of his garden, he dug a hole, the earth cool between his fingers as he buried the talent, hiding it away from risk and loss.

Years passed, and the master returned, his presence once again commanding respect and attention. He summoned his servants to account for their stewardship. The first came forward, presenting his accomplishment with pride. **“Lord, thou deliveredst unto me five talents: behold, I have gained beside them five talents more.”** The master beamed with approval. **“Well done, thou good and faithful servant,”** he said, satisfaction in his voice. **“Thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.”**

The second servant approached with similar news, his modesty masking his achievement. **“Lord, thou deliveredst unto me two talents: behold, I have gained two other talents beside them.”** His reward mirrored the first, a testament to his loyalty and effort.

Then came the third, his steps heavy with apprehension. **“Lord, I knew thee that thou art an hard man,”** he began, his words tumbling out in a rush of fear. **“I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth: lo, there thou hast that is thine.”** The master’s face darkened with disappointment. **“Thou wicked and slothful servant,”** he rebuked, his voice a sharp contrast to the earlier praise. **“Thou oughtest therefore to have put my money to the exchangers.”**

In a swift judgment, the talent was taken from the third servant and given to the first. The master’s decree was final, his disappointment clear. **“For unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance: but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath.”** The third servant was cast into darkness, the weight of squandered opportunity heavy on his shoulders, a cautionary shadow against the brilliance of the others' success.

stories.title: The Sheep and the Goats
stories.keyVerse: "And before him shall be gathered all nations: and he shall separate them one from another, as a shepherd divideth his sheep from the goats:"
stories.text:
When the Son of man shall come in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, then shall he sit upon the throne of his glory:
And before him shall be gathered all nations: and he shall separate them one from another, as a shepherd divideth
his sheep from the goats:
And he shall set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left.
Then shall the King say unto them on his right hand, Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world:
For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in:
Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me.
Then shall the righteous answer him, saying, Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, and fed
thee? or thirsty, and gave
thee
drink?
When saw we thee a stranger, and took
thee in? or naked, and clothed
thee?
Or when saw we thee sick, or in prison, and came unto thee?
And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done
it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done
it unto me.
Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels:
For I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me no drink:
I was a stranger, and ye took me not in: naked, and ye clothed me not: sick, and in prison, and ye visited me not.
Then shall they also answer him, saying, Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, or athirst, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister unto thee?
Then shall he answer them, saying, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye did
it not to one of the least of these, ye did
it not to me.
And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal.
stories.retelling:
The scene unfolds with a profound sense of anticipation. The sky is a canvas of ethereal light as the Son of Man arrives in his glory, surrounded by an entourage of celestial beings. There's an awe-inspiring majesty to his presence as he takes his seat upon a grand, resplendent throne. Below him, a vast multitude gathers—people of every nation and language, each one waiting with bated breath.

In this moment of ultimate reckoning, the King surveys the crowd. There's a quiet intensity in the air, heightened by the sheer enormity of the gathering. Then, with the precision of a shepherd tending his flock, he begins to separate them. On his right, he places the sheep, while the goats stand to his left.

Addressing those on his right, his voice carries the warmth and tenderness of a long-awaited homecoming. **"Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world,"** he announces. The words resonate with a profound sense of fulfillment and promise.

He recounts their deeds with a tone of gratitude that fills the space between them. **"For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in,"** he says, highlighting the intimate acts of kindness they showed when they least expected recognition. The sheep, humbled and bewildered, ask when they had ever seen him in need and acted. The King responds with earnest sincerity, **"Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me."**

As the spirit of compassion and grace settles over the right side, the King turns to those on his left. The shift in atmosphere is palpable, as if a shadow has crossed the sun. His voice, now firm and unwavering, delivers the solemn decree: **"Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels."** The words strike a chord of finality and regret.

He recounts their absence of compassion with equal clarity. **"I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me no drink,"** he recites, detailing their failures to act when it was most needed. The goats, in their defense, question when they ever saw him in such states of need. But his response is unwavering, **"Inasmuch as ye did it not to one of the least of these, ye did it not to me."**

And so, with an air of inevitability, the separation concludes. The righteous move towards a realm of eternal life, their hearts lightened by the promise fulfilled. Meanwhile, those on the left face a different fate, one marked by eternal punishment. The scene draws to a close, leaving behind a powerful testament to the weight of choices and the echo of actions.

stories.title: The Anointing at Bethany
stories.keyVerse: "Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, there shall also this, that this woman hath done, be told for a memorial of her."
stories.text:
And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished all these sayings, he said unto his disciples,
Ye know that after two days is
the feast of the passover, and the Son of man is betrayed to be crucified.
Then assembled together the chief priests, and the scribes, and the elders of the people, unto the palace of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas,
And consulted that they might take Jesus by subtilty, and kill
him.
But they said, Not on the feast
day, lest there be an uproar among the people.
Now when Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper,
There came unto him a woman having an alabaster box of very precious ointment, and poured it on his head, as he sat
at meat.
But when his disciples saw
it, they had indignation, saying, To what purpose
is this waste?
For this ointment might have been sold for much, and given to the poor.
When Jesus understood
it, he said unto them,
Why trouble ye the woman? for she hath wrought a good work upon me.
For ye have the poor always with you; but me ye have not always.
For in that she hath poured this ointment on my body, she did
it for my burial.
Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world,
there shall also this, that this woman hath done, be told for a memorial of her.Then one of the twelve, called Judas Iscariot, went unto the chief priests,
And said
unto them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver.
And from that time he sought opportunity to betray him.
stories.retelling:
The air was thick with anticipation as Jesus spoke to his disciples, his words carrying the weight of looming inevitability. "You know that after two days, the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified," he announced, his voice calm yet laden with the gravity of what was to come. Unbeknownst to them, not far away, the chief priests, scribes, and elders gathered in the opulent courtyard of Caiaphas, the high priest. Their minds were entwined with schemes, plotting in hushed tones to seize Jesus by deceit and execute him. Yet, they hesitated, wary of the uproar that might erupt if they acted during the feast.

Meanwhile, in the village of Bethany, a different scene unfolded. Inside the home of Simon the leper, the room was filled with the comforting hum of conversation. Jesus reclined at the table, surrounded by his disciples. The aroma of freshly prepared food mingled with the scent of costly perfume as a woman approached him, cradling an alabaster jar. Without a word, she broke open the jar and poured the precious ointment over Jesus' head, the fragrance enveloping the room in a poignant reminder of her devotion.

The disciples watched, their expressions shifting from surprise to indignation. Murmurs of discontent rippled through the group. "Why this waste?" one of them questioned, the words heavy with judgment. "This ointment could have been sold for a high price and given to the poor."

Perceiving their displeasure, Jesus spoke with a gentle rebuke, his eyes resting on the woman with gratitude. **"Why trouble ye the woman? for she hath wrought a good work upon me,"** he said, acknowledging her act of love and foresight. **"For ye have the poor always with you; but me ye have not always."** His words hung in the air, a reminder of his transient time among them. **"For in that she hath poured this ointment on my body, she did it for my burial."**

The room fell silent, the significance of her gesture sinking in. Jesus, with quiet certainty, added, **"Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, there shall also this, that this woman hath done, be told for a memorial of her."** His words transformed the moment into an eternal testament to her faith.

In stark contrast to this intimate scene, Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve, slipped away and sought out the chief priests. Driven by his own motives, he proposed a deal, asking, "What are you willing to give me, that I should deliver him to you?" The clinking of thirty pieces of silver echoed his betrayal, sealing his fate as he began to watch for the moment to hand Jesus over to them.

stories.title: Jesus Washes the Disciples' Feet
stories.keyVerse: "After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples’ feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith he was girded."
stories.text:
Now before the feast of the passover, when Jesus knew that his hour was come that he should depart out of this world unto the Father, having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end.
And supper being ended, the devil having now put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s
son, to betray him;
Jesus knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he was come from God, and went to God;
He riseth from supper, and laid aside his garments; and took a towel, and girded himself.
After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples’ feet, and to wipe
them with the towel wherewith he was girded.
Then cometh he to Simon Peter: and Peter saith unto him, Lord, dost thou wash my feet?
Jesus answered and said unto him,
What I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt know hereafter.
Peter saith unto him, Thou shalt never wash my feet. Jesus answered him,
If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me.
Simon Peter saith unto him, Lord, not my feet only, but also
my
hands and
my head.
Jesus saith to him,
He that is washed needeth not save to wash
his feet, but is clean every whit: and ye are clean, but not all.
For he knew who should betray him; therefore said he,
Ye are not all clean.
So after he had washed their feet, and had taken his garments, and was set down again, he said unto them,
Know ye what I have done to you?
Ye call me Master and Lord: and ye say well; for so I am.
If I then,
your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another’s feet.
For I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you.
Verily, verily, I say unto you, The servant is not greater than his lord; neither he that is sent greater than he that sent him.
If ye know these things, happy are ye if ye do them.          I speak not of you all: I know whom I have chosen: but that the scripture may be fulfilled, He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me.
Now I tell you before it come, that, when it is come to pass, ye may believe that I am
he.
Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that receiveth whomsoever I send receiveth me; and he that receiveth me receiveth him that sent me.
When Jesus had thus said, he was troubled in spirit, and testified, and said,
Verily, verily, I say unto you, that one of you shall betray me.
Then the disciples looked one on another, doubting of whom he spake.
Now there was leaning on Jesus’ bosom one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved.
Simon Peter therefore beckoned to him, that he should ask who it should be of whom he spake.
He then lying on Jesus’ breast saith unto him, Lord, who is it?
Jesus answered,
He it is, to whom I shall give a sop, when I have dipped
it. And when he had dipped the sop, he gave
it
to Judas Iscariot,
the son of Simon.
And after the sop Satan entered into him. Then said Jesus unto him,
That thou doest, do quickly.
Now no man at the table knew for what intent he spake this unto him.
For some
of them thought, because Judas had the bag, that Jesus had said unto him, Buy
those things that we have need of against the feast; or, that he should give something to the poor.
He then having received the sop went immediately out: and it was night.
stories.retelling:
The room was filled with the warm glow of oil lamps flickering against the stone walls. The air was thick with the aroma of roasted lamb and freshly baked bread, remnants of the Passover feast. Jesus, knowing that his time was drawing near, looked around at his disciples, each one absorbed in their own thoughts, unaware of the gravity of the moment. Judas Iscariot, sitting among them, had already set his heart on betrayal, though none but Jesus knew.

Rising from the table, Jesus quietly removed his outer garment, and with a purposeful calm, took a towel and wrapped it around his waist. The room fell silent as he poured water into a basin, the sound echoing softly. The disciples watched in confusion as he knelt down before them. One by one, he began to wash their feet, the cool water running over their skin, the towel absorbing the droplets as he dried them.

When Jesus reached Simon Peter, the disciple's eyes widened in disbelief. **“Lord, dost thou wash my feet?”** Peter's voice broke the silence, a mix of surprise and resistance. Jesus looked up at him with a gentle assurance. **“What I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt know hereafter.”**

Peter shook his head, adamant. **“Thou shalt never wash my feet.”**

Jesus met his gaze, a hint of sadness in his eyes. **“If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me.”** 

The realization struck Peter, his resolve crumbling. **“Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head.”** His voice was earnest, a plea for inclusion in whatever Jesus was offering.

With a quiet smile, Jesus responded, **“He that is washed needeth not save to wash his feet, but is clean every whit.”** His words were a soft reassurance, a tender reminder of their bond.

Once he had washed all their feet, Jesus returned to his place at the table, the room still with anticipation. **“Know ye what I have done to you?”** he asked, his voice steady and filled with purpose. He explained that as their Teacher and Lord, he had set an example for them to follow. **“If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another’s feet.”**

The room absorbed his words, the gravity of his actions sinking in. But the moment was marred by a shadow. Jesus' voice grew somber as he spoke of betrayal, his spirit troubled. **“Verily, verily, I say unto you, that one of you shall betray me.”** The disciples exchanged anxious glances, uncertainty gripping them.

Leaning close to Jesus, the beloved disciple asked quietly, **“Lord, who is it?”**

Jesus responded, his voice barely above a whisper, revealing the betrayer through a simple gesture of giving a piece of bread to Judas. As Judas accepted it, a chill crept through the room. Jesus turned to him, his words laced with an urgency and inevitability. **“That thou doest, do quickly.”**

Judas left the room, the door closing behind him with a heavy thud. Outside, the night was dark and foreboding, the weight of his choice hanging in the air. Inside, the disciples were left in silence, the profound lesson of service and the shadow of betrayal lingering in their hearts.

stories.title: The Last Supper
stories.keyVerse: And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat; this is my body.
stories.text:
Now the first
day of the
feast of unleavened bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying unto him, Where wilt thou that we prepare for thee to eat the passover?
And he said,
Go into the city to such a man, and say unto him, The Master saith, My time is at hand; I will keep the passover at thy house with my disciples.
And the disciples did as Jesus had appointed them; and they made ready the passover.
Now when the even was come, he sat down with the twelve.
And as they did eat, he said,
Verily I say unto you, that one of you shall betray me.
And they were exceeding sorrowful, and began every one of them to say unto him, Lord, is it I?
And he answered and said,
He that dippeth
his hand with me in the dish, the same shall betray me.
The Son of man goeth as it is written of him: but woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed! it had been good for that man if he had not been born.
Then Judas, which betrayed him, answered and said, Master, is it I? He said unto him,
Thou hast said.And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed
it,
and brake
it, and gave
it to the disciples, and said,
Take, eat; this is my body.
And he took the cup, and gave thanks, and gave
it to them, saying,
Drink ye all of it;
For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.
But I say unto you, I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine, until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom.
And when they had sung an hymn, they went out into the mount of Olives.
Then saith Jesus unto them,
All ye shall be offended because of me this night: for it is written, I will smite the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered abroad.
But after I am risen again, I will go before you into Galilee.
Peter answered and said unto him, Though all
men shall be offended because of thee,
yet will I never be offended.
Jesus said unto him,
Verily I say unto thee, That this night, before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice.
Peter said unto him, Though I should die with thee, yet will I not deny thee. Likewise also said all the disciples.
stories.retelling:
Darkness had gently settled over Jerusalem, wrapping the city in a cool, quiet embrace. Inside a modest room, the flickering light of oil lamps cast long shadows on the walls, where Jesus and his twelve disciples gathered around a simple wooden table.
