The air was filled with the warmth of freshly baked bread and the earthy scent of wine. It was the first day of the feast of unleavened bread, a time to celebrate and remember the deliverance of their ancestors.  

The disciples had been diligent, following Jesus' instructions to prepare a place for the Passover meal. They found a man in the city, just as Jesus had described, and arranged to use his home for this sacred gathering. Now, as they reclined together, an air of anticipation mixed with a touch of unease filled the room.  

As the meal progressed, Jesus, with a calm yet grave demeanor, broke the silence. **“Verily I say unto you, that one of you shall betray me.”** His words struck like a thunderclap, sending ripples of shock across the table. The disciples exchanged worried glances, their hearts pounding with a mix of disbelief and fear. Each one, with a voice tinged with desperation, asked, “Lord, is it I?”  

Jesus, with a sorrowful gaze, gestured towards the shared dish. **“He that dippeth his hand with me in the dish, the same shall betray me.”** The weight of his words hung heavily in the air. Judas, trying to maintain his composure, asked, “Master, is it I?” Jesus met his eyes and replied, **“Thou hast said.”**  

As the tension simmered, Jesus took a loaf of bread. His hands moved with deliberate grace as he blessed and broke it, sharing it among them. **“Take, eat; this is my body.”** The bread passed from hand to hand, its symbolic weight deepening the moment.  

He then lifted a cup of wine, his voice steady and filled with a solemn promise. **“Drink ye all of it; for this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.”** The disciples drank, each sip a shared pledge in this new covenant.  

The meal drew to a close with a hymn, voices blending in a chorus of faith and uncertainty. Together, they left the warmth of the room and ventured into the night, walking towards the Mount of Olives. The stars above seemed to watch silently as Jesus turned to them, his voice carrying the weight of prophecy.  

**“All ye shall be offended because of me this night,”** he said, a hint of sadness in his tone. Peter, full of fervor, declared, “Though all men shall be offended because of thee, yet will I never be offended.” Jesus looked at him with a knowing sadness. **“Verily I say unto thee, That this night, before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice.”**  

The night pressed on, filled with promises and the looming shadow of betrayal, as the disciples followed their teacher, each step drawing them nearer to an uncertain fate.

stories.title: I Am the Way
stories.keyVerse: “I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.”
stories.text:
Therefore, when he was gone out, Jesus said,
Now is the Son of man glorified, and God is glorified in him.
If God be glorified in him, God shall also glorify him in himself, and shall straightway glorify him.
Little children, yet a little while I am with you. Ye shall seek me: and as I said unto the Jews, Whither I go, ye cannot come; so now I say to you.
A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another.
By this shall all
men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.Simon Peter said unto him, Lord, whither goest thou? Jesus answered him,
Whither I go, thou canst not follow me now; but thou shalt follow me afterwards.
Peter said unto him, Lord, why cannot I follow thee now? I will lay down my life for thy sake.
Jesus answered him,
Wilt thou lay down thy life for my sake? Verily, verily, I say unto thee, The cock shall not crow, till thou hast denied me thrice.          Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God, believe also in me.
In my Father’s house are many mansions: if
it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you.
And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and receive you unto myself; that where I am,
there ye may be also.
And whither I go ye know, and the way ye know.
Thomas saith unto him, Lord, we know not whither thou goest; and how can we know the way?
Jesus saith unto him,
I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
If ye had known me, ye should have known my Father also: and from henceforth ye know him, and have seen him.
Philip saith unto him, Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us.
Jesus saith unto him,
Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou
then, Shew us the Father?
Believest thou not that I am in the Father, and the Father in me? the words that I speak unto you I speak not of myself: but the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the works.
Believe me that I
am in the Father, and the Father in me: or else believe me for the very works’ sake.
Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me, the works that I do shall he do also; and greater
works than these shall he do; because I go unto my Father.
And whatsoever ye shall ask in my name, that will I do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son.
If ye shall ask any thing in my name, I will do
it.          If ye love me, keep my commandments.
And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever;
Even the Spirit of truth; whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth him not, neither knoweth him: but ye know him; for he dwelleth with you, and shall be in you.
I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you.
Yet a little while, and the world seeth me no more; but ye see me: because I live, ye shall live also.
At that day ye shall know that I
am in my Father, and ye in me, and I in you.
He that hath my commandments, and keepeth them, he it is that loveth me: and he that loveth me shall be loved of my Father, and I will love him, and will manifest myself to him.
Judas saith unto him, not Iscariot, Lord, how is it that thou wilt manifest thyself unto us, and not unto the world?
Jesus answered and said unto him,
If a man love me, he will keep my words: and my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him.
He that loveth me not keepeth not my sayings: and the word which ye hear is not mine, but the Father’s which sent me.
These things have I spoken unto you, being
yet present with you.
But the Comforter,
which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you.
Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.
Ye have heard how I said unto you, I go away, and come
again
unto you. If ye loved me, ye would rejoice, because I said, I go unto the Father: for my Father is greater than I.
And now I have told you before it come to pass, that, when it is come to pass, ye might believe.
Hereafter I will not talk much with you: for the prince of this world cometh, and hath nothing in me.
But that the world may know that I love the Father; and as the Father gave me commandment, even so I do. Arise, let us go hence.
stories.retelling:
In the dim glow of the upper room, Jesus had just finished sharing a meal with his disciples. The atmosphere was thick with anticipation and a hint of unease. Judas had slipped out into the night, leaving behind an air of betrayal that lingered in the shadows. Jesus looked around at his friends, their faces etched with concern and confusion. He began to speak, his voice calm yet carrying the weight of the moment. He spoke of glory, of God, and of a future beyond their understanding.  

He referred to them lovingly as his "little children," telling them that his time with them was drawing to a close. Confusion flickered across their faces as he explained, **"Whither I go, ye cannot come; so now I say to you."** Then, he gave them a new commandment that would define them: **"That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another."** The room was silent, the gravity of his words sinking in.  

Impulsively, Peter spoke up, his voice a mix of determination and desperation, **“Lord, whither goest thou?”** Jesus replied gently, **“Whither I go, thou canst not follow me now; but thou shalt follow me afterwards.”** The tension in Peter’s voice was palpable as he protested, **“Lord, why cannot I follow thee now? I will lay down my life for thy sake.”** A somber expression crossed Jesus’ face as he predicted Peter's imminent denial.  

Sensing the growing anxiety in the room, Jesus offered words of comfort, telling them not to let their hearts be troubled. He painted a picture of his Father's house, a place with many rooms, a place he was going to prepare for them. Thomas, ever the realist, voiced the question on all their minds: **“Lord, we know not whither thou goest; and how can we know the way?”**  

Jesus' response was both profound and reassuring, **“I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.”** His words hung in the air, challenging and comforting all at once.  

Still, the disciples struggled with understanding. Philip, yearning for clarity, asked, **“Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us.”** Jesus, eyes filled with a gentle reproach, explained that seeing him was seeing the Father, emphasizing their inseparable connection.  

He promised them a Counselor, the Spirit of truth, who would never leave their side. He assured them of his peace, a peace unlike any the world could offer. His words were like a balm, soothing their troubled hearts, reminding them of the deep love that bound them all.  

As the night deepened, Jesus prepared to lead them from the room, a resolve in his voice as he concluded, **“Arise, let us go hence.”** In that moment, the disciples stood on the brink of a new understanding, poised at the edge of a journey they could scarcely comprehend.

stories.title: The True Vine
stories.keyVerse: "I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing."
stories.text:
I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.
Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every
branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit.
Now ye are clean through the word which I have spoken unto you.
Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me.
I am the vine, ye
are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered; and men gather them, and cast
them into the fire, and they are burned.
If ye abide in me, and my words abide in you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you.
Herein is my Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit; so shall ye be my disciples.
As the Father hath loved me, so have I loved you: continue ye in my love.
If ye keep my commandments, ye shall abide in my love; even as I have kept my Father’s commandments, and abide in his love.
These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and
that your joy might be full.
This is my commandment, That ye love one another, as I have loved you.
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
Ye are my friends, if ye do whatsoever I command you.
Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you.
Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye should go and bring forth fruit, and
that your fruit should remain: that whatsoever ye shall ask of the Father in my name, he may give it you.
These things I command you, that ye love one another.
If the world hate you, ye know that
it hated me before it hated you.
If ye were of the world, the world would love his own: but because ye are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hateth you.
Remember the word that I said unto you, The servant is not greater than his lord. If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they have kept my saying, they will keep yours also.
But all these things will they do unto you for my name’s sake, because they know not him that sent me.
If I had not come and spoken unto them, they had not had sin: but now they have no cloke for their sin.
He that hateth me hateth my Father also.
If I had not done among them the works which none other man did, they had not had sin: but now have they both seen and hated both me and my Father.
But
this cometh to pass, that the word might be fulfilled that is written in their law, They hated me without a cause.
But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father,
even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me:
And ye also shall bear witness, because ye have been with me from the beginning.
stories.retelling:
On an evening thick with the warmth of companionship, Jesus gathered with his disciples, his presence gentle yet commanding. A soft breeze rustled the leaves around them, and the air carried the scent of earth and growing things. His eyes, deep and knowing, met each of theirs, drawing them into the heart of his message. 

He spoke with clarity, painting a picture as vivid as the gardens they had strolled through. "I am the true vine," he began, the words weaving through the group like a thread connecting each soul to the next. "My Father is the gardener." His voice was steady, each word deliberate, like the careful tending of a vineyard.

Jesus continued, explaining that in this vineyard, every branch that bore no fruit would be removed, while those that did would be pruned to yield even more. His gaze moved among them, his tone tender yet firm. They were already clean, he assured them, made so by the words he had shared.

"Remain in me, and I in you," he urged, a plea wrapped in promise. They were the branches, he the vine, and apart from him, they could achieve nothing. The metaphor was clear—without their connection to him, their efforts would wither like discarded branches on a forest floor.

His voice dropped to a softer, more intimate tone, as if sharing a secret between friends. **"If ye abide in me, and my words abide in you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you."** The promise of divine support was both an invitation and a challenge, calling them to deepen their commitment.

The evening shadows lengthened as he spoke of love, a love that began with the Father and flowed through him to them. **"Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends,"** he said, his words resonating with a truth they felt in their bones. No longer were they merely followers; he called them friends, a title that bore the weight of shared knowledge and trust.

As the world outside their circle held its breath, Jesus warned of the challenges to come. The world, he said, would not understand them, just as it had not understood him. Persecution would follow. Yet, the connection they shared with him and with each other would sustain them.

In the quiet that followed, a sense of purpose settled over the disciples. Jesus spoke of the Spirit of truth, the Counselor who would come, a promise of presence even in his absence. They would testify, he said, because they had been with him from the beginning, and in that mission, they would find their strength.

The conversation waned, but the message lingered, a vine rooted deep within their hearts, ready to bear fruit in the world beyond.

stories.title: The Work of the Holy Spirit
stories.keyVerse: "These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world."
stories.text:
These things have I spoken unto you, that ye should not be offended.
They shall put you out of the synagogues: yea, the time cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service.
And these things will they do unto you, because they have not known the Father, nor me.
But these things have I told you, that when the time shall come, ye may remember that I told you of them. And these things I said not unto you at the beginning, because I was with you.
But now I go my way to him that sent me; and none of you asketh me, Whither goest thou?
But because I have said these things unto you, sorrow hath filled your heart.
Nevertheless I tell you the truth; It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you.
And when he is come, he will reprove the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment:
Of sin, because they believe not on me;
Of righteousness, because I go to my Father, and ye see me no more;
Of judgment, because the prince of this world is judged.
I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now.
Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth: for he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear,
that shall he speak: and he will shew you things to come.
He shall glorify me: for he shall receive of mine, and shall shew
it unto you.
All things that the Father hath are mine: therefore said I, that he shall take of mine, and shall shew
it unto you.
A little while, and ye shall not see me: and again, a little while, and ye shall see me, because I go to the Father.
Then said
some of his disciples among themselves, What is this that he saith unto us, A little while, and ye shall not see me: and again, a little while, and ye shall see me: and, Because I go to the Father?
They said therefore, What is this that he saith, A little while? we cannot tell what he saith.
Now Jesus knew that they were desirous to ask him, and said unto them,
Do ye enquire among yourselves of that I said, A little while, and ye shall not see me: and again, a little while, and ye shall see me?
Verily, verily, I say unto you, That ye shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice: and ye shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy.
A woman when she is in travail hath sorrow, because her hour is come: but as soon as she is delivered of the child, she remembereth no more the anguish, for joy that a man is born into the world.
And ye now therefore have sorrow: but I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man taketh from you.
And in that day ye shall ask me nothing. Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, he will give
it
you.
Hitherto have ye asked nothing in my name: ask, and ye shall receive, that your joy may be full.
These things have I spoken unto you in proverbs: but the time cometh, when I shall no more speak unto you in proverbs, but I shall shew you plainly of the Father.
At that day ye shall ask in my name: and I say not unto you, that I will pray the Father for you:
For the Father himself loveth you, because ye have loved me, and have believed that I came out from God.
I came forth from the Father, and am come into the world: again, I leave the world, and go to the Father.
His disciples said unto him, Lo, now speakest thou plainly, and speakest no proverb.
Now are we sure that thou knowest all things, and needest not that any man should ask thee: by this we believe that thou camest forth from God.
Jesus answered them,
Do ye now believe?
Behold, the hour cometh, yea, is now come, that ye shall be scattered, every man to his own, and shall leave me alone: and yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me.
These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.
stories.retelling:
The room was dimly lit, a flickering flame casting shadows that danced across the walls. Jesus sat among his disciples, their faces etched with concern and anticipation. The air was thick with tension as he prepared them for the trials ahead. His voice was calm, yet carried the weight of what was to come. He warned them of the challenges they would face, of being cast out from synagogues, and of how some would even think they were serving God by persecuting them. Their expressions turned to confusion and dismay.

He paused, letting his words sink in, then continued. **“But now I go my way to him that sent me; and none of you asketh me, Whither goest thou?”** he said, noting their silence. The sorrow in their hearts was almost palpable, and he addressed it with a promise of comfort. **“It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you.”**

The disciples exchanged glances, struggling to grasp the full meaning of his words. Jesus spoke of the Spirit of truth, who would guide them when he was gone. This Spirit would reveal the world's errors in judgment and righteousness, a beacon in their darkest times. His words painted a picture of a future where they would not be alone, where the Spirit would lead them into all truth.

As he spoke of his departure, he assured them of his return. **“A little while, and ye shall not see me: and again, a little while, and ye shall see me.”** The mystery of his words left them whispering among themselves, trying to decipher his meaning. Jesus, perceiving their confusion, likened their forthcoming sorrow to a woman in labor—intense yet temporary, leading to joy beyond measure.

He promised that their hearts would rejoice, and no one could take that joy from them. The room seemed to brighten slightly as a glimmer of hope ignited within them. Jesus told them they would no longer need to ask him questions; instead, they could ask the Father directly in his name. This new relationship was built on love and belief, a foundation that would sustain them.

Finally, as he spoke plainly, the disciples felt a wave of clarity. **“Lo, now speakest thou plainly, and speakest no proverb,”** they acknowledged, their faith in him solidifying. Yet, Jesus knew what lay ahead. **“Behold, the hour cometh... that ye shall be scattered, every man to his own, and shall leave me alone.”** Despite this, he reassured them, **“I am not alone, because the Father is with me.”**

His closing words were a balm to their troubled hearts. **“In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.”** In those words, they found strength, a promise of peace amidst the storm, and a reminder that victory was already theirs.

stories.title: Jesus' High Priestly Prayer
stories.keyVerse: "Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee:"
stories.text:
These words spake Jesus, and lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said,
Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee:
As thou hast given him power over all flesh, that he should give eternal life to as many as thou hast given him.
And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.
I have glorified thee on the earth: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do.
And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was.
I have manifested thy name unto the men which thou gavest me out of the world: thine they were, and thou gavest them me; and they have kept thy word.
Now they have known that all things whatsoever thou hast given me are of thee.
For I have given unto them the words which thou gavest me; and they have received
them, and have known surely that I came out from thee, and they have believed that thou didst send me.
I pray for them: I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; for they are thine.
And all mine are thine, and thine are mine; and I am glorified in them.
And now I am no more in the world, but these are in the world, and I come to thee. Holy Father, keep through thine own name those whom thou hast given me, that they may be one, as we
are.
While I was with them in the world, I kept them in thy name: those that thou gavest me I have kept, and none of them is lost, but the son of perdition; that the scripture might be fulfilled.
And now come I to thee; and these things I speak in the world, that they might have my joy fulfilled in themselves.
I have given them thy word; and the world hath hated them, because they are not of the world, even as I am not of the world.
I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil.
They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world.
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.
As thou hast sent me into the world, even so have I also sent them into the world.
And for their sakes I sanctify myself, that they also might be sanctified through the truth.
Neither pray I for these alone, but for them also which shall believe on me through their word;
That they all may be one; as thou, Father,
art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me.
And the glory which thou gavest me I have given them; that they may be one, even as we are one:
I in them, and thou in me, that they may be made perfect in one; and that the world may know that thou hast sent me, and hast loved them, as thou hast loved me.
Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me where I am; that they may behold my glory, which thou hast given me: for thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world.
O righteous Father, the world hath not known thee: but I have known thee, and these have known that thou hast sent me.
And I have declared unto them thy name, and will declare
it:
that the love wherewith thou hast loved me may be in them, and I in them.
stories.retelling:
In the dim light of the upper room, where shadows flickered against the walls from the faint glow of oil lamps, Jesus stood among his disciples. The air was heavy with the weight of what lay ahead, a tension palpable enough to still every heart. He lifted his eyes toward the heavens, a profound calm enveloping him, as if drawing strength from the very source of creation.

**"Father, the hour is come,"** he began, his voice a quiet yet commanding presence that filled the space. The disciples watched in silence, their eyes fixed on him as he spoke intimately with God, laying bare the depths of his heart.

This was a moment of transition, a bridge between the life he had lived on earth and the eternal purpose he was about to fulfill. Jesus spoke of glory—not the kind found in earthly accolades, but a divine glory that transcends time, a radiance he shared with the Father before the world began. He had accomplished what he came to do, revealing God’s nature to those he had gathered, and now he sought the Father’s presence to be restored fully to him.

Pausing, he glanced at his disciples—those who had walked with him, laughed with him, and learned from him. What he felt for them was a deep, abiding love, a commitment that would endure beyond the physical world. He prayed for them, not for escape from the world’s struggles, but for protection from the darkness that threatened their light. **"Holy Father, keep through thine own name those whom thou hast given me, that they may be one, as we are,"** he prayed, his words a shield against the trials to come.

The room was quiet, save for the steady rhythm of breathing, as Jesus continued. He knew they would face hatred and hostility because they were not of the world, just as he was not. Yet he did not ask for their removal from these challenges; instead, he sought their sanctification through truth, the very essence of God’s word.

His prayer expanded beyond the room, reaching into the future. He prayed not only for those present but for all who would come to believe through their message, envisioning a unity that would testify to the world of God’s love. **"That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee,"** he said, his voice filled with a hope that transcended time.

As the prayer drew to a close, Jesus expressed his desire for his followers to witness his glory, a glory rooted in a love that predated the world itself. The disciples sat in the glow of his words, a warmth that promised that even in their separation, his presence would remain within them.

With his heart laid bare, Jesus concluded, knowing he had passed on to them not just teachings, but a living presence, a connection to the divine love he had known. The room, once heavy with foreboding, now felt lighter, infused with the anticipation of the unfolding story of redemption.

stories.title: Gethsemane
stories.keyVerse: "And he went a little farther, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt."
stories.text:
Then cometh Jesus with them unto a place called Gethsemane, and saith unto the disciples,
Sit ye here, while I go and pray yonder.
And he took with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, and began to be sorrowful and very heavy.
Then saith he unto them,
My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death: tarry ye here, and watch with me.
And he went a little farther, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying,
O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou
wilt.
And he cometh unto the disciples, and findeth them asleep, and saith unto Peter, What, could ye not watch with me one hour?
Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed
is willing, but the flesh
is weak.
He went away again the second time, and prayed, saying,
O my Father, if this cup may not pass away from me, except I drink it, thy will be done.
And he came and found them asleep again: for their eyes were heavy.
And he left them, and went away again, and prayed the third time, saying the same words.
Then cometh he to his disciples, and saith unto them,
Sleep on now, and take
your rest: behold, the hour is at hand, and the Son of man is betrayed into the hands of sinners.
Rise, let us be going: behold, he is at hand that doth betray me.
And while he yet spake, lo, Judas, one of the twelve, came, and with him a great multitude with swords and staves, from the chief priests and elders of the people.
Now he that betrayed him gave them a sign, saying, Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he: hold him fast.
And forthwith he came to Jesus, and said, Hail, master; and kissed him.
And Jesus said unto him,
Friend, wherefore art thou come? Then came they, and laid hands on Jesus, and took him.
And, behold, one of them which were with Jesus stretched out
his
hand, and drew his sword, and struck a servant of the high priest’s, and smote off his ear.
Then said Jesus unto him,
Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
Thinkest thou that I cannot now pray to my Father, and he shall presently give me more than twelve legions of angels?
But how then shall the scriptures be fulfilled, that thus it must be?
In that same hour said Jesus to the multitudes,
Are ye come out as against a thief with swords and staves for to take me? I sat daily with you teaching in the temple, and ye laid no hold on me.
But all this was done, that the scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled.
Then all the disciples forsook him, and fled.
stories.retelling:
Under the cloak of night, Jesus led his disciples along a well-trodden path to a garden called Gethsemane. The air was thick with the scent of olive trees, and the moonlight cast long shadows across the ground. Here, at this quiet retreat, he paused and turned to his followers, his face lined with the weight of impending sorrow. He instructed them to sit and wait, as he needed solitude to pray. But he did not go alone; he chose Peter and the two sons of Zebedee to accompany him a little further. 

These three disciples watched as the burden of grief visibly settled over Jesus, his demeanor heavy with an unseen load. **“My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death: tarry ye here, and watch with me,”** he implored, his voice a raw whisper in the stillness. Then, leaving them behind, he moved a short distance away.

In the solitude of the night, Jesus fell to the ground, his heart pouring out in anguished prayer. **“O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.”** The words hung in the air, a plea for relief from the inexorable path he faced, yet simultaneously a surrender to a higher will.

Returning to his disciples, he found them asleep, their eyelids heavy with exhaustion. Disappointment flickered across his face as he addressed Peter, **“What, could ye not watch with me one hour?”** The gentle rebuke was filled with understanding of human frailty. He urged them to stay vigilant, warning, **“The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”**

A second time, Jesus withdrew to pray, wrestling once more with the weight of his impending sacrifice. **“O my Father, if this cup may not pass away from me, except I drink it, thy will be done.”** Despite the agony of the moment, there was a resolve, a quiet acceptance in his words.

Again, he returned to find his disciples overcome by sleep. Their inability to stay awake was an echo of the isolation growing between them. For the third time, he retreated to pray, repeating his earnest words, a surrender to divine purpose.

Finally, he returned and woke them gently. **“Sleep on now, and take your rest: behold, the hour is at hand,”** he said, as a rustle in the garden foretold the arrival of his betrayer.

As he spoke, Judas appeared, leading a crowd armed with swords and clubs. The kiss of betrayal sealed his intentions. Jesus, with calm resolve, greeted him, **“Friend, wherefore art thou come?”** With those words, the betrayal was complete, and the mob surged forward, laying hands on him.

In a brief, chaotic moment, one of Jesus’ followers drew a sword, striking the servant of the high priest. But Jesus, unwavering, instructed him to sheath the weapon, reminding them all of the futility of violence. **“Thinkest thou that I cannot now pray to my Father, and he shall presently give me more than twelve legions of angels?”** Yet, he accepted the unfolding events, knowing they fulfilled the prophecies.

As the disciples scattered into the night, leaving Jesus alone in the hands of his captors, the garden fell silent once more, a witness to the beginning of the end.

stories.title: Jesus Before Caiaphas, Peter's Denial
stories.keyVerse: "Then began he to curse and to swear, saying, I know not the man. And immediately the cock crew."
stories.text:
And they that had laid hold on Jesus led
him away to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and the elders were assembled.
But Peter followed him afar off unto the high priest’s palace, and went in, and sat with the servants, to see the end.
Now the chief priests, and elders, and all the council, sought false witness against Jesus, to put him to death;
But found none: yea, though many false witnesses came,
yet
found they none. At the last came two false witnesses,
And said, This
fellow said, I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to build it in three days.
And the high priest arose, and said unto him, Answerest thou nothing? what
is it which these witness against thee?
But Jesus held his peace. And the high priest answered and said unto him, I adjure thee by the living God, that thou tell us whether thou be the Christ, the Son of God.
Jesus saith unto him,
Thou hast said: nevertheless I say unto you, Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven.
Then the high priest rent his clothes, saying, He hath spoken blasphemy; what further need have we of witnesses? behold, now ye have heard his blasphemy.
What think ye? They answered and said, He is guilty of death.
Then did they spit in his face, and buffeted him; and others smote
him with the palms of their hands,
Saying, Prophesy unto us, thou Christ, Who is he that smote thee?
Now Peter sat without in the palace: and a damsel came unto him, saying, Thou also wast with Jesus of Galilee.
But he denied before
them all, saying, I know not what thou sayest.
And when he was gone out into the porch, another
maid saw him, and said unto them that were there, This
fellow was also with Jesus of Nazareth.
And again he denied with an oath, I do not know the man.
And after a while came unto
him they that stood by, and said to Peter, Surely thou also art
one of them; for thy speech bewrayeth thee.
Then began he to curse and to swear,
saying, I know not the man. And immediately the cock crew.
And Peter remembered the word of Jesus, which said unto him,
Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. And he went out, and wept bitterly.
stories.retelling:
The night air was tense as Jesus was led through the narrow streets, his captors' torches casting flickering shadows on the walls. They brought him to the high priest Caiaphas, where the city's religious elite had gathered, their faces set with grim determination. In the courtyard, Peter lingered in the shadows, his heart heavy, watching from a distance as the scene unfolded.

Inside, the atmosphere was charged with a mix of anticipation and hostility. The high priest and council members were desperate for a reason, any reason, to condemn Jesus. Witness after witness came forward, but their testimonies crumbled under scrutiny, lacking coherence and consistency. Finally, two men stepped forward, claiming, “This man said, ‘I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to build it in three days.’”

Caiaphas stood, his voice cutting through the murmurs. “Have you no answer?” he demanded, his eyes fixed on Jesus, who remained silent, a calm center amid the storm of accusations. Pressing further, Caiaphas insisted, **“I adjure thee by the living God, that thou tell us whether thou be the Christ, the Son of God.”**

Jesus spoke, his voice steady and clear, **“Thou hast said: nevertheless I say unto you, Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven.”** At this, Caiaphas tore his robes in a dramatic display of outrage. “Blasphemy!” he declared. The council swiftly reached a grim consensus: Jesus was guilty of death.

The room erupted in chaos. Some spat at him, others struck him, taunting, “Prophesy unto us, thou Christ, Who is he that smote thee?” The mockery echoed through the halls, a bitter chorus of cruelty.

Meanwhile, Peter sat outside in the courtyard, his mind a whirl of confusion and fear. A servant girl approached, peering at him curiously. “You were also with Jesus of Galilee,” she said, her voice cutting through the night. Peter's heart raced, and he blurted out, “I don’t know what you are talking about.”

He moved away, trying to blend into the shadows, but another servant pointed him out. “This man was also with Jesus of Nazareth,” she insisted. Again, Peter shook his head, denying with an oath, “I don’t know the man.”

Time stretched, and the world seemed to close in on Peter. A group of bystanders approached, their eyes narrowing. “Surely you are also one of them; your accent gives you away.” Panic surged through Peter, and he cursed, his voice rising in desperation, **“I know not the man.”** At that moment, a rooster crowed, its call piercing the night.

The sound jolted Peter, bringing a wave of cold realization. Jesus’ words flashed in his mind: “Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” Overcome with guilt and sorrow, Peter stumbled out into the darkness, tears streaming down his face as he wept bitterly.

stories.title: Jesus Before Pilate
stories.keyVerse: "When Pilate saw that he could prevail nothing, but that rather a tumult was made, he took water, and washed his hands before the multitude, saying, I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it."
stories.text:
When the morning was come, all the chief priests and elders of the people took counsel against Jesus to put him to death:
And when they had bound him, they led
him away, and delivered him to Pontius Pilate the governor.
Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders,
Saying, I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood. And they said, What
is that to us? see thou
to that.
And he cast down the pieces of silver in the temple, and departed, and went and hanged himself.
And the chief priests took the silver pieces, and said, It is not lawful for to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood.
And they took counsel, and bought with them the potter’s field, to bury strangers in.
Wherefore that field was called, The field of blood, unto this day.
Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet, saying, And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him that was valued, whom they of the children of Israel did value;
And gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord appointed me.
And Jesus stood before the governor: and the governor asked him, saying, Art thou the King of the Jews? And Jesus said unto him,
Thou sayest.
And when he was accused of the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing.
Then said Pilate unto him, Hearest thou not how many things they witness against thee?
And he answered him to never a word; insomuch that the governor marvelled greatly.
Now at
that feast the governor was wont to release unto the people a prisoner, whom they would.
And they had then a notable prisoner, called Barabbas.
Therefore when they were gathered together, Pilate said unto them, Whom will ye that I release unto you? Barabbas, or Jesus which is called Christ?
For he knew that for envy they had delivered him.
When he was set down on the judgment seat, his wife sent unto him, saying, Have thou nothing to do with that just man: for I have suffered many things this day in a dream because of him.
But the chief priests and elders persuaded the multitude that they should ask Barabbas, and destroy Jesus.
The governor answered and said unto them, Whether of the twain will ye that I release unto you? They said, Barabbas.
Pilate saith unto them, What shall I do then with Jesus which is called Christ?
They all say unto him, Let him be crucified.
And the governor said, Why, what evil hath he done? But they cried out the more, saying, Let him be crucified.
When Pilate saw that he could prevail nothing, but
that rather a tumult was made, he took water, and washed
his hands before the multitude, saying, I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye
to it.
Then answered all the people, and said, His blood
be on us, and on our children.
Then released he Barabbas unto them: and when he had scourged Jesus, he delivered
him to be crucified.
stories.retelling:
As dawn broke over Jerusalem, a tense and resolute group of chief priests and elders gathered with a singular mission: the death of Jesus. They bound him tightly, leading him through the dusty streets, each step echoing their grim determination. Their destination was the imposing residence of Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor.  

Inside, amidst the ornate columns and guarded by Roman soldiers, Jesus stood before Pilate. The governor, accustomed to wielding power, gazed at Jesus with a mixture of curiosity and skepticism. "Are you the King of the Jews?" he asked, his voice carrying a blend of authority and disbelief. Jesus met his eyes calmly, replying, **"Thou sayest."**  

Outside, the city was stirring with the news of Jesus' trial, and the air buzzed with anticipation. Meanwhile, Judas, tormented by remorse, approached the temple with the thirty pieces of silver clinking heavily in his pocket. He confronted the priests, his voice shaking, **"I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood."** Their response was cold and dismissive: **"What is that to us? see thou to that."** Overcome with despair, Judas flung the silver to the ground, the coins scattering across the temple floor, and fled into the shadows, where he would meet his tragic end.  

Back at Pilate's residence, the tension in the air was palpable. The governor was perplexed by Jesus' silence amidst the accusations hurled by the priests and elders. "Don't you hear how many things they testify against you?" Pilate pressed, but Jesus remained silent, his composure unbroken, leaving Pilate marveling at his restraint.  

The festival tradition of releasing a prisoner offered Pilate a potential solution. The crowd gathered, and Pilate presented them with a choice: Jesus or Barabbas, a notorious prisoner. While Pilate's wife sent an urgent message, plagued by a haunting dream, urging him to have nothing to do with "that righteous man," the crowd was stirred by the chief priests and elders to demand Barabbas' release.  

"Which of the two do you want me to release to you?" Pilate asked, his voice ringing out over the murmurs. "Barabbas!" they cried. Pilate, pressing his luck, asked, "What shall I do then with Jesus, who is called Christ?" The crowd roared, "Let him be crucified!"  

Pilate, seeing the growing unrest and realizing he could not sway the crowd, sought to absolve himself of the responsibility. He called for water, washing his hands before the multitude, declaring, **"I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it."** The crowd responded with chilling resolve, "May his blood be on us, and on our children!"  

With a resigned nod, Pilate released Barabbas. Jesus was handed over to be scourged, the harsh sound of the lash echoing against the stones. As the sun climbed higher in the sky, the weight of the moment settled heavily over Jerusalem, the city holding its breath for what was to come.

stories.title: The Crucifixion
stories.keyVerse: "Jesus, when he had cried again with a loud voice, yielded up the ghost."
stories.text:
Then the soldiers of the governor took Jesus into the common hall, and gathered unto him the whole band
of soldiers.
And they stripped him, and put on him a scarlet robe.
And when they had platted a crown of thorns, they put
it
upon his head, and a reed in his right hand: and they bowed the knee before him, and mocked him, saying, Hail, King of the Jews!
And they spit upon him, and took the reed, and smote him on the head.
And after that they had mocked him, they took the robe off from him, and put his own raiment on him, and led him away to crucify
him.
And as they came out, they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name: him they compelled to bear his cross.
And when they were come unto a place called Golgotha, that is to say, a place of a skull,
They gave him vinegar to drink mingled with gall: and when he had tasted
thereof, he would not drink.
And they crucified him, and parted his garments, casting lots: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, They parted my garments among them, and upon my vesture did they cast lots.
And sitting down they watched him there;
And set up over his head his accusation written, THIS IS JESUS THE KING OF THE JEWS.
Then were there two thieves crucified with him, one on the right hand, and another on the left.
And they that passed by reviled him, wagging their heads,
And saying, Thou that destroyest the temple, and buildest
it
in three days, save thyself. If thou be the Son of God, come down from the cross.
Likewise also the chief priests mocking
him, with the scribes and elders, said,
He saved others; himself he cannot save. If he be the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him.
He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he will have him: for he said, I am the Son of God.
The thieves also, which were crucified with him, cast the same in his teeth.
Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour.
And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying,
Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say,
My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
Some of them that stood there, when they heard
that, said, This
man calleth for Elias.
And straightway one of them ran, and took a spunge, and filled
it with vinegar, and put
it on a reed, and gave him to drink.
The rest said, Let be, let us see whether Elias will come to save him.
Jesus, when he had cried again with a loud voice, yielded up the ghost.
And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent;
And the graves were opened; and many bodies of the saints which slept arose,
And came out of the graves after his resurrection, and went into the holy city, and appeared unto many.
Now when the centurion, and they that were with him, watching Jesus, saw the earthquake, and those things that were done, they feared greatly, saying, Truly this was the Son of God.
And many women were there beholding afar off, which followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering unto him:
Among which was Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James and Joses, and the mother of Zebedee’s children.
stories.retelling:
The air was tense, filled with the crackling anticipation of an unfolding tragedy. Soldiers led Jesus into the Praetorium, an echoing hall that seemed to amplify their jeers. They stripped him and draped a scarlet robe over his shoulders, a mockery of royalty. A cruel crown of thorns was pressed onto his head, the sharp points biting into his skin. They placed a reed in his hand as a scepter and knelt before him in feigned reverence, their voices dripping with sarcasm as they shouted, **“Hail, King of the Jews!”** The mockery continued, their spit landing on his face, the reed used to strike him.

Once they had their fill of this cruel spectacle, they returned his own clothes and led him away to be crucified. Outside the city, they seized a man named Simon from Cyrene, forcing him to carry the heavy wooden cross to Golgotha, the Place of the Skull. The area was barren, the ground dry and unyielding underfoot.

At Golgotha, they offered Jesus a bitter concoction of vinegar mixed with gall. He tasted but refused to drink. The soldiers went about their grim task, nailing him to the cross. They gambled for his clothes, casting lots under a sky that seemed to grow darker with each passing moment.

Above him, a sign declared his supposed crime: “THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS.” On either side, two criminals hung, sharing his fate. Passersby hurled insults, shaking their heads in disdain. **“Thou that destroyest the temple, and buildest it in three days, save thyself,”** they taunted. **“If thou be the Son of God, come down from the cross.”**

The chief priests and scribes joined in the mockery, their voices a chorus of scorn. **“He saved others; himself he cannot save,”** they sneered. **“If he be the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him.”** Even the criminals beside him joined in the derision.

As the hours passed, darkness enveloped the land, a palpable shroud that lingered from noon until three in the afternoon. Then, breaking through the oppressive silence, Jesus cried out with a heart-wrenching plea, **“Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?”** His voice echoed, a cry of profound abandonment.

Some bystanders misunderstood, thinking he called for Elijah. One rushed to give him a sponge soaked in vinegar, but others held back, curious if Elijah would indeed come.

Finally, with an agonizing cry, Jesus released his hold on life. The earth itself seemed to respond, quaking violently. The temple veil tore from top to bottom, rocks split apart, and graves opened, releasing saints who appeared in the city.

The centurion and those with him, witnesses to these extraordinary events, were filled with dread. **“Truly this was the Son of God,”** they murmured in awe.

From a distance, his followers watched, among them the women who had accompanied him from Galilee—Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and the mother of Zebedee’s children—mourning the loss of their beloved teacher.

stories.title: The Burial of Jesus
stories.keyVerse: And when Joseph had taken the body, he wrapped it in a clean linen cloth,
stories.text:
When the even was come, there came a rich man of Arimathaea, named Joseph, who also himself was Jesus’ disciple:
He went to Pilate, and begged the body of Jesus. Then Pilate commanded the body to be delivered.
And when Joseph had taken the body, he wrapped it in a clean linen cloth,
And laid it in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out in the rock: and he rolled a great stone to the door of the sepulchre, and departed.
And there was Mary Magdalene, and the other Mary, sitting over against the sepulchre.
Now the next day, that followed the day of the preparation, the chief priests and Pharisees came together unto Pilate,
Saying, Sir, we remember that that deceiver said, while he was yet alive, After three days I will rise again.
Command therefore that the sepulchre be made sure until the third day, lest his disciples come by night, and steal him away, and say unto the people, He is risen from the dead: so the last error shall be worse than the first.
Pilate said unto them, Ye have a watch: go your way, make
it
as sure as ye can.
So they went, and made the sepulchre sure, sealing the stone, and setting a watch.
stories.retelling:
As the sun dipped below the horizon, painting the sky in hues of deep orange and purple, the bustling streets of Jerusalem began to quiet down. A man named Joseph, wealthy and respected, made his way through the dimly lit alleys. Though a member of the council, Joseph was secretly a follower of Jesus. Tonight, his heart was heavy with grief and determination. He had a mission to complete.

Arriving at the governor's residence, Joseph approached the guards with a composed yet urgent demeanor. He requested an audience with Pilate. After a brief wait, he was ushered into the presence of the Roman governor. Joseph's voice was steady but laced with sorrow as he made his request. **“I beg of thee, let me have the body of Jesus.”** Pilate, perhaps relieved to have the matter of Jesus’ body handled, gave a brief nod, allowing Joseph to take custody.

With permission granted, Joseph hurried to the site of Golgotha. His heart ached at the sight of Jesus’ lifeless body, still hanging on the cross. Gently, with reverence and care, Joseph and a few trusted helpers lowered Jesus. The air was cool and still, filled with the scent of earth and lingering incense, as they wrapped Him in a clean linen cloth. The fabric was soft to the touch, a stark contrast to the harsh wood and iron that had been Jesus' final earthly companions.

The group moved solemnly to Joseph's own tomb, a freshly hewn cave set into the rocky hills. The moon cast a pale light on the stone, highlighting the newness of the tomb. It was a quiet place, removed from the noise and chaos of the city—a fitting resting place for a man of peace. With great effort, they laid Jesus inside, the linen shrouding His form.

Mary Magdalene and the other Mary watched from a distance, their faces etched with grief and a quiet determination. They had followed Jesus to the end and would do so even now, in His death.

Joseph, with a final, lingering glance at the tomb, rolled a massive stone into place, sealing the entrance. The sound of stone grating against stone echoed into the night, a heavy finality to it all.

The next day, the atmosphere changed as the chief priests and Pharisees gathered before Pilate. Their faces were tense with urgency and fear. They reminded Pilate of Jesus’ prophecy, their voices tinged with disdain as they called Him a deceiver. Their concern was palpable: **“Command therefore that the sepulchre be made sure until the third day.”** 

Pilate, a man weary of the whole affair, waved them off. **“Ye have a watch: go your way, make it as sure as ye can.”** 

With that, they secured the tomb, sealing the stone and setting a guard. The air was thick with anticipation and tension, as if the earth itself was holding its breath, waiting for what might come next.

stories.title: The Resurrection
stories.keyVerse: "He is not here: for he is risen, as he said. Come, see the place where the Lord lay."
stories.text:
In the end of the sabbath, as it began to dawn toward the first
day of the week, came Mary Magdalene and the other Mary to see the sepulchre.
And, behold, there was a great earthquake: for the angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and came and rolled back the stone from the door, and sat upon it.
His countenance was like lightning, and his raiment white as snow:
And for fear of him the keepers did shake, and became as dead
men.
And the angel answered and said unto the women, Fear not ye: for I know that ye seek Jesus, which was crucified.
He is not here: for he is risen, as he said. Come, see the place where the Lord lay.
And go quickly, and tell his disciples that he is risen from the dead; and, behold, he goeth before you into Galilee; there shall ye see him: lo, I have told you.
And they departed quickly from the sepulchre with fear and great joy; and did run to bring his disciples word.
And as they went to tell his disciples, behold, Jesus met them, saying,
All hail. And they came and held him by the feet, and worshipped him.
Then said Jesus unto them,
Be not afraid: go tell my brethren that they go into Galilee, and there shall they see me.
stories.retelling:
As the first light of dawn stretched across the horizon on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary made their way quietly through the garden. The air was crisp and still, the world holding its breath in the delicate silence of early morning. They approached the tomb where Jesus had been laid to rest, their hearts heavy with grief but determined to honor him with their presence.

Suddenly, the ground beneath them trembled violently. An earthquake shook the earth, and they stumbled, clutching each other for support. In that moment, a celestial being descended from the sky, an angel whose presence seemed to electrify the very air around them. His appearance was blinding, like lightning, and his clothes glimmered white as untouched snow.

With effortless strength, the angel rolled the massive stone away from the tomb's entrance and sat upon it, his expression calm and authoritative. The guards stationed at the tomb were paralyzed with fear, their bodies rigid as if lifeless.

Mary and the other woman stood frozen, eyes wide with awe and fear. The angel turned to them, his voice both gentle and commanding as he reassured them, **"Fear not ye: for I know that ye seek Jesus, which was crucified."** His words hung in the air, a promise of hope and unexpected wonder. **"He is not here: for he is risen, as he said. Come, see the place where the Lord lay."**

Trembling with a mix of emotions, the women peered inside the tomb. The stone slab was empty, the linens that had wrapped Jesus lying undisturbed but devoid of their precious occupant. The angel's message echoed in their minds as he urged them, **"Go quickly, and tell his disciples that he is risen from the dead."**

With hearts pounding, they turned and ran from the tomb, their steps driven by both fear and an overwhelming joy. The path ahead seemed to blur as they raced to deliver this miraculous news.

As they hurried through the garden, Jesus appeared before them. His presence was warm and familiar, dispelling any lingering doubts. **"All hail,"** he greeted them, his voice a balm to their souls. Overcome, they fell to their knees, clutching his feet, tears mingling with laughter as they worshiped him.

Jesus gazed at them with love and reassurance, **"Be not afraid: go tell my brethren that they go into Galilee, and there shall they see me."** His words were a gentle command, a promise of reunion and new beginnings.

The women rose, their spirits lifted by the reality of his resurrection. They set forth, eager to share the incredible news with the others, their hearts alight with the dawn of a new hope.

stories.title: Mary Magdalene Sees the Lord
stories.keyVerse: "Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master."
stories.text:
The first
day of the week cometh Mary Magdalene early, when it was yet dark, unto the sepulchre, and seeth the stone taken away from the sepulchre.
Then she runneth, and cometh to Simon Peter, and to the other disciple, whom Jesus loved, and saith unto them, They have taken away the Lord out of the sepulchre, and we know not where they have laid him.
Peter therefore went forth, and that other disciple, and came to the sepulchre.
So they ran both together: and the other disciple did outrun Peter, and came first to the sepulchre.
And he stooping down,
and looking in, saw the linen clothes lying; yet went he not in.
Then cometh Simon Peter following him, and went into the sepulchre, and seeth the linen clothes lie,
And the napkin, that was about his head, not lying with the linen clothes, but wrapped together in a place by itself.
Then went in also that other disciple, which came first to the sepulchre, and he saw, and believed.
For as yet they knew not the scripture, that he must rise again from the dead.
Then the disciples went away again unto their own home.
But Mary stood without at the sepulchre weeping: and as she wept, she stooped down,
and looked into the sepulchre,
And seeth two angels in white sitting, the one at the head, and the other at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain.
And they say unto her, Woman, why weepest thou? She saith unto them, Because they have taken away my Lord, and I know not where they have laid him.
And when she had thus said, she turned herself back, and saw Jesus standing, and knew not that it was Jesus.
Jesus saith unto her,
Woman, why weepest thou? whom seekest thou?
She, supposing him to be the gardener, saith unto him, Sir, if thou have borne him hence, tell me where thou hast laid him, and I will take him away.
Jesus saith unto her,
Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master.
Jesus saith unto her,
Touch me not; for I am not yet ascended to my Father: but go to my brethren, and say unto them, I ascend unto my Father, and your Father; and
to my God, and your God.
Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and
that he had spoken these things unto her.
stories.retelling:
The chill of the early morning clung to Mary Magdalene as she moved through the shadows, the first light of dawn barely brushing the horizon. Her heart pounded with both anticipation and dread as she approached the tomb where Jesus had been laid. But as she neared, her breath caught— the massive stone sealing the entrance had been rolled away. 

Panic surged through her, and she turned, running as fast as her feet could carry her to find Simon Peter and John, the disciple whom Jesus loved. Breathless, she reached them, words tumbling out in a rush. **“They have taken away the Lord out of the sepulchre, and we know not where they have laid him.”** 

The two disciples exchanged a glance of shock and disbelief before they broke into a sprint towards the tomb. John, younger and faster, reached the site first. He peered inside, hesitating at the threshold. The linen cloths were there, but Jesus was not. 

Simon Peter arrived moments later, his breath ragged, and pushed past John into the tomb. He too saw the linen cloths and the head covering, now neatly rolled up and set aside. John followed, and as he stepped inside, understanding dawned upon him, a belief settling deep within his heart, though the full meaning eluded them both. 

Confused and unsettled, the disciples left, returning to their homes. But Mary, overcome with grief and confusion, remained. She stood outside the tomb, tears streaming down her face. She bent down to look inside once more, and this time, she saw two angels dressed in radiant white, positioned where Jesus’ body had once lain. 

They asked her gently, **“Woman, why weepest thou?”** Her voice breaking, she replied, **“Because they have taken away my Lord, and I know not where they have laid him.”**

Turning away from the tomb, she suddenly saw a man standing nearby. Her eyes, blurred with tears, did not recognize him. He asked her softly, **“Woman, why weepest thou? Whom seekest thou?”** Supposing him to be the gardener, she pleaded, **“Sir, if thou have borne him hence, tell me where thou hast laid him, and I will take him away.”**

Then, with a single word, everything changed. **“Mary,”** the man said. The voice struck her heart like a lightning bolt, and she turned to him, recognition flooding her soul. **“Rabboni!”** she exclaimed, the word a mixture of astonishment and joy. 

Jesus instructed her gently not to hold onto him, for he had not yet ascended to the Father. Instead, he gave her a mission: to go to his brethren and tell them that he was ascending to his Father and their Father, to his God and their God. 

With renewed purpose and a heart brimming with joy, Mary Magdalene ran to the disciples, proclaiming, “I have seen the Lord,” and shared with them the words he had spoken to her.

stories.title: The Road to Emmaus
stories.keyVerse: "And their eyes were opened, and they knew him; and he vanished out of their sight."
stories.text:
And, behold, two of them went that same day to a village called Emmaus, which was from Jerusalem
about threescore furlongs.
And they talked together of all these things which had happened.
And it came to pass, that, while they communed
together and reasoned, Jesus himself drew near, and went with them.
But their eyes were holden that they should not know him.
And he said unto them,
What manner of communications
are
these that ye have one to another, as ye walk, and are sad?
And the one of them, whose name was Cleopas, answering said unto him, Art thou only a stranger in Jerusalem, and hast not known the things which are come to pass there in these days?
And he said unto them,
What things? And they said unto him, Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, which was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people:
And how the chief priests and our rulers delivered him to be condemned to death, and have crucified him.
But we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel: and beside all this, to day is the third day since these things were done.
Yea, and certain women also of our company made us astonished, which were early at the sepulchre;
And when they found not his body, they came, saying, that they had also seen a vision of angels, which said that he was alive.
And certain of them which were with us went to the sepulchre, and found
it even so as the women had said: but him they saw not.
Then he said unto them,
O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken:
Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
And they drew nigh unto the village, whither they went: and he made as though he would have gone further.
But they constrained him, saying, Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent. And he went in to tarry with them.
And it came to pass, as he sat at meat with them, he took bread, and blessed
it, and brake, and gave to them.
And their eyes were opened, and they knew him; and he vanished out of their sight.
And they said one to another, Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?
And they rose up the same hour, and returned to Jerusalem, and found the eleven gathered together, and them that were with them,
Saying, The Lord is risen indeed, and hath appeared to Simon.
And they told what things
were done in the way, and how he was known of them in breaking of bread.
stories.retelling:
The sun hung low in the sky, casting long shadows across the dusty road that led from Jerusalem to Emmaus. Two men trudged along, their hearts heavy with confusion and sorrow. The events of the past days weighed on them like a shroud, and they spoke in hushed tones, trying to make sense of the whirlwind of rumors and emotions that had consumed their city.

As they walked, a stranger joined them, matching their pace. He seemed an ordinary traveler, yet something about him was compelling. The men were too engrossed in their own despair to recognize him. The stranger asked, **“What manner of communications are these that ye have one to another, as ye walk, and are sad?”** His question pierced their melancholy, and they stopped in their tracks, a mix of surprise and curiosity washing over them.

One of the men, Cleopas, turned to the stranger with incredulity. **“Art thou only a stranger in Jerusalem, and hast not known the things which are come to pass there in these days?”** The stranger’s eyes held a twinkle of mystery as he replied, **“What things?”** A flood of words poured from Cleopas as he recounted the story of Jesus of Nazareth, a mighty prophet in both action and word, betrayed and condemned by the very leaders they had trusted. Their hopes had been dashed against the rocks of reality when he was crucified.

As Cleopas spoke, the stranger listened intently, his expression a blend of empathy and quiet understanding. He then began to speak, his words weaving a tapestry from the ancient prophecies, illuminating the scriptures in ways that set their hearts aflame. The men found themselves captivated, the stranger’s voice resonating with a truth that stirred something deep within them.

The village of Emmaus came into view just as the day began to give way to evening. The stranger seemed intent on continuing his journey, but the men, drawn to his presence, implored him, **“Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent.”** He accepted their invitation, and together they made their way to a modest dwelling.

Inside, the table was set with simple fare. As they sat down, the stranger took the bread, blessed it, and broke it. At that moment, a veil lifted from the men’s eyes, and they recognized him—it was Jesus. A breathless instant passed before he vanished from their sight, leaving them in stunned silence.

Heartbeats quickened with the realization. **“Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?”** Cleopas exclaimed. Without hesitation, they rose from the table, the urgency of their revelation propelling them back to Jerusalem. Their feet barely touched the ground as they hurried to share the miraculous encounter with the others, their spirits no longer burdened by grief, but buoyed by hope.

stories.title: Thomas Believes
stories.keyVerse: "Then saith he to Thomas, Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing."
stories.text:
Then the same day at evening, being the first
day of the week, when the doors were shut where the disciples were assembled for fear of the Jews, came Jesus and stood in the midst, and saith unto them,
Peace
be unto you.
And when he had so said, he shewed unto them
his hands and his side. Then were the disciples glad, when they saw the Lord.
Then said Jesus to them again,
Peace
be unto you: as
my Father hath sent me, even so send I you.
And when he had said this, he breathed on
them, and saith unto them,
Receive ye the Holy Ghost:
Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them;
and
whose soever
sins ye retain, they are retained.But Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came.
The other disciples therefore said unto him, We have seen the Lord. But he said unto them, Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe.
And after eight days again his disciples were within, and Thomas with them:
then came Jesus, the doors being shut, and stood in the midst, and said,
Peace
be unto you.
Then saith he to Thomas,
reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust
it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.
And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.
Jesus saith unto him,
Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed
are they that have not seen, and
yet have believed.And many other signs truly did Jesus in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book:
But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name.
stories.retelling:
The sun was setting on the first day of the week, casting long shadows across the room where the disciples huddled together. The air was thick with tension and fear, the locked doors a testament to their anxiety about the Jewish leaders. Yet, in the midst of their apprehension, Jesus appeared among them, his presence as sudden as it was reassuring. **"Peace be unto you,"** he greeted them, his voice calm, cutting through the fear like a balm.

He showed them the wounds in his hands and side, tangible proof of his identity. Relief and joy surged through the disciples, their hearts lifted by the undeniable sight of their risen Lord. Jesus spoke again, his words a gentle command, **"As my Father hath sent me, even so send I you."** He breathed on them, a symbolic gesture that filled the room with a sense of purpose and empowerment. **"Receive ye the Holy Ghost,"** he instructed, setting them on a path of forgiveness and spiritual authority.

But Thomas, one of their own, was absent from this miraculous gathering. When the others recounted the event, their excitement barely contained, Thomas was skeptical. **"Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe,"** he insisted, his voice edged with doubt.

Eight days passed, a stretch of time filled with anticipation and whispered discussions. The disciples were gathered again in the same locked room, and this time, Thomas was with them. Without warning, Jesus appeared once more in their midst. **"Peace be unto you,"** he said, his eyes seeking Thomas.

Turning to the doubting disciple, Jesus invited him to reach out and touch the evidence he needed. **"Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing."** The room held its breath as Thomas approached, his skepticism melting away in the face of undeniable truth.

Overwhelmed, Thomas declared, **"My Lord and my God."** The words were a confession, a proclamation of faith forged through doubt. Jesus responded with a gentle reminder, **"Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed."**

In that locked room, the air was transformed from fear to faith, from doubt to belief. Jesus had performed many signs, but this moment, etched into the hearts of his disciples, was more than a miracle—it was an invitation to trust in what could not always be seen. The disciples would carry this lesson with them, a testament written not just on parchment, but in the living history of their lives.

stories.title: Breakfast by the Sea
stories.keyVerse: "Jesus saith unto them, Come and dine. And none of the disciples durst ask him, Who art thou? knowing that it was the Lord."
stories.text:
After these things Jesus shewed himself again to the disciples at the sea of Tiberias; and on this wise shewed he
himself.
There were together Simon Peter, and Thomas called Didymus, and Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, and the
sons of Zebedee, and two other of his disciples.
Simon Peter saith unto them, I go a fishing. They say unto him, We also go with thee. They went forth, and entered into a ship immediately; and that night they caught nothing.
But when the morning was now come, Jesus stood on the shore: but the disciples knew not that it was Jesus.
Then Jesus saith unto them,
Children, have ye any meat? They answered him, No.
And he said unto them,
Cast the net on the right side of the ship, and ye shall find. They cast therefore, and now they were not able to draw it for the multitude of fishes.
Therefore that disciple whom Jesus loved saith unto Peter, It is the Lord. Now when Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he girt
his
fisher’s coat
unto him, (for he was naked,) and did cast himself into the sea.
And the other disciples came in a little ship; (for they were not far from land, but as it were two hundred cubits,) dragging the net with fishes.
As soon then as they were come to land, they saw a fire of coals there, and fish laid thereon, and bread.
Jesus saith unto them,
Bring of the fish which ye have now caught.
Simon Peter went up, and drew the net to land full of great fishes, and hundred and fifty and three: and for all there were so many, yet was not the net broken.
Jesus saith unto them,
Come
and dine. And none of the disciples durst ask him, Who art thou? knowing that it was the Lord.
Jesus then cometh, and taketh bread, and giveth them, and fish likewise.
This is now the third time that Jesus shewed himself to his disciples, after that he was risen from the dead.
stories.retelling:
The sky was a deep indigo, the early morning light just beginning to tease the horizon over the sea of Tiberias. A chilled breeze swept across the water, whispering against the boat where Simon Peter and his companions—Thomas, Nathanael, the sons of Zebedee, and two other disciples—were huddled. The night had been long, and the toll of it showed in their weary eyes as they worked the nets with little to show for their labor.

As dawn's first light touched the sea, a figure appeared on the distant shore. The disciples barely noticed him at first, their minds clouded with fatigue. The stranger called out, his voice cutting through the morning haze, **"Children, have ye any meat?"** The simple question hung in the air, a reminder of their empty nets. They responded with a disheartened, "No."

The figure on the shore spoke again, his voice carrying an unexpected authority, **"Cast the net on the right side of the ship, and ye shall find."** Skepticism mingled with hope as the disciples obeyed. The moment the net hit the water, it was as though the sea itself had come alive. The net swelled with a throng of fish, so heavy they could scarcely pull it in.

John, the disciple whom Jesus loved, turned to Peter with sudden clarity. "It is the Lord," he declared, his voice a mixture of awe and joy. At that, Peter sprang into action, hastily wrapping his coat around him and plunging into the sea. The cold water embraced him as he swam fervently towards the shore, his heart pounding with anticipation.

The other disciples, not far behind, rowed the boat back, dragging the miraculous catch with them. As they reached the shore, the aroma of a fire greeted them—a fire already set with fish and bread warming over the coals. Jesus stood there, his presence both familiar and extraordinary.
